Photograph the individual in situ from multiple angles, record location and habitat notes, and follow permitting requirements before any handling or sampling.
Collect the frog and transport it to the nearest office for safekeeping until you can seek advice.

questions.prompt: Your passive acoustic recorders captured calls that might indicate a bat species of management concern. How should you proceed to validate the detection?

options.text: Rely on automated call ID software outputs without manual checking to speed reporting.
Delete low-quality recordings and only report high-confidence automated IDs.
Report all automated IDs as confirmed detections to the client to be conservative.
Manually review and verify call recordings with an experienced bat acoustician and cross-reference metadata such as time and location before inclusion in the report.

questions.prompt: During a spotlighting survey you detect a nocturnal bird species at the edge of the survey block but outside the mapped study area. What is the right course of action for data recording and reporting?

options.text: Record the detection with GPS coordinates and note it as incidental outside the survey block, including habitat context for reporting and potential follow-up.
Exclude the record entirely since it is outside the mapped study area to avoid affecting survey statistics.
Adjust the mapped study area boundaries to include the sighting retroactively without documenting the change.
Signal the team to stop spotlighting to relocate the individual into the study area for a valid detection.

questions.prompt: You are designing a trapping program for small mammals where non-target species are common. Which design choice minimises risk to non-target fauna while still achieving survey objectives?

options.text: Use larger cage traps and bait attractive to a wide range of species to maximise captures.
Select trap types, bait, and placement informed by target species ecology to reduce non-target captures and implement daily checks and release protocols.
Place traps only in open areas to avoid catching burrow-dwelling non-targets.
Avoid setting traps at all and rely solely on indirect surveys even if detection probability for target species is low.

questions.prompt: A contractor asks you to shorten the recommended survey duration to save costs. What is the most appropriate professional response?

options.text: Agree to the change and proceed, noting cost savings in the invoice.
Refuse outright without discussion to maintain your original plan.
Explain how reduced duration will lower detectability and outline the risks to results, then propose an evidence-based compromise or escalation to the client if necessary.
Proceed with fewer nights but increase team size to make up effort without telling the client.

questions.prompt: While entering data from field datasheets, you notice inconsistent species codes used by different observers for similar records. What quality assurance step best addresses this?

options.text: Standardise codes post hoc without documenting changes to streamline the dataset.
Leave the inconsistencies to avoid altering original observer entries.
Delete records with inconsistent codes to avoid confusion in analysis.
Cross-check original datasheets, reconcile discrepancies using a coded glossary, document decisions in a data-cleaning log, and consult observers if needed.

questions.prompt: You must select survey sites across a construction corridor where some patches of habitat are privately owned and access is uncertain. What is the best planning approach?

options.text: Map all habitat patches, seek permissions early, and develop alternative survey locations and justification criteria if access is denied, documenting decisions.
Only include publicly accessible patches to avoid permission delays.
Assume access will be granted and schedule surveys, dealing with permissions later.
Exclude privately owned patches from the assessment without notifying stakeholders.

questions.prompt: During a daytime bird survey, team members report differing IDs for a fast-moving raptor. Which action best addresses this uncertainty in final records?

options.text: Choose the species the senior observer suggested and record it as confirmed.
Record the observation at the highest confident taxonomic level (e.g., genus or ‘raptor sp.’), include descriptive notes and any photos or sketches.
Omit the observation because it lacks consensus.
Assign the most common regional species to the sighting to maintain consistency with expected species lists.

questions.prompt: Your survey detected tracks and scats suggesting presence of a medium-sized carnivore of potential conservation interest, but no direct sightings. What evidence hierarchy action should be taken before reporting presence?

options.text: Treat tracks and scats as definitive proof of presence and include them as confirmed records.
Ignore indirect signs because they are unreliable.
Collect detailed field measurements, photographs, GPS locations, and, where permitted, non-invasive samples (e.g., hair) to support identification, noting uncertainty level in the report.
Recreate tracks in the office for comparison rather than collecting field data.

questions.prompt: You are preparing the methods section for a fauna survey report. Which detail is most critical to include to allow peer reviewers to assess survey adequacy?

options.text: The name of the client commissioning the survey.
High-level statements that standard methods were used without specifics.
Only species lists and final conclusions to keep the report concise.
Comprehensive descriptions of survey timing, effort (hours, traps/nights), methods, observer experience, and environmental conditions.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist proposes using a single short-duration camera deployment to infer absence of a nocturnal marsupial. What technical judgement should you provide?

options.text: Advise that single short deployments have low power to infer absence and recommend multiple cameras, longer deployment periods, and complementary methods to increase detection probability.
Agree; one camera is sufficient if placed at a likely spot.
Recommend replacing camera surveys entirely with spotlighting only.
Suggest inferring absence from habitat condition alone without further surveys.

questions.prompt: You discover a dead individual of a species of interest during a survey. What is the appropriate immediate step regarding chain of custody and evidence?

options.text: Move the carcass into your vehicle and store it until you decide what to do.
Photograph the carcass in situ, record precise location and condition, secure the site if required, and follow jurisdictional protocols before any removal.
Burn the carcass to prevent disease spread.
Ignore it and continue surveying to avoid time delays.

questions.prompt: An acoustic detector malfunctioned for two nights of a planned five-night bat survey. How should you account for this in analysis and reporting?

options.text: Exclude the entire survey from analysis because of missing nights.
Assume species were absent on lost nights and proceed with analysis.
Note the equipment failure, quantify lost effort, and adjust detection probability estimates or interpret results cautiously, proposing follow-up deployment if necessary.
Fill gaps by duplicating calls from other sites to make the dataset complete.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether to use live trapping or pitfall arrays for small ground-dwelling reptiles in a sandy dune system. Which factor most strongly informs your technical choice?

options.text: The contractor’s preference that causes least disturbance.
Cost per unit of equipment only.
Using the same method as a previous unrelated project for convenience.
Species ecology (movement patterns, size), substrate suitability, expected detectability, and welfare risks of each method in that environment.

questions.prompt: A landowner asks for immediate verbal results about potential protected species before final report. What is the correct communication approach?

options.text: Offer to share preliminary observations with clear caveats about their provisional nature and commit to providing formal conclusions in the final report after analysis.
Provide speculative conclusions verbally to reassure the landowner.
Refuse all communication until the final report is delivered.
Forward raw datasheets to the landowner without explanation.

questions.prompt: While reviewing historical records for the study area, you find ambiguous older records with vague locality descriptions. What is the best practice for using these in survey planning?

options.text: Treat them as precise and use them to prioritise sites without further verification.
Flag them as historical but uncertain, use their general habitat information to inform targeted searches, and document uncertainties in the data sources.
Discard historical records because they are not exact contemporary sightings.
Assume the species is no longer present due to lack of precise recent records.

questions.prompt: You need to decide whether a single detection of a species by camera trap constitutes occupancy in a small habitat patch slated for clearing. Which consideration most strongly affects your decision?

options.text: The species’ conservation status alone justifies immediate classification as occupied.
Treat any single detection as definitive occupancy regardless of context.
Consider detection reliability (false-positive risk), species movement ecology (transient use vs resident), and available supplementary evidence before concluding occupancy.
Ignore the detection because it is only one record.

questions.prompt: During a wet-season amphibian survey heavy rain causes flash flooding risk. What is the appropriate risk management action?

options.text: Continue surveys because amphibians are more active in the rain.
Leave staff unsupervised in the field to maintain data continuity.
Switch to night surveys immediately without reassessing hazards.
Suspend fieldwork, move personnel to safe locations, reassess weather forecasts and site conditions, and only resume once safe and documented in the site risk register.

questions.prompt: You are asked to use an unfamiliar species identification key in the field. What is the best approach to ensure accurate IDs during the survey?

options.text: Familiarise yourself with the key before fieldwork, take reference material and photographic guides, and record uncertain IDs for later expert review.
Use the key quickly without cross-referencing and trust your immediate judgement.
Postpone all surveys until you have completed formal training on the key.
Ask local residents to identify species based on casual observation.

questions.prompt: A client requests omission of incidental non-target species records to shorten the report. How should you respond?

options.text: Exclude incidental records to satisfy the client’s request.
Explain that incidental records are part of the survey dataset, discuss the implications of omission, and propose a concise way to present them while retaining transparency.
Fabricate alternate summaries that hide the incidental records.
Refuse to submit any report.

questions.prompt: You must escalate a potential detection of a highly restricted species to a senior specialist. What information should you prioritise in your escalation?

options.text: Your personal opinion about the species’ importance.
Only the species name and the site name.
Precise location, date/time, method of detection, supporting evidence (photos, recordings, samples), observer details, and any immediate management concerns.
A summary of unrelated survey findings to provide context.

questions.prompt: You’ve completed multiple nights of surveys with varying weather. How should you incorporate weather variability into your detectability analysis?

options.text: Ignore weather variation as it complicates analysis.
Average all weather conditions into one descriptor and use it for all nights.
Only include nights with ideal weather and discard the rest.
Record weather variables each survey night and include them as covariates or discuss their influence on detectability in analysis and reporting.

questions.prompt: A colleague suggests using souvenir photographs of specimens taken by volunteers as survey evidence. What is the appropriate data quality response?

options.text: Assess photographs for diagnostic features, verify metadata (date/location), document volunteer observer details, and only include records that meet evidence standards.
Use the photographs without verification to expand your dataset.
Discard volunteer photos because volunteers are not qualified.
Ask volunteers to resubmit staged photos for clarity.

questions.prompt: You need to report uncertainty around absence findings. Which reporting phrase best balances clarity and scientific caution?

options.text: Species is absent from the site.
No detections were recorded during the survey; given the survey effort and methods, this provides limited confidence of absence and further targeted surveys are recommended if required.
It is doubtful the species ever occurred here.
Absence is proven beyond doubt.

questions.prompt: During a review, you find that GIS coordinates in the dataset are in different coordinate systems. What is the correct QA step?

options.text: Ignore the discrepancy and use the coordinates as-is.
Delete records with coordinates that are not in the preferred system.
Convert all coordinates to a common standard using documented transformation parameters and note the original systems in metadata.
Estimate locations by eyeballing them on a map without conversion.

questions.prompt: A field team reports finding a nest of a ground-nesting bird in an area scheduled for vegetation clearing next week. What immediate action should you recommend?

options.text: Proceed with clearing to keep to schedule; nests are natural and can be relocated later.
Mark the nest with a sign and continue clearing elsewhere on the site.
Capture and move the chicks yourself to a safe location to allow clearing.

Flag the location, advise temporarily halting clearing in the immediate area, notify project manager and specialist ecologist to assess and determine mitigations in line with permit or regulatory obligations.

questions.prompt: You are validating presence records from multiple observers for a report. Which approach best ensures credibility of species identifications?

options.text: Prioritise records with diagnostic evidence (photographs, specimens, recordings), cross-check less certain records with experts, and document validation decisions.
Accept all observer records equally to avoid conflict.
Only accept records from senior staff.
Remove any record that is not accompanied by a photograph.

questions.prompt: A development timetable requires fauna surveys completed before a critical decision date, but seasonal windows for some target species are later. What is the appropriate project-level recommendation?

options.text: Complete early-season surveys and state confidently that results are final.

Communicate limitations clearly, recommend staged surveys with later seasonal surveys for target species, and advise decision-makers of residual uncertainty and potential need for conditions or offsets.
Refuse to perform any surveys until all seasonal windows pass, delaying the project.
Conduct rapid unseasonal surveys and extrapolate findings to the full season.

questions.prompt: You plan to use volunteer observers for daytime surveys to increase coverage. Which measure best maintains data quality when using volunteers?

options.text: Let volunteers work independently without training to maximise numbers.
Only assign volunteers to trivial tasks like carrying equipment.
Provide targeted training, standardised datasheets, supervised initial visits, and a validation process for volunteer records.
Accept volunteer observations without question because community involvement is valuable.

questions.prompt: A senior reviewer requests removal of a low-confidence detection from the draft report to avoid potential regulatory complications. How should you handle this request?

options.text: Remove it silently to expedite approval.
Refuse to change the report under any circumstances.
Replace the detection with a fabricated non-sensitive species record.
Discuss the rationale with the reviewer, present the evidence and uncertainty, and agree on whether to retain the record with qualification or remove it, documenting the decision.

questions.prompt: You are designing a survey to detect a cryptic ground frog known to call only during sporadic heavy rain events. Which multi-method design best increases detection probability?

options.text: Combine opportunistic rapid-response surveys during rain events, automated acoustic recorders deployed across the landscape, and targeted daytime habitat searches.
Schedule surveys only on sunny days and rely on searching microhabitats.
Use only pitfall traps because they operate continuously.
Rely solely on historical records to infer current presence.

questions.prompt: While conducting mark-recapture, you notice the marking method might cause abrasion on small marsupials. What immediate technical judgement should you make?

options.text: Continue marking as planned because data are needed.
Stop marking immediately, assess welfare impacts, switch to a less harmful marking method or non-invasive alternative, and document the welfare concern and corrective action.
Increase the number of captures to dilute the effect.
Ignore welfare issues to complete the dataset.

questions.prompt: You are compiling a species list for the report and must prioritise which records to highlight in the executive summary. Which criteria best guides selection?

options.text: Highlight species that are most charismatic to appeal to stakeholders.
Only list species that are common and familiar to the public.
Emphasise records of statutory conservation significance, species with high management relevance to the project, and new or unexpected detections, with context on confidence.
Include every incidental sighting with equal prominence.

questions.prompt: You find a repeatable identification key error in your species dataset that affects several records. What QA action should you take before finalising the report?

options.text: Ignore the error because correcting will delay the report.
Delete all affected records to avoid explanation.
Re-run analyses without addressing the error.
Trace the error source, correct affected records, run consistency checks across the dataset, and document the correction and its implications in the report.

questions.prompt: During stakeholder engagement, a local Indigenous representative raises concerns about survey methods disturbing culturally sensitive areas. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Pause activities in the specified areas, consult with the representative to understand concerns, adjust survey methods or access routes accordingly, and document agreements.
Proceed without changes because surveys are ecologically necessary.
Dismiss the concerns as irrelevant to fauna surveys.
Terminate the survey entirely.

questions.prompt: You receive automated sensor data that indicate nocturnal activity spikes inconsistent with observer records. How should you reconcile these discrepancies?

options.text: Discard automated data because observers are more reliable.
Investigate sensor calibration, time synchronisation, and environmental noise, compare raw files with field notes, and, if necessary, consult technical support before deciding on inclusion.
Assume observer records are incorrect and overwrite them with sensor outputs.
Average both datasets and report the mean activity.

questions.prompt: A junior team member suggests using social media sightings to supplement your survey. What protocols should you put in place to responsibly use such records?

options.text: Include all social media sightings without verification to increase sample size.
Prohibit any use of social media as a source.
Screen social media records for verifiable photographs and metadata, attempt to contact observers for additional information, and apply the same validation standards as for other incidental records.
Only accept social media records if they are from official organisations.

questions.prompt: You must document survey limitations for a governance review. Which statement best captures limitations relevant to fauna surveys?

options.text: Surveys were flawless with no limitations.
Only financial constraints affected the survey quality.
Limitations are not relevant to the final conclusions and need not be recorded.

Limitations include seasonal constraints, weather-driven detectability variability, equipment failures, access restrictions to some habitats, and observer variability; these were documented and considered in interpreting results.

title: Flora Habitat and Threatened Flora Survey Fundamentals

questions.prompt: You are preparing for a threatened flora survey on private land in temperate NSW. What is the most appropriate first action in planning the field survey?

options.text: Contact the landowner to confirm access times and any recent land management activities.
Draft a species list based on regional floras and previous records only.
Book the survey team for a full day without site reconnaissance.
Begin laboratory identification protocols for samples you might collect.

questions.prompt: On arrival at a survey site you note recent heavy grazing has removed most understorey. For locating threatened herbs known from the area, what is the most appropriate immediate field response?

options.text: Assume the species is now absent and mark the site as negative and depart.
Adjust your search to focus on undisturbed microhabitats such as rocky outcrops, fence lines and remnant patches.
Collect multiple soil samples for seedbank analysis and leave without exhaustive searching.
Install exclusion fencing to prevent further grazing before completing the survey.

questions.prompt: During a survey you find an unfamiliar plant that could be a threatened species. What is the most defensible approach to record this observation in your field data?

options.text: Record only the GPS point and a single wide-angle photo to minimise disturbance.
Transplant the specimen to a safer nearby location for later identification.
Photograph diagnostic features, geolocate the plant, take detailed field notes, and collect a voucher if permitted and necessary for ID.
Mark the location and return later with a botanist without further data collection.

questions.prompt: Your survey brief requires you to map extents of remnant vegetation patches that may contain threatened plants. Which mapping method is most appropriate given limited field time?

options.text: Delineate patches solely from desktop satellite imagery without field verification.
Walk a random transect across the entire property without using imagery to avoid bias.
Digitise boundaries from historical maps produced ten years ago because they are readily available.
Use targeted ground-truthing of patch boundaries guided by high-resolution aerial imagery and GPS waypoints.

questions.prompt: While conducting timed searches for a cryptic threatened orchid, the surveyor is interrupted by a landowner asking for immediate results. What is the correct professional response?

options.text: Explain that survey results require completion of surveys and later verification; offer a brief description of activities and a follow-up report timeframe.
Provide an immediate definitive statement about presence or absence based on partial search to satisfy the landowner.
Decline to speak and continue the survey to avoid distraction.
Ask the landowner to sign a waiver so you can share preliminary data on site.

questions.prompt: You plan surveys timed to coincide with a threatened shrub's flowering period, but seasonal conditions have delayed flowering. What adjustment to methodology is most appropriate?

options.text: Proceed with standard surveys regardless of phenology, recording only obvious plants.
Reschedule targeted surveys to the peak flowering window and use opportunistic searches in the interim to document vegetative individuals.
Cancel the project and report inability to complete it due to phenology.
Use historical flowering dates without checking current conditions and proceed.

questions.prompt: A threatened plant population occurs along a roadside verge. What risk-management action should you take during survey to protect specimens?

options.text: Move plants further from the road edge to protect them from future maintenance.
Clear surrounding vegetation to improve visibility for future monitoring.
Keep to existing vehicle tracks, minimise trampling, and avoid driving or parking over plants while positioning equipment and personnel.
Install unofficial markers to deter road maintenance crews from the area.

questions.prompt: You are compiling field records for threatened flora and must decide data fields to include. Which set is most essential for later verification and regulatory use?

options.text: Just species and number of plants observed, leaving other details for the final report.
Only photographs and a sketch map, as visual evidence will suffice.
Habitat description and soil type only, because location is sensitive information.
Species identification (with confidence), GPS coordinates, date/time, habitat description, abundance estimate, photographs, observer name.

questions.prompt: While performing a quadrat-based abundance estimate, you find many juvenile plants hard to distinguish from a common species. What is the best technical judgement?

options.text: Record ambiguous individuals as 'juvenile/uncertain' and collect detailed photos and notes for later expert verification.
Ignore juveniles and count only mature individuals to avoid errors.
Assume all juveniles are the threatened species to be precautionary.
Collect several juvenile specimens without permission to identify them in the lab.

questions.prompt: You need to prioritise areas for targeted searches within a large property where time is limited. Which criterion is most appropriate for prioritisation?

options.text: Areas closest to the property entrance to maximise convenience.
Areas with highest likelihood of suitable microhabitat based on species habitat requirements, previous records and landscape connectivity.
Randomly chosen grids to remove professional bias irrespective of habitat suitability.
Areas already extensively cleared because they are easiest to walk.

questions.prompt: During data entry you notice GPS coordinates for several observations are identical to the surveyors' start location. What is the most appropriate QA step?

options.text: Assume the records are fine and publish them as-is because location error is common.
Delete the suspect records to avoid including erroneous data.
Return to the field notes and photographs to cross-check waypoints, and if unresolved, contact the surveyor for clarification before finalising records.
Adjust the coordinates to nearby suitable habitat based on aerial imagery without consulting the field team.

questions.prompt: A threatened species' identification hinges on seed capsule characters that are not present during your visit. What is the appropriate survey strategy?

options.text: Declare the population absent because key characters were missing.
Rely on vegetative characters alone and report a confirmed identification.
Collect immature seeds to force them to develop in a greenhouse for identification.
Plan repeat visits to coincide with the stage when diagnostic fruiting structures are present or use other confirming traits with expert input.

questions.prompt: You find a population of a locally rare plant but cannot be certain of its taxonomic status in the field. For reporting to a regulator, what is the correct course of action?

options.text: Report the observation as an uncertain identification with supporting evidence and recommend expert taxonomic review.
Classify it as the nationally threatened taxon to ensure maximum protection.
Omit the observation to avoid possible misreporting.
Assign a new species name in the report to reflect uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Your field team must use herbicide control on invasive grass during monitoring. What immediate consideration is most critical before proceeding?

options.text: Apply herbicide ASAP to improve visibility for monitoring.
Confirm herbicide type, application method and timing will not harm nearby threatened flora and obtain necessary approvals from landowner and relevant authorities.
Burn the invasive grass instead because fire is a common control method.
Spread herbicide broadly across the area to ensure complete removal.

questions.prompt: During a survey you observe machinery damage to habitat near a known threatened plant. Who should you escalate this to first?

options.text: Directly notify national media to raise awareness.
Immediately report to the police regardless of the situation.
The project ecologist or supervisor responsible for the site to assess immediate mitigation and reporting obligations.
Ignore it because the damage is already done.

questions.prompt: In planning surveys for multiple threatened species with different detectability, how should you allocate limited daily field effort?

options.text: Spend equal time on each species regardless of detectability or phenology.
Concentrate on the easiest-to-find species to maximise positive records.
Survey only one species per day to reduce complexity.
Allocate effort proportionally, focusing morning visits on species detectable in cool conditions and afternoons on others, informed by species-specific detectability windows.

questions.prompt: You are asked to collect a voucher specimen of a threatened plant. What is the correct protocol before collecting?

options.text: Confirm legal and permit requirements, assess population size and conservation impact, and obtain written permission from relevant authorities before collection.
Collect several specimens to ensure identification, then seek retrospective permission.
Avoid collecting and rely solely on photos to save time.
Collect only seeds because they are less destructive than whole specimens.

questions.prompt: While verifying historical records, you find an old herbarium specimen labelled with a locality that no longer matches current land features. What is the best approach to interpret this record?

options.text: Discard the record as unusable because the location cannot be exactly matched.
Compare the specimen's habitat notes and historical maps, consult local experts, and treat the record as plausible but with spatial uncertainty in planning surveys.
Assume the species no longer occurs there and reallocate resources elsewhere.
Assign the record to the nearest modern suburb as a shortcut.

questions.prompt: You complete a threatened flora report that includes sensitive location data. What is the appropriate way to manage that data in the report for external stakeholders?

options.text: Include full coordinates in the public report for transparency.
Omit location information entirely from all documents to be safe.
Provide general habitat descriptions in the public report and supply precise coordinates only in appendices for authorised recipients with clear data sensitivity controls.
Publish precise locations on public social media to support community engagement.

questions.prompt: A junior surveyor records an abundance estimate using a method different from what was in the project brief. What QA action should you take?

options.text: Overwrite the data to match the brief without consulting the surveyor.
Reject all the survey data and repeat the entire survey.
Ignore the deviation because methodologies always vary in the field.
Discuss the discrepancy with the surveyor, document the deviation, assess if data remain comparable, and note any impacts in the report.

questions.prompt: You detect a population at low density and need to estimate total abundance across rugged terrain. Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Use stratified sampling with transects or quadrats targeting representative habitat strata and extrapolate with clear confidence intervals.
Walk the entire area and count every individual without a structured method.
Estimate abundance visually from the air using a drone without ground verification.
Use a single large quadrat and multiply by area to estimate total.

questions.prompt: A threatened grass has a key diagnostic hair pattern visible only under magnification. In field surveys, what equipment and practice best supports accurate identification?

options.text: Rely on macro photographs taken with a phone from three metres distance.
Carry a hand lens (10x), take high-resolution close-up photos, and note microhabitat and associated species to support ID and later verification.
Collect multiple specimens without documentation to compare later under microscopes.
Estimate identity based on surrounding vegetation structure only.

questions.prompt: You are asked to design a monitoring program for a threatened perennial. Which monitoring frequency is most defensible given resource constraints and the species' life history?

options.text: Monitor daily for a month each year to maximise data.
Monitor once every ten years because resources are limited.
Monitor annually during peak detectability years, with less frequent intervals if population is stable and life history supports longer intervals, justified in the plan.
Monitor only when a complaint is received about potential impacts.

questions.prompt: On a survey you find evidence of fungal infection affecting a threatened plant. What is the appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Dig out affected plants to stop spread.
Spray fungicide broadly across the area without expert input.
Ignore the infection because disease is natural.
Record symptoms in detail, take photos and samples where permitted, minimise spread by disinfecting equipment, and escalate to senior ecologist for assessment.

questions.prompt: During a threatened flora survey you encounter Aboriginal cultural heritage items. What is the correct immediate course of action?

options.text: Cease intrusive activities in the immediate area, record the location and notify the project lead and appropriate cultural heritage representatives for guidance.
Continue the survey but avoid photographing the items.
Remove items to protect them from damage.
Ignore them and proceed because the survey is ecological, not cultural.

questions.prompt: A threatened species has irregular recruitment tied to fire. The client asks whether a small prescribed burn could help. As an early-career ecologist what is your best response?

options.text: Recommend burning immediately as recruitment is likely to follow.
Explain that fire effects are species-specific; recommend consulting the supervising ecologist and fire ecology experts and reviewing the species' ecological literature before advising on management.
Advise against any burning because it is always harmful to threatened plants.
Provide detailed burn prescriptions based on a single observation from the current survey.

questions.prompt: You are writing the methods section of a threatened flora survey report. Which detail is essential to include to allow reproducibility?

options.text: Only the total number of hours spent in the field.
A general statement that ‘standard methods’ were used without specifics.
Survey dates and times, personnel, search effort (person-hours), methods (transect/quadrat/timed search), and phenological conditions.
Photographs of the survey team at work to demonstrate effort.

questions.prompt: A threatened plant population is adjacent to a development footprint. The developer requests immediate confidential preliminary counts. What is the correct balance between timeliness and data quality?

options.text: Give the developer unverified numbers to avoid delays.
Refuse to share any preliminary information until final report is complete.
Agree to hide population locations to expedite approvals.
Provide a preliminary summary with caveats about survey limitations and commit to providing validated counts after data QA and verification.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether to disclose exact locations of a newly discovered threatened plant to a contractor undertaking earthworks on-site. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Share location information with the contractor under strict supervision and clear instructions to avoid disturbance, and document the disclosure and mitigation measures.
Refuse to provide any information and tell the contractor to stop work.
Publish the coordinates to the contractor's online forum.
Provide vague directions to the contractor so they cannot avoid the area.

questions.prompt: A field crew reports suspected illegal collection of plants near your survey area. What is the immediate practical step for the ecology team?

options.text: Confront the suspected collectors directly in the field.
Secure your own survey data and site markers, record evidence (photos, descriptions), notify the project supervisor and follow agreed incident reporting procedures to escalate appropriately.
Ignore it because enforcement is not the ecology team's responsibility.
Remove any remaining plants to a safe location.

questions.prompt: You are validating historical herbarium determinations for use in a current threatened flora assessment. Which approach best increases confidence in record reliability?

options.text: Use the specimen labels without further verification because herbarium records are always accurate.
Exclude all historical records older than five years.
Re-examine herbarium specimens where possible, verify determinations with taxonomic keys or experts, and cross-check collection dates and localities.
Assign modern GPS points to old records based solely on the collector's name.

questions.prompt: An ecological survey team must avoid spreading Phytophthora. What field practice is most effective at minimising this risk during threatened flora surveys?

options.text: Wear the same boots all day and rinse them in a creek between sites.
Use herbicide on boots to sterilise them.
Avoid any documentation to reduce personnel movement.
Clean and disinfect footwear and equipment between sites, avoid working in wet soil conditions where possible, and follow a documented hygiene protocol.

questions.prompt: You must communicate uncertain species presence to a client. Which phrasing best balances clarity and technical accuracy?

options.text: We recorded plants with features consistent with Species X; identification remains provisional pending specialist verification and targeted follow-up during its diagnostic phenophase.
Species X is definitely present; no further work is needed.
We could not identify anything of interest; no species present.
There might be a species similar to X; you decide what to do next.

questions.prompt: While conducting quadrat counts, team members disagree on what constitutes a single clump for a tufted perennial. What is the best way to resolve this in the field?

options.text: Each member should use their own judgement and average the counts later.
Agree on a consistent operational definition (e.g. individuals separated by >X cm) before continuing and document that definition in field notes.
Stop the survey and return another day with a different team.
Count every leaf as a separate individual to be conservative.

questions.prompt: A threatened plant is known from very few records. For public reporting, what is the appropriate approach to mapping that species' distribution?

options.text: Plot exact points on a public map to maximise transparency.
Omit the species from the distribution maps entirely to avoid attention.
Display generalised occurrence zones and note the existence of precise records in controlled datasets, avoiding publishing exact locality points.
Show the species as present across the whole region to be cautious.

questions.prompt: You are training a new field assistant on threatened flora survey ethics. Which instruction is most important to emphasise?

options.text: Collect at least one specimen of each interesting plant regardless of permit status.
Always clear surrounding vegetation to make plants more visible for future surveys.
Keep findings secret to protect the species.
Avoid unnecessary disturbance: do not remove plants, minimise trampling, photograph rather than collect unless permitted, and always record precise context for any sampling.

questions.prompt: You need to estimate detection probability for a threatened annual during surveys. Which approach will give the most useful estimate?

options.text: Conduct repeated timed searches at the same sites under similar conditions and use occupancy/detection modelling to estimate detection probability.
Assume detection probability is 1 because plants are visible when present.
Use a single survey and treat non-detections as absences.
Base detection probability on expert opinion without field data.

questions.prompt: If you need specialist taxonomic advice for a potential threatened plant outside your expertise, what is the appropriate action?

options.text: Make the determination yourself to avoid delays.
Contact a recognised taxonomic expert or herbarium curator with specimen images and data, and request a formal verification.
Use an online forum and accept any identification offered.
Ignore taxonomy and proceed with management recommendations.

questions.prompt: You must decide on sampling intensity for baseline surveys of a vascular plant community with potential threatened species. What sampling design principle should primarily guide your decision?

options.text: Use the same fixed number of samples regardless of habitat variation.
Only sample areas where previous surveys reported presence to conserve resources.
Sample to capture habitat heterogeneity and the spatial distribution of target species, increasing effort in rare or high-value microhabitats.
Sample randomly without regard to habitat because that avoids bias.

questions.prompt: After completing a threatened flora field season you identify systematic inconsistencies in identification confidence among surveyors. What quality assurance measure is most appropriate for future surveys?

options.text: Require junior surveyors to defer identifications to seniors without training.
Ignore the inconsistencies as inevitable and proceed.
Remove confidence scores from data collection to simplify records.
Implement a calibration exercise and identification workshops using reference specimens and paired-field surveys to align surveyor skills and confidence scoring.

questions.prompt: You are preparing an ecological report for a proposed development site. During planning, you realise the desktop survey lacks recent aerial imagery for parts of the site. What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Obtain more recent aerial imagery or satellite data and update the desktop assessment before fieldwork.
Proceed with the report using the available older imagery and note the limitation in the methods section.
Delay the entire project timeline and request permission from the client to cancel the survey.
Rely on local knowledge and anecdotal reports from neighbours to supplement the outdated imagery.

questions.prompt: During field surveys for a vegetation community, you encounter an area with ambiguous boundary lines between two vegetation types. For the report, what is the most appropriate approach to document this?

options.text: Assign the whole area to the dominant vegetation type without further documentation to simplify mapping.
Map the boundary as a transitional zone, describe the field indicators used, and include uncertainty in the report maps.
Exclude the ambiguous area from mapping to avoid introducing potential errors.
Create multiple map versions showing different boundary interpretations but do not explain differences in the text.

questions.prompt: A client requests an ecological report that claims no threatened species occur on site, but your initial reconnaissance found signs potentially indicating a threatened species. How should you respond in the report?

options.text: State confidently that no threatened species occur, to meet the client's request.
Omit mention of the signs to avoid delaying approvals and focus on other constraints.
Report the observed signs, outline targeted follow-up surveys required, and recommend adaptive management pending results.
Advise the client that the signs are inconclusive and present no further actions.

questions.prompt: When selecting the structure of an ecological report for a regulatory submission, which element is most important to include early in the document?

options.text: A detailed methodology appendix only accessible at the end of the document.
A long literature review before any findings or recommendations are presented.
Photographs of the site as the first section without context or captions.
An executive summary that states key findings, recommended actions, and uncertainty levels.

questions.prompt: You must present species detection results in the report where several targeted surveys were negative. How should negative results be best conveyed?

options.text: Present negative detections alongside survey effort, timing, detection probability considerations, and remaining uncertainty.
State that species are absent without caveats since no detections were made.
Only report positive detections and omit negative survey outcomes to keep the report concise.
Replace negative results with historical occurrence records to fill gaps.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist provides raw data tables with inconsistent species names and no metadata. For quality assurance before finalising the report, what should you do first?

options.text: Use the data as-is and include a note that names were reported by the junior ecologist.
Standardise species names using accepted taxonomic sources, create metadata, and document any assumptions.
Discard the raw data and repeat the entire field survey to obtain clean data.
Convert tables into charts and include them without cleaning since visualisation hides inconsistencies.

questions.prompt: While drafting a report, you identify a potential significant ecological impact not included in the original scope. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Ignore it because it lies outside the original scope and finalise the report.
Add a brief paragraph recommending mitigation without further fieldwork or client consultation.
Document the potential impact, advise the client of scope limitations, and recommend additional assessment and scope amendment.
Delay the report until the client commissions a new, broader project without noting the issue now.

questions.prompt: Your report will include maps showing habitat types. To ensure maps are useful for compliance and field teams, what should you include?

options.text: Only a single-colour outline for the study area without legend or scale to keep the map simple.
High-resolution aerial photo without overlaying habitat classifications.
A stylised artistic map prioritising visual appeal over spatial accuracy.
Clear legend, scale bar, north arrow, coordinate grid, and symbology explanations for habitat types and survey points.

questions.prompt: A peer reviewer flags that your report conclusions rely heavily on a single short-duration survey. How should you address this in the final report?

options.text: Acknowledge the limitation, describe potential effects on conclusions, and recommend follow-up survey timing and methods.
Remove discussion of the issue and stand by the original conclusions.
Replace the survey data with modelled predictions to avoid admitting the short duration.
Add an appendix with extra raw photos to strengthen the appearance of effort.

questions.prompt: When reporting mitigation measures, how should you present their expected effectiveness and monitoring requirements?

options.text: List mitigation measures without expected outcomes or monitoring because predictions are uncertain.
Describe each measure, provide a rationale for expected effectiveness, outline monitoring metrics, frequency, and adaptive triggers.
State that mitigation will be effective and omit monitoring to avoid additional obligations for the client.
Provide only a high-level commitment to mitigate and leave details to later contractors.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether to include raw survey playback recordings in appendices. What is the best practice?

options.text: Include all raw recordings unedited to maximise transparency, even if file sizes are large.
Exclude any audio to avoid legal or privacy issues and only report detected species lists.
Provide representative audio samples with timestamps and metadata, and offer full raw files on request with storage details.
Transcribe all recordings into text and include only the transcripts in the appendix.

questions.prompt: A regulatory officer asks for the confidence level of your species absence statement. How should you present this in the report?

options.text: Claim absolute certainty of absence since no evidence was found.
Avoid giving any confidence indication and defer to the regulator to interpret the data.
Include a numeric probability without explaining how it was derived.
Provide a qualitative confidence statement supported by survey effort, methods, seasonality, detectability, and residual uncertainty.

questions.prompt: During data analysis you notice a species record that conflicts with known range expectations. What should you do prior to finalising the report?

options.text: Verify the record by checking voucher specimens, photos, observer notes, and consult taxonomic references or specialists if needed.
Include the record unquestioned to avoid altering field data.
Delete the record to prevent confusion.
Relocate the record to an unlabelled appendix without comment.

questions.prompt: Your client requests an expedited report for an ecological assessment but you lack time to complete peer review. What is the most professionally responsible option?

options.text: Skip peer review, finalise the report, and deliver on the expedited timeline.
Explain the risks of delivering without peer review, seek an extended timeline, or provide a preliminary report clearly labelled as draft pending peer review.
Use peer reviewers from unrelated disciplines to speed the process.
Deliver the report with a note that peer review was performed internally but not documented.

questions.prompt: You must communicate complex uncertainty about predicted habitat loss to a non-technical client. Which approach will be most effective in the report?

options.text: Provide dense statistical descriptions without simplification to be thorough.
Exclude uncertainty discussion to avoid confusing the client.
Use plain language summaries, visual confidence indicators, and clear implications for project decisions.
Include only technical annexes and ask the client to consult them if interested.

questions.prompt: A draft report lists mitigation costs that are rough estimates. Before issuing the final report, what should you do regarding cost statements?

options.text: Leave rough estimates as-is without qualification to avoid delaying the report.
Remove all cost information to prevent potential client disagreements.
Inflate the costs slightly to ensure adequate budget allocation.
Label the estimates as preliminary, describe the basis and assumptions, and recommend obtaining detailed costings for implementation.

questions.prompt: You become aware of confidential cultural heritage information relevant to habitat constraints. How should this be handled in the ecological report?

options.text: Discuss ecological implications generally, withhold sensitive cultural details, and follow legal and client protocols for confidentiality and escalation.
Publish the cultural details in full to ensure ecological implications are transparent.
Omit any mention of cultural heritage to avoid dealing with sensitivities.
Include the cultural information but mark it as 'for internal use only' without consulting custodians.

questions.prompt: When presenting cumulative impacts in a report, what is the appropriate way to characterise them?

options.text: Ignore cumulative impacts because the assessment scope is limited to the site footprint.
Describe potential cumulative effects from the project combined with other known developments, explain assumptions and data sources, and identify key uncertainties.
Assume cumulative impacts are the same as the project impacts and present no separate analysis.
Speculate on all possible future developments without referencing data or spatial relevance.

questions.prompt: Your report includes recommendations for an ongoing monitoring program. How should triggers for adaptive management be framed?

options.text: State that adaptive management will be applied but avoid defining specific triggers to remain flexible.
Set triggers as vague targets such as 'if things get worse' without metrics.
Define measurable ecological thresholds or indicators, specify monitoring frequency, and outline actions to be taken when triggers are met.
Recommend immediate mitigation without monitoring to prevent the need for triggers.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder disputes a habitat classification in your report based on local traditional knowledge. How should you address this dispute within the report?

options.text: Dismiss the stakeholder's input if it conflicts with your field classification.
Remove your habitat classification and adopt the stakeholder's view without verification.
Note the disagreement but state you will not change the report because local observations are anecdotal.
Document the stakeholder's observations, compare them to your methods and evidence, and propose ways to reconcile differences or recommend further collaborative investigation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best way to present statistical biodiversity metrics in a report for varied audiences?

options.text: Provide clear summaries of key metrics in plain language, include visual aids, and place detailed tables in appendices.
Only include the detailed statistical tables and expect readers to interpret them.
Convert statistics into qualitative labels like 'high' or 'low' without definitions.
Exclude metrics and rely solely on descriptive species lists.

questions.prompt: You need to document field constraints that limited survey coverage (e.g. flooded access routes). How should these be presented in the methods and results?

options.text: Omit mention of constraints to avoid undermining the credibility of the survey.
Clearly describe constraints, areas not surveyed, potential implications for findings, and how constraints were mitigated or will be addressed.
Only mention constraints verbally to the client and leave them out of the report.
Claim that alternate routes were used even if they were not to maintain an impression of full coverage.

questions.prompt: A report section relies on external datasets from a government database. What is the correct way to reference and qualify those data in the ecological report?

options.text: Cite the dataset without describing date accessed or limitations.
Include a screenshot of the database page in the report as the only citation.
Cite the dataset with version/date accessed, describe known limitations or gaps, and state how you used the data.
Paraphrase the database information without formal citation to streamline the report.

questions.prompt: While finalising the report you find a minor arithmetic error in a habitat area calculation. It does not change conclusions but affects a table value. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it since it does not affect conclusions to save time.
Change related figures elsewhere to match the incorrect value for consistency.
Highlight the error prominently and withdraw the entire report.
Correct the arithmetic error, rerun any dependent calculations, and document the correction in an errata or revision note.

questions.prompt: Your draft report includes habitat suitability modelling with several assumptions. How should those assumptions be treated in the final report?

options.text: Explicitly state all key assumptions, parameter choices, and sensitivity of results to those assumptions.
Leave the modelling assumptions implicit to avoid cluttering the text.
Replace assumptions with optimistic values to make outcomes more favourable.
Present only the model outputs without discussing assumptions or limitations.

questions.prompt: An ecological report reviewer requests raw GPS tracks for your transects. How should you supply spatial data to support reproducibility?

options.text: Refuse to provide GPS tracks to protect your field team’s methods.
Provide GPS tracks with metadata (device, datum, accuracy), explain any processing, and offer formats suitable for GIS review.
Provide only a simplified map without the raw track files.
Supply approximate waypoint coordinates typed into the report body.

questions.prompt: You must escalate a likely occurrence of a high-risk invasive species found on site. Which escalation path is most appropriate to include in the report?

options.text: List internal office staff only and expect the client to contact authorities if required.
Treat the species as unimportant and recommend no action to avoid alarm.
Describe the immediate steps taken in the field, notify the client, and advise contacting the relevant government biosecurity authority with recommended contact options.
Wait for the regulatory authority to discover the issue independently.

questions.prompt: When including photographs in the report, what best practice should you follow?

options.text: Insert photos without captions to let readers interpret them freely.
Use only stock images that resemble site conditions to make the report visually consistent.
Include full-resolution images embedded in the main text regardless of file size.
Provide clear captions with date, location (coordinates), subject, photographer, and relevance to the assessment.

questions.prompt: Your report must recommend timing windows to avoid fauna breeding seasons. What is the appropriate way to justify those windows?

options.text: Provide timing windows based on best-available literature, local observations, and note any uncertainties and the need for confirmation.
Propose a fixed avoidance period with no supporting evidence to be conservative.
Suggest no timing restrictions because compliance is the client's responsibility.
Use breeding dates from a different ecoregion without qualification.

questions.prompt: A section of your report summarises stakeholder concerns incorporated during consultation. How should these be presented?

options.text: List concerns verbatim without context or how they influenced your assessment.
Summarise key concerns, indicate how they were considered in the assessment, and note any unresolved matters or follow-up actions.
Only include stakeholder concerns that support your conclusions.
Omit stakeholder input to maintain an objective scientific tone.

questions.prompt: In writing species impact statements, how should you treat indirect impacts (e.g. edge effects, noise) in the report?

options.text: Ignore indirect impacts as they are speculative and difficult to quantify.
Combine indirect impacts with direct impacts without distinguishing them.
Describe plausible indirect impacts, provide supporting evidence or analogues, and indicate uncertainty and management options.
State that indirect impacts will be negligible without assessment.

questions.prompt: How should you document the chain of custody for physical samples (e.g. voucher specimens) in the report?

options.text: Mention that samples were collected but provide no further details to maintain brevity.
Only note the final repository without documenting earlier handlers.
State that samples are available upon request without giving custody details.
Record collection details, preservative, storage location, accession numbers if deposited, and who handled samples through to deposition.

questions.prompt: During synthesis of results, you find conflicting interpretations between two survey teams. What is the proper approach in the report?

options.text: Present both interpretations, explain the reasons for divergence, evaluate supporting evidence, and recommend resolution steps (e.g. targeted re-survey or expert review).
Choose the interpretation that best supports project approval.
Discard both interpretations and avoid drawing any conclusions.
Assign blame to one team and favour the other without further analysis.

questions.prompt: Your report will be used by contractors to implement mitigation. How should mitigation instructions be written?

options.text: Provide high-level objectives only and leave specific actions to contractors.
Provide clear, actionable instructions, roles and responsibilities, timing windows, and performance criteria that contractors can follow.
Write instructions in technical jargon only accessible to ecologists.
Include optional mitigation measures and allow contractors to choose preferred approaches.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to handle proprietary or sensitive data provided by the client for inclusion in the report?

options.text: Publish all proprietary data without permission to ensure completeness.
Refuse to use proprietary data and rely only on public sources.
Seek client approval for inclusion, indicate data restrictions in the report, and provide summaries where full data cannot be published.
Alter proprietary data to anonymise it without consulting the client.

questions.prompt: A methodological innovation used in your assessment differs from standard protocols. How should this be addressed in the report?

options.text: Omit methodological details to avoid scrutiny of the innovation.
State that the innovation is proprietary and provide no further information.
Claim that the innovation follows standard protocols even if it does not.
Describe the method in detail, justify deviations from standard protocols, present validation or limitations, and recommend peer review.

questions.prompt: When reporting on ecological risk, how should likelihood and consequence be combined?

options.text: Provide a qualitative rationale linking likelihood and consequence with explicit criteria and examples rather than a bare label.
Give only numerical scores without explanation so readers can infer their meaning.
Rank risks by consequence only and ignore likelihood.
Present likelihood and consequence randomly to avoid bias.

questions.prompt: Your report must be reviewed by a qualified reviewer. Which statement best describes an appropriate reviewer selection?

options.text: Choose a reviewer from the same project team to speed sign-off.
Select an independent reviewer with relevant technical expertise and no conflict of interest, and document their qualifications and review scope.
Ask a junior staff member to perform the review since they are available.
Use a reviewer recommended by the client regardless of their expertise.

questions.prompt: After report finalisation, a new recent study emerges that may affect your conclusions. What is the most appropriate post-delivery action?

options.text: Ignore the new study because the report is already finalised.
Retract the report immediately without evaluation.
Assess the implications of the new study, advise the client if it materially affects conclusions, and recommend updating the assessment if needed.
Wait for the regulator to raise the issue instead of informing the client.

questions.prompt: Which practice best ensures transparency about expert judgements used in the report (e.g. habitat value scoring)?

options.text: Provide final scores without explaining the criteria or expert reasoning.
Keep scoring methods confidential as intellectual property.
Present scores as consensus without recording dissenting expert opinions.
Describe the scoring criteria, expert qualifications, any weighting applied, and provide worked examples or supporting evidence for key judgements.

questions.prompt: You are preparing for a morning survey to identify native plant species in a coastal heath remnant. What is the most important pre-field action to improve accuracy of species identification?

options.text: Print and carry regional field guides and recent floras covering coastal heath species.
Contact landholder for an informal list of species they recall seeing on the property.
Prepare a generic plant identification cheat-sheet with common names only.
Plan to rely on photos taken in the field and identify species later in the office.

questions.prompt: During a fauna survey you encounter a small possum you suspect is a juvenile of a native species with two similar congeners in the area. What should you do to support species-level identification?

options.text: Attempt to capture and handle the animal to compare dental and cranial features to keys in the field.
Record high-quality photos from multiple angles, note habitat and behaviour, and collect measurements where possible without handling the animal.
Release the animal immediately and rely on memory to describe distinguishing features in the report.
Assume the most common species in the region and annotate the record accordingly.

questions.prompt: You must survey a wetland for aquatic plant species, some of which fruit seasonally. It's outside the peak fruiting season. How should you adjust your survey approach?

options.text: Postpone all surveys until the next fruiting season to ensure definitive species lists.
Record species as 'not identified' and proceed with habitat impact assessments without further action.
Use vegetative keys, take detailed morphological photographs, and schedule a follow-up survey during peak fruiting if identification remains uncertain.
Collect whole plants from the wetland for lab-based identification regardless of permit requirements.

questions.prompt: On a licence-constrained site you find a tree that could be a protected native species requiring special handling. You lack a clear species ID. What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Proceed with planned works but avoid cutting the tree unless it obstructs equipment.
Assume it is not protected because you cannot confirm in the field and continue work.
Cut a small branch for later identification without consulting site management.
Photograph diagnostic features, record GPS location and microhabitat, and suspend any work near the tree until a specialist confirms identification.

questions.prompt: While surveying reptiles you locate shed skin that may belong to a locally uncommon snake species. Which data-recording practice best supports later confirmation?

options.text: Photograph the shed skin against a scale, note orientation and substrate, collect the shed in a sealed bag as non-invasive evidence, and log GPS coordinates.
Discard the shed skin after taking a single distant photo as evidence is rarely needed.
Handle the shed heavily to flatten it for a clearer photo, then leave it on-site in case the snake returns.
Move the shed to a central location to make it easier for others to find.

questions.prompt: You are training a new field ecologist on identifying native orchids. Which mentoring method most effectively improves their identification skills in the field?

options.text: Give them a list of species and ask them to read descriptions before solo surveys.
Go on guided surveys together, demonstrating key morphological features and explaining variability and look-alikes in situ.
Assign them to photograph orchids and correct IDs later without on-site discussion.
Tell them to rely on automated plant ID apps during surveys.

questions.prompt: During a survey you observe two visually similar frog species calling. How should you collect evidence to support species identification?

options.text: Rely solely on visual observation of a distant silhouette at night to identify species.
Play back recordings of one species to elicit a response and assume a match based on any reply.
Record high-quality audio of the calls with time and weather notes, and note microhabitat and calling behaviour.
Mark the location and leave immediately to avoid disturbing the amphibians.

questions.prompt: You must prepare a species list for a client. Some identifications were made by non-expert staff. What quality-assurance step is most appropriate before delivering the list?

options.text: Include all identifications as recorded but add a disclaimer that some were by non-experts.
Remove all records made by non-expert staff to avoid potential errors.
Accept non-expert records if they match common species in the region without further checks.
Review non-expert identifications against reference specimens or expert-confirmed photographs and escalate uncertain records for specialist verification.

questions.prompt: A field team reports finding a plant that matches the description of a threatened native species but photos are blurry. What is the appropriate escalation?

options.text: Request clearer images or arrange a targeted revisit by a botanist to obtain diagnostic characters before confirming the record.
Report the record immediately as the threatened species to the client without further verification.
Discard the observation since the photos are inadequate and do not mention it in deliverables.
Ask the team to collect seeds for later identification without confirming permits.

questions.prompt: While documenting birds, you note a plumage variant not covered in your regional guide. What should you do to support accurate identification?

options.text: Assume it is a juvenile form of a common species and record it as such without further evidence.
Capture detailed photos, record behaviour and vocalisations, compare with multiple authoritative sources, and consult an ornithological specialist if uncertain.
Ignore the record because variants are rarely important for ecological assessments.
Use only range maps to assign species identity.

questions.prompt: A land-clearing contractor requests a quick ID of a dense understory to confirm whether clearing can proceed. How should you respond as an early-career ecologist?

options.text: Provide an immediate verbal clearance based on a brief glance to keep the project on schedule.
Tell them to clear the area and report any notable plants afterwards.
Explain you need time for proper survey and identification, perform a focused assessment documenting key diagnostic features, and advise pausing clearance until confirmed.
Refer the contractor to an online plant photo without conducting a site assessment.

questions.prompt: During a diurnal mammal survey you set camera traps that capture an ambiguous small carnivore. What is the best practice for classifying this detection in your dataset?

options.text: Assign the species to the most likely common carnivore and include it as a confirmed detection.
Exclude the record from the dataset due to uncertainty.
Enhance the image digitally to infer species identity and record that as confirmed.
Classify the record as 'unconfirmed species - cryptic' with attached images and notes, and seek specialist review for confirmation.

questions.prompt: You're tasked with producing a vegetation map. A polygon contains a mix of native grass species that are difficult to separate in the field. How should you represent this in mapping?

options.text: Map the polygon as a native grass-dominated unit and annotate species-level uncertainties, planning targeted sampling for species composition if required.
Split the polygon into species-specific units based on visual guesses to increase perceived precision.
Label the entire area as 'unknown vegetation' to avoid misclassification.
Exclude grasses from the map since they are hard to identify.

questions.prompt: An early-career ecologist must identify leaf-miner damage to assign host plant species. Which approach yields the most reliable host ID?

options.text: Assume any leaf-miner in the area uses the most abundant plant species.
Collect and photograph the leaf mines, record the host plant morphology, and, if necessary, rear larvae to adult for specialist identification.
Ignore the leaf mines as they are not relevant to vegetation mapping.
Use only leaf shape to assign host species without considering mines or insect life stage.

questions.prompt: During nocturnal surveys you need to identify microbat species by echolocation. What is an appropriate evidence standard?

options.text: Make a best-guess identification in the field by ear without recordings.
Rely solely on the time of night as an indicator of species presence.
Record high-quality ultrasonic calls with calibrated detectors, note location and habitat, and compare with regional call libraries and expert opinion.
Use a smartphone app recording audible sound to capture echolocation.

questions.prompt: You are verifying historical herbarium records to inform current surveys. A specimen label lists an old locality name that no longer exists. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Discard the record because the locality name is obsolete and therefore unreliable.
Assume the specimen came from the nearest town and use that for distribution mapping.
Treat the record as modern and add it to recent occurrence data without comment.
Georeference the specimen using historical maps and notes, document uncertainty, and use it to guide targeted field searches.

questions.prompt: In a survey of native freshwater fish you capture specimens similar to two species that require scale counts to distinguish. You cannot perform counts in the field. What is the proper procedure?

options.text: Photograph lateral view with a scale bar, measure and release specimens if permitted, and arrange laboratory verification or preserved voucher specimens under permits.
Identify to the genus level only and omit species records entirely.
Handle specimens roughly to obtain scale samples without permits to speed up identification.
Estimate scale counts visually and record the most likely species.

questions.prompt: You're compiling a report and must present confidence levels for field identifications. Which method is most defensible for native species IDs?

options.text: State that all identifications are confident without providing evidence or criteria.
Use a standard confidence rubric (e.g. confirmed, probable, possible) tied to evidence types like specimens, photos, or audio and list criteria for each level.
Exclude confidence information to avoid drawing attention to uncertain records.
Provide numeric confidence scores without explaining what evidence supports them.

questions.prompt: A field ecologist finds a plant that matches a native species listed on an advisory list but the match is not exact. What is the appropriate communication to the client?

options.text: Label it as the advisory-listed species in the report to trigger immediate management measures.
Omit the observation to avoid causing concern for the client.
Report the observation as a possible match, include supporting photos and notes, and recommend specialist confirmation before any management actions.
Advise the client verbally that no action is needed until you complete the full report.

questions.prompt: You are tasked with photographic documentation of diagnostic features for sedge species. Which photographic technique is best practice?

options.text: Capture only wide-angle landscape photos showing general sedge cover.
Photograph random leaves without including diagnostic reproductive structures.
Use flash-only macro shots that overexpose delicate floral detail.
Take close-up images of inflorescences, ligules, leaf cross-sections, and overall habit with scale bars and notes on substrate.

questions.prompt: During a vegetation survey you must record occurrences of a native shrub that hybridises frequently. How should hybrid-looking individuals be recorded?

options.text: Record them as 'putative hybrids' with detailed notes on the mixed traits and collect voucher material or photos for specialist analysis.
Force identification to one parent species based on majority traits.
Exclude hybrid individuals from species counts to avoid distorting results.
List them as a new species in the report due to intermediate features.

questions.prompt: A client requests a rapid baseline species list from a 2-hectare woodland outside peak survey season. How should you manage expectations about native species identification?

options.text: Deliver a complete species list based on a single rapid visit to satisfy the client timeline.
Provide a provisional list noting seasonal limitations, species likely missed, and recommend targeted seasonal surveys for a comprehensive inventory.
Decline to produce any list until exhaustive year-round surveys are completed.
Use regional checklist data to compile a species list without field verification.

questions.prompt: You detect a large population of a native wildflower with subtle distinguishing traits from an invasive look-alike. What risk management step should you take before management actions?

options.text: Treat all similar plants as invasive to expedite control operations.
Delay all management indefinitely due to uncertainty without seeking verification.
Confirm native species identity through specimen-based verification or specialist confirmation before any removal, and document the decision pathway.
Apply herbicide treatments broadly across the area and note outcomes later.

questions.prompt: While conducting invertebrate surveys, you encounter a beetle that could be a locally rare native. What is the best immediate documentation practice?

options.text: Take a single distant photo and assume species status based on habitat.
Squash and discard the beetle to prevent misidentification.
Record it as a common beetle to avoid triggering further investigations.
Photograph dorsal and ventral views, note microhabitat and host plants, and collect a voucher specimen under relevant permits for expert verification.

questions.prompt: You need to standardise species identification methods across multiple early-career field staff. Which approach best increases consistency?

options.text: Develop a field identification protocol with exemplar photos, decision keys, and minimum evidence standards, then run competency checks.
Allow each staff member to use their preferred methods and compare results at project end.
Rely on senior staff to re-identify all finds after fieldwork without training juniors.
Use different identification guides for each team to encourage diverse opinions.

questions.prompt: You're reviewing a colleague's plant ID that is questionable. What is an appropriate review action?

options.text: Delete the record from the dataset without discussion to maintain data quality.
Compare their records and images against reference literature and herbarium specimens, discuss discrepancies with the colleague, and suggest specialist input if unresolved.
Accept the identification to avoid conflict and move on.
Publicly correct the colleague in a client meeting without internal consultation.
