Recommend that the Stage 1 memo conclusions, uncertainties and recommended actions be reviewed by a designated senior ecologist and the project environmental manager, with outcomes recorded and communicated to the client.

questions.prompt: You are preparing for a field survey to map vegetation plots with geolocated points. Which pre-field action best ensures GPS units will record accurate positions during the survey?

options.text: Charge unit batteries, calibrate compass settings on each device, and load site boundary polygons before departure.
Rely on smartphone GPS only and plan to average multiple readings per location in the field.
Turn on devices at the office to warm them up for 30 minutes before starting at the first plot.
Download satellite imagery to the device after arriving on site to get the latest basemap.

questions.prompt: During a nocturnal fauna survey you need to log precise locations of detections using a handheld GPS. Which on-the-spot recording practice best minimises location error?

options.text: Record the GPS waypoint immediately and move on to the next point to reduce disturbance.
Pause at the detection location for at least 60 seconds to allow satellite acquisition and then record the averaged coordinate.
Stand near the detection but under dense canopy to avoid disturbing animals and take a quick fix.
Take a photo of the animal and geotag it later from memory in the office.

questions.prompt: You are mapping a threatened plant population with a GNSS receiver capable of real-time correction. What is the best way to document positional accuracy in the field record?

options.text: Note the number of satellites visible and assume sub-metre accuracy if more than 10 are logged.
Enter a standard 5 m accuracy value for all waypoints to simplify data entry.
Record the reported horizontal dilution of precision (HDOP) and estimated horizontal error value from the receiver at each waypoint.
Take duplicate waypoints five metres apart and average them later.

questions.prompt: While collecting point data with handheld devices, you notice the device clock is set two minutes behind the surveyor's watch. Why is synchronising timestamps important and what should you do?

options.text: Timestamps are irrelevant; continue surveying as location is the priority.
Reset the field watch to the device time since the device records positions.
Record both times in each field note and decide later which to use.
Synchronise the device clock to the standard field time and note the correction in metadata so time-stamped photos and GPS points align.

questions.prompt: You find a deep canyon where satellite reception drops intermittently while transecting. Which technique best mitigates positional uncertainty for your transect line?

options.text: Use conspicuous landmarks with known coordinates to mark transect endpoints and interpolate positions between them in the office.
Abort the transect and sample an alternative area with better reception.
Record fixes only at the start and end of the canyon section and assume a straight line between them.
Carry out the transect but do not record any locations within the canyon to avoid bad data.

questions.prompt: A junior surveyor collected numerous waypoints using a mobile app but forgot to attach surveyor initials to records. For data chain-of-custody, what is the best immediate action?

options.text: Accept the data as anonymous and proceed to analysis.
Ask the surveyor to review the original device and add their identification and a brief note explaining the omission before submission.
Delete the suspect waypoints and resurvey the site at a later date.
Add a general team name to all records rather than individual initials to avoid singling anyone out.

questions.prompt: You are validating a third-party dataset of geolocated fauna sightings for use in your report. Which verification step is most appropriate before integration?

options.text: Integrate all records but flag them as external data with no further checks.
Convert coordinates to your projection and trust they are accurate if they plot within the expected area.
Cross-check a random subset of records against original photos, timestamp metadata, or field notes to assess reliability.
Remove records lacking an accuracy field to ensure only high-quality data remain.

questions.prompt: Your survey plan requires georeferencing historic hand-drawn transects. Which method best preserves accuracy when digitising these features?

options.text: Trace the hand-drawn lines directly in the GIS by eye to reproduce the transects.
Enter approximate coordinates from the map scale verbally into the dataset.
Ignore historic transects and design new transects with GPS.
Scan the maps, georeference the raster using multiple control points from current reliable coordinates, then digitise transects from the georeferenced image.

questions.prompt: While using a GNSS receiver you notice its antenna was knocked and the casing bent earlier in the season. What is the most appropriate action before relying on its positions?

options.text: Ground-check the unit against known control points and document any systematic offsets before using it for important surveys.
Continue using the unit; physical damage rarely affects accuracy.
Only use the device under open sky conditions where damage will not matter.
Replace the unit immediately with a smartphone and resume work.

questions.prompt: You're required to collect geotagged photos for each survey plot. Which practice ensures photos are reliably linked to the correct plot?

options.text: Take photos liberally and match them to plots later by visual similarity.
Capture a reference photo of the plot marker with the GPS device visible in-frame showing coordinates and timestamp for each plot.
Filename photos sequentially in the camera and assume order matches field notes.
Only collect photos when time allows; rely on written descriptions otherwise.

questions.prompt: During data collection, battery power is limited and a surveyor must choose between GPS recording frequency or continuous camera use. What should guide their decision?

options.text: Conserve GPS by switching it off and take as many photos as possible for later geolocation.
Alternate between GPS and camera every 10 minutes to balance usage.
Prioritise more frequent GPS fixes if location precision is critical to the survey objectives, and reduce photo capture accordingly.
Use only one device and estimate missing data from nearby fixes.

questions.prompt: You need to transcribe field GPS waypoints into the project GIS. Which data-recording practice least preserves traceability?

options.text: Import the raw GNSS export file (.gpx) and retain original attributes.
Attach exported waypoints to observation records and keep the original file in the archive.
Record the export file name and processing steps in the dataset metadata.
Manually retype coordinates into a spreadsheet and delete the original GNSS files.

questions.prompt: A surveyor reports a single point with unexpectedly high positional error in the GNSS log. What is the most appropriate data-quality response?

options.text: Retain the point but flag it and add a note describing the high error and any contextual observations.
Automatically erase any points exceeding the project's nominal accuracy threshold.
Adjust the coordinate to match neighbouring points to improve apparent consistency.
Convert the point to a polygon to disguise the inaccuracy.

questions.prompt: You are designing a field form for recording geolocated observations. Which required field will best support post-field spatial QA?

options.text: Observer's favourite species.
Device or app used and its reported horizontal accuracy in metres for each point.
Estimated distance walked during the day.
Weather description in narrative form only.

questions.prompt: While leading a team, you notice inconsistent naming conventions for waypoint IDs across surveyors. What is the best immediate management action?

options.text: Ignore the inconsistency; it will be clear during data processing.
Allow each surveyor to continue with their format and merge later manually.
Stop fieldwork briefly, communicate a standard waypoint ID format, and require surveyors to update recent entries where feasible.
Create a mapping table in the office after the survey to reconcile names.

questions.prompt: A contractor asks whether to use WAAS/EGNOS correction for a coastal survey where some areas have tree cover. What advice should you give based on geolocated field data practices?

options.text: Avoid correction services because they introduce complexity and do not work over water.
Rely solely on smartphone GPS instead of correction services for consistency.
Switch off all corrections to maintain raw data integrity.
Use the correction service where available to improve horizontal accuracy, but document locations where coverage or multipath under canopy may still affect fixes.

questions.prompt: You must combine multiple geolocated datasets collected in different projections. What is the most defensible first step?

options.text: Identify the coordinate reference systems (CRS) used for each dataset, document them, and reproject all data to a common project CRS before analysis.
Overlay the layers without transforming and visually inspect alignment.
Convert everything to latitude/longitude decimals without recording the original CRS.
Randomly choose a CRS that looks right in the GIS and reproject all layers to it.

questions.prompt: A landowner challenges the location of a mapped boundary you recorded with a handheld device. What escalation route is most appropriate?

options.text: Defend the mapping by insisting your GPS is correct without further checks.
Explain the positional accuracy and limitations recorded in the survey metadata and propose verification using higher-accuracy control points or cadastral records.
Offer to move the boundary on the map to match the landowner's claim immediately.
Ignore the complaint and proceed with reporting.

questions.prompt: During a rapid assessment after rain, you need to capture ephemeral wetland extents with limited time. Which geolocation strategy balances speed and acceptable accuracy?

options.text: Walk the entire wetland perimeter taking high-frequency GNSS fixes regardless of time.
Estimate the extent by sketching on a paper map and digitise later without GPS.
Collect waypoint fixes at key corners and representative points, photograph the shoreline with device coordinates visible, and recollect complete perimeters later if needed.
Delay the assessment until you can schedule a full GPS survey.

questions.prompt: You suspect your handheld GPS shows a consistent 3 m eastward bias compared with survey control. For reporting, what is the best technical judgement?

options.text: Apply a blanket 3 m westward correction to all field points without noting it.
Discard all data collected with that device and resurvey.
Ignore the bias and proceed since 3 m is negligible.
Document the observed bias, present results with raw coordinates, and, if appropriate, apply and document a correction in the QA record so readers understand the adjustment.

questions.prompt: A survey requires capturing acoustic detections logged by a recorder with time but no GPS. What's the best practical approach to geolocate these detections?

options.text: Assign the recorder's deployment GPS coordinate to all detections and record the recorder position and its accuracy in metadata.
Guess coordinates based on where the recorder was likely placed in dense vegetation.
Exclude the acoustic data because it lacks per-detection geolocation.
Create a random distribution of points around the recorder to represent uncertainty.

questions.prompt: You are training new staff in using an app that auto-rounds coordinates to 6 decimal places. Which guidance best reflects good data practice?

options.text: Allow rounding since 6 decimals is always precise enough for ecological surveys.
Explain the app's rounding behaviour, record device settings in metadata, and where higher precision is required use devices or exports that retain full precision.
Disable the app and use paper notes only to avoid rounding.
Manually add extra digits based on estimation to increase apparent precision.

questions.prompt: A field crew collected overlapping transects with different start IDs causing duplicates in the database. Which remediation maintains data integrity?

options.text: Merge duplicate transects automatically and keep the version with more points.
Delete all duplicates and leave only one random record to simplify the dataset.
Compare duplicated records, reconcile attributes against field notes and raw GNSS files, then assign unique IDs and document the reconciliation steps.
Rename all transects using a new numbering system without consulting field logs.

questions.prompt: You must collect geolocated data in an area with known magnetic anomalies affecting compass-based bearings. How should you adapt field procedures?

options.text: Ignore compass bearings and rely solely on estimated distances from previous maps.
Use a stronger magnetic compass to overcome anomalies.
Cancel the survey until a full geophysical study is completed.
Use GNSS-derived bearings where possible, note locations affected by magnetic anomalies, and avoid relying on magnetic compass bearings for critical alignment.

questions.prompt: Your field device records coordinates in the local grid but your office GIS uses GDA2020. What is the correct data handling step?

options.text: Identify the recorded grid and apply an appropriate datum transformation to GDA2020, documenting the method used.
Import coordinates without transformation and relabel the layer as GDA2020.
Convert coordinates by applying a simple offset based on eyeballing alignment.
Discard the field coordinates and resurvey in GDA2020.

questions.prompt: You notice two surveyors recorded the same nest using slightly different waypoint coordinates and different species codes. What is the most appropriate QA review action?

options.text: Keep both entries to reflect observer variability.
Review both field notes and photos, reconcile species code using evidence, merge duplicate waypoints as a single record, and document the decision.
Delete the older record to avoid duplicates.
Average the coordinates and randomly choose one species code.

questions.prompt: A remote survey uses satellite-linked GPS collars transmitting locations irregularly. For analytical integrity, what metadata is most critical to retain?

options.text: Only the animal ID and landcover type at each fix.
Battery level of the collar at each transmission only.
Timestamp of each fix, reported positional accuracy, fix type (2D/3D), and transmission method to interpret temporal and spatial gaps.
The colour of the collar for identification in photos.

questions.prompt: You must document chain-of-custody for raw GNSS files collected by contractors. Which practice best fulfils this requirement?

options.text: Ask the contractor to email CSV exports and accept those without further checks.
Request screenshots of waypoints instead of files for convenience.
Collect only aggregated summaries of coordinates rather than raw files.
Require contractors to provide original raw GNSS files, a manifest listing filenames/timestamps, and a signed statement confirming no post-collection edits.

questions.prompt: During a survey you detect multipath errors near metal fencing causing erratic GNSS points. Which field adjustment reduces multipath impact?

options.text: Move several metres away from the fence to a clearer location, record the point, and note the offset distance and direction.
Increase the frequency of waypoint recording to capture more data.
Hold the antenna closer to the metal to stabilise signals.
Record the points only during cloudy weather to reduce interference.

questions.prompt: You are tasked with producing a map for a client showing GPS-derived survey points with stated confidence. How should confidence be presented?

options.text: Do not state confidence; leave interpretation to the client.
Include a legend indicating reported horizontal accuracy ranges (e.g., <1 m, 1–5 m, >5 m) derived from device metadata and note the methods used to calculate them.
Show points with error bars of arbitrary size to demonstrate uncertainty.
Present points only where accuracy is below an arbitrary 2 m threshold and omit others.

questions.prompt: A field team is unsure whether to collect an observed feature as a point or small polygon. Which decision best supports future analysis?

options.text: Always record as a point to save time during fieldwork.
Make the decision later in the office without collecting any spatial data in the field.
Record as a polygon in the field when the feature's extent is relevant to the survey objective; otherwise capture a point with a clear note and photo.
Capture multiple points around the feature and leave it to the GIS operator to decide.

questions.prompt: You need to archive field GNSS data for long-term access. Which practice ensures future usability?

options.text: Store the files only on the surveyor's personal device.
Convert all data to PDF reports and delete raw files.
Email files to the project manager and rely on their inbox for storage.
Save original raw GNSS files and exports, record device and software versions, coordinate reference system, and store them in a managed, backed-up repository with descriptive metadata.

questions.prompt: A survey includes recording rare orchid locations with high legal significance. What escalation is appropriate if you suspect inaccurate GPS readings at a reported location?

options.text: Pause reporting, notify your supervisor, and schedule a verification visit using higher-accuracy equipment or reference control points before finalising the location in the report.
Proceed with the report and ignore the inconsistency to meet deadlines.
Change the recorded GPS coordinates to match earlier records without verification.
Publish the suspect locations but annotate them as approximate.

questions.prompt: During a coastal bird survey you used a handheld GPS in a pocket under clothing and now have systematically poor accuracy. What QA note should accompany these points?

options.text: No note is necessary; GPS is always accurate enough.
Document that GPS devices were carried in pockets, likely degrading reception, include device-reported accuracy values, and flag points for potential low reliability.
Replace the coordinates with values estimated from maps.
Claim the dataset used an external base station to improve accuracy.

questions.prompt: You are QA reviewing a mobile-app export where some coordinates fall outside the surveyed property polygon. What is the best immediate review step?

options.text: Assume the app GPS drifted and delete the outlying points.
Shift the entire dataset to fit within the property boundary.
Check raw GNSS logs, timestamps, and field notes for those points to determine whether they were recorded outside the property or are erroneous.
Ignore the discrepancy since minor outside points are common.

questions.prompt: A field survey records many species occurrences but no coordinate accuracy values. What is the most practical remediation step?

options.text: Delete all records lacking accuracy data to avoid uncertain locations.
Assume the highest accuracy of the best device used on the project for all records.
Randomly assign accuracy values based on habitat type.
Consult the surveyors to obtain device type and typical accuracy settings, then assign conservative accuracy estimates in metadata and flag records for caution.

questions.prompt: When preparing field GPS devices for an upcoming survey, what documentation should accompany each device to support quality control in the field?

options.text: A device checklist including serial number, firmware/software version, antenna type, recent calibration or testing results, and default settings to be used during the survey.
Only the device serial number written on a sticky note.
A photo of the device in its case.
No documentation; users are expected to know the device details.

questions.prompt: You are asked to provide evidence that geolocated points were collected on the stated survey dates. Which combination of records best supports this claim?

options.text: Only the final GIS layer with dates edited to match the report.
Original GNSS raw files with timestamps, geotagged photographs, field sheets with signatures, and device metadata retained in the project archive.
An email from the team leader stating the dates.
A client invoice showing payment dates.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist proposes using a drone to map small habitat patches and integrate drone-derived coordinates with handheld GNSS points. What is the key consideration to ensure datasets align?

options.text: Assume drone GPS is more accurate and overwrite handheld points.
Use the drone without ground control and scale the image to fit handheld data visually.
Ensure the drone-derived orthomosaic is georeferenced using ground control points surveyed with compatible datum and document transformation parameters for integration with handheld GNSS points.
Collect drone data on a different day to avoid duplication.

questions.prompt: Your project requires export of survey points for regulatory submission. Which export practice best minimises misinterpretation by the regulator?

options.text: Export coordinates without metadata in the regulator's preferred file type to reduce file size.
Embed coordinates in a PDF map only and omit raw files.
Send a screenshot of points overlaid on a basemap for clarity.

Provide coordinate exports in the regulator's required format accompanied by metadata describing coordinate system, accuracy/error metrics, device types, timestamps and any spatial processing applied.

title: Fieldwork Planning WHS and Remote Work

questions.prompt: You are organising a two-day ecological survey at a remote riparian site requiring helicopter access. What is the first planning action you should take specific to WHS and remote logistics?

options.text: Prepare a site-specific risk assessment including helicopter landing zones, landing protocols and emergency evacuation procedures.
Book the helicopter and pilot directly based on availability to secure transport windows.
Send a generic trip checklist to all team members and ask them to pack personal protective equipment (PPE).
Confirm flora and fauna survey methods with the client to determine equipment needs.

questions.prompt: An early-career ecologist is drafting a field safety plan for overnight remote work. Which detail is most important to include to support emergency communication reliability?

options.text: A list of mobile phone numbers for all team members and the client contact.
The planned satellite communication device type, registration details, expected coverage limitations and check-in schedule.
The radio channels used by local recreational clubs in the area.
A hard copy map showing the approximate location of the campsite.

questions.prompt: During pre-field planning, you identify potential heat stress for a summer day survey. Which control is most appropriate to reduce heat-related injury risk for the team?

options.text: Advise team members to drink water when they feel thirsty and bring sunscreen.
Require all team members to wear long-sleeved shirts and full-length trousers at all times regardless of conditions.
Schedule surveys for early morning and late afternoon, include enforced rest breaks in shade, and limit continuous work during peak heat.
Reduce team size to minimise the number of people exposed to heat.

questions.prompt: You’re preparing equipment for an inland wetland survey where daytime temperatures drop suddenly at night. What evidence should be recorded to justify clothing and equipment choices in the field record?

options.text: A note that 'team members chose appropriate clothing' without specifics.
A statement from the team leader saying cold is unlikely and no extra gear was needed.
An email from the client approving the budget for extra clothing.
Photographs of packed gear, a list of issued thermal layers, weather forecast screenshots and rationale for choices in the field log.

questions.prompt: On arrival at a remote property you discover additional hazards (livestock and uneven access tracks). What is the correct immediate technical judgement for the survey team leader?

options.text: Stop and conduct a rapid site-specific risk assessment, modify access routes or controls, and communicate changes to the team before continuing.
Proceed with the planned survey route to maintain the schedule and record hazards in the post-field report.
Ask the landowner to remove livestock temporarily and then proceed as planned.
Return to base to await further instructions rather than assess on site.

questions.prompt: A team member reports feeling unwell with suspected dehydration mid-survey in a remote area. What escalation step should the team leader take first?

options.text: Continue the survey while monitoring the team member closely.
Administer oral fluids, move the person to shade, implement the emergency response plan and if no improvement follow protocol for medical evacuation.
Delay treatment until returning to base to access better supplies.
Ask the person to rest alone while the rest of the team finishes the survey.

questions.prompt: Which record is most important to retain after a multi-day remote fauna survey for WHS compliance and future quality assurance?

options.text: A signed timesheet for each team member.
The raw species datasheets only, without WHS documents.
Completed site-specific risk assessments, incident/near-miss reports, daily check-in logs and equipment maintenance records.
Photographs of survey locations with no supporting documentation.

questions.prompt: You must choose vehicles for a field team heading into remote, unsealed tracks. Which selection demonstrates sound WHS and operational planning?

options.text: Use the client’s vehicle because it is closest, without checking condition.
Use standard sedans to maximise fuel economy and reduce costs.
Allow volunteers to drive any available vehicle provided they have a licence.
Select 4WD vehicles with current maintenance checks, recovery gear, communication equipment, and driver competence records for off-road driving.

questions.prompt: During planning you must set a check-in schedule for a remote solo observer overnight. Which schedule balances risk and practicality?

options.text: Regular check-ins via satellite device every 2–4 hours overnight with an agreed escalation if missed.
A single check-in time the next day to avoid disturbing the observer.
No formal check-in; rely on the observer to call if there is a problem.
Ask the observer to check in only when they return to mobile coverage.

questions.prompt: Which control is most appropriate when planning surveys in areas with venomous snakes during warm months?

options.text: Advise team members to wear fashionable boots and hope for the best.
Require gaiters or high boots, provide snake bandage and first aid training, plan routes to avoid long grass and include snakebite emergency procedures.
Ban fieldwork during warm months entirely regardless of project deadlines.
Rely on local landowner knowledge only and proceed without PPE.

questions.prompt: You’re preparing a remote vegetation plot survey with multiple teams. How should data integrity and WHS be managed in planning?

options.text: Allow each team to use their preferred datasheets and safety procedures for flexibility.
Prioritise data protocols and omit WHS briefings to save time.
Standardise datasheets, digital data-entry protocols, and include a section in the safety briefing for site-specific hazards and mutual aid arrangements between teams.
Require teams to send data at the end of the week rather than during the field period.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist is unsure whether to proceed when weather forecasts predict severe winds on the day of a canopy access survey. What is the appropriate course of action?

options.text: Proceed because the site has been accessed previously without incident.
Proceed but reduce the number of workers in the canopy to one.
Switch to a different site with similar canopy characteristics without further assessment.
Postpone or reschedule the canopy access survey until forecasts improve, consult the supervisor and document the decision with risk rationale.

questions.prompt: Which element is essential in a field inspection record to demonstrate technical judgement about flora survey timing?

options.text: Dates and times of survey, phenological observations, weather conditions and rationale for timing decisions recorded in the field log.
A statement that 'timing was suitable' without supporting data.
A photograph of a flowering specimen alone.
An estimate of species detectability based on memory after returning to the office.

questions.prompt: You are compiling a fieldwork WHS debrief after a remote project. Which action best supports continuous improvement?

options.text: Record only positive outcomes to maintain client confidence.
Document incidents, near-misses, control effectiveness, team feedback and recommended changes to procedures, then update plans and training accordingly.
File the debrief with no distribution to avoid criticism.
Rely on memory for improvements rather than records.

questions.prompt: Which communication is most appropriate to send to landholders before accessing a remote property for an ecological survey?

options.text: A brief text asking permission without specifying dates, team composition or biosecurity measures.
No communication; simply arrive early to complete the survey quickly.
A detailed email including visit dates and times, team names, vehicle details, biosecurity requirements, access routes and emergency contact information.
A generic brochure about your company services.

questions.prompt: During field planning you identify that a survey requires working alone in a remote wetland for several hours. Which control best reduces solo-worker risk while maintaining survey integrity?

options.text: Keep the solo worker but require them to carry a phone only.
Double the survey area for the solo worker to reduce time on-site.
Cancel the survey as solo work is strictly prohibited.
Use a buddy system rotating short solo periods, or provide scheduled overlap with another team member, plus satellite check-ins and a rescue plan.

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence best demonstrates that vehicle safety was considered for a remote field project?

options.text: Written vehicle pre-departure checklists, maintenance records, recovery gear inventory and driver accreditation records kept with the project files.
A verbal assurance from the driver that the vehicle is fine.
A fuel receipt showing a full tank before departure.
A photo of the vehicle parked at the site.

questions.prompt: A field team encounters a previously unknown Aboriginal cultural heritage marker on-site. What is the appropriate immediate action under good field practice?

options.text: Continue the survey avoiding the marker and note it in the report later.
Cease work in the immediate area, secure the site, contact the supervisor and follow the organisation’s cultural heritage procedure, seeking guidance on escalation.
Move the marker to a safer location to allow survey completion.
Ignore it as it is not part of the ecological survey.

questions.prompt: Which quality assurance step should be included in the field plan to ensure technical data collected by early-career staff are robust?

options.text: Trust that all staff follow their training and avoid further checks.
Only review unusual records after project completion.
Include paired sampling or periodic senior staff audits of data collection, standard operating procedures and calibration checks for equipment.
Delegate QA responsibility to the client.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible way to document an on-site change to the agreed survey methodology due to unexpected conditions?

options.text: Make the change and mention it casually in the final report appendix.
Proceed without recording and hope the change is not noticed.
Ask team members to remember the change and discuss it verbally at the next team meeting.
Record the change in the field log with date, time, rationale, who authorised it, and retain any supporting data or photos.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist is planning night-time spotlighting. Which control should be prioritised to manage WHS risks unique to night surveys?

options.text: Conduct a daytime reconnaissance to identify hazards, provide high-visibility clothing, robust lighting systems, and enforce buddy checks and check-in times.
Use the same daytime route and expect no additional hazards.
Rely on the novelty of night surveys to keep team members alert.
Require observers to use personal torches only and avoid radios.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct escalation route if a team identifies an unsafe bridge used to access a survey area and immediate repair is not possible?

options.text: Cross the bridge cautiously to keep the schedule and report it later.
Suspend access via that bridge, notify the supervisor and landholder, identify alternative safe access, and document the decision in the site record.
Ask team volunteers to test the bridge before everyone uses it.
Avoid the area altogether and cancel the project without consulting stakeholders.

questions.prompt: Which approach best ensures biosecurity risks are managed for multiple site visits across properties?

options.text: Clean boots between properties only when they look muddy.
Rely solely on landholder instructions per property.
Implement and document a biosecurity protocol: vehicle and equipment washdown, disposable boot covers or boot cleaning stations, and a log of cleaning actions between properties.
Wait to address biosecurity at project end to save time during fieldwork.

questions.prompt: An early-career ecologist needs to decide whether to use a drone for a remote vegetation mosaic survey. What consideration is most critical from a WHS and technical perspective?

options.text: Using a drone is always faster and should be used without further checks.
Only check the drone’s camera resolution.
Plan to launch the drone from the vehicle without securing a clear launch area to save time.
Confirm operator competency, battery and maintenance status, emergency procedures for drone failure, airspace restrictions and how drone data integrates with ground-truthing protocols.

questions.prompt: Which documentation is most important to include in the handover when transferring field responsibilities between teams at a remote site?

options.text: A written handover including current tasks, outstanding hazards, equipment status, check-in schedule, locations of personnel and any incidents.
A verbal update only to save time.
Only a map of the site with no additional notes.
A list of personal favourite snacks for the incoming team.

questions.prompt: You notice a junior team member is not following PPE requirements in the field. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Ignore it to avoid upsetting the team dynamic.
Politely but firmly stop work, correct the PPE issue, explain the safety rationale, and record the intervention in the site WHS log.
Send the person home without explanation.
Complain to the client after the survey is finished.

questions.prompt: Which action best demonstrates appropriate risk-based scheduling for fieldwork in flood-prone regions?

options.text: Schedule surveys during the wet season to get the best data regardless of safety.
Proceed as scheduled and monitor the river visually only when on-site.
Use historical flood data and short-term forecasts to avoid high-risk windows, plan alternative dates and include flood contingency procedures in the field plan.
Only consider flood risk once the team is already at the site.

questions.prompt: When planning sample transport from a remote site back to the laboratory, what WHS and quality step is essential?

options.text: Place all samples together in a single bag for convenience.
Leave samples in the vehicle overnight for pickup the next morning.
Allow each team member to handle samples without documentation.
Use labelled, secure containers with appropriate cool-chain control where required, documented chain-of-custody, and secure storage in vehicles to prevent spills and contamination.

questions.prompt: A field team member reports a near-miss when their ankle twisted on loose rocks. What is the correct immediate and short-term course of action?

options.text: Provide first aid assessment, adjust tasks to avoid further strain, document the near-miss in the incident log, and review footing controls for the site before continuing work.
Encourage them to continue to finish the day and report the incident later.
Send them home immediately without recording details.
Ask them to self-assess and only report if pain persists.

questions.prompt: Which planning step is most important to ensure cultural and environmental restrictions are respected during remote survey timing?

options.text: Assume no restrictions unless the client mentions them.
Engage stakeholders early (including Indigenous representatives and landholders), identify seasonal or access restrictions and include constraints explicitly in the field schedule.
Plan according to staff availability only.
Ignore potential restrictions and proceed if access is physically possible.

questions.prompt: Which indicator in daily field records best supports later QA review of biodiversity survey effort?

options.text: Only total number of species recorded each day.
A single summary sentence stating that 'sufficient effort was applied'.
Start and end times of survey effort, transect lengths, weather conditions, observer names and methods used for each recording session.
Photographs of the team at work with no metadata.

questions.prompt: You plan to use contractors for remote fauna trapping. What WHS and quality assurance requirement must be included in pre-engagement checks?

options.text: Hire the cheapest contractors to reduce project costs.
Assume contractors follow best practice and only review their output later.
Allow contractors to use their own unvetted equipment for convenience.
Verify contractor licences and insurance, check their trapping protocols align with project SOPs, ensure they have first aid and rescue plans, and document induction completion.

questions.prompt: Which action best mitigates the risk of data loss when using field tablets in remote locations?

options.text: Use tablets with offline-capable data-entry apps, enable automatic backups to encrypted external drives or staggered cloud syncs when connectivity is available, and carry spare batteries.
Trust the tablet battery and save data locally until end of trip.
Rely solely on paper datasheets and no digital copies.
Have one team member be solely responsible for all data backups mentally without documentation.

questions.prompt: A senior ecologist requests that you deviate from the field safety plan to finish a survey before a forecast storm. What is the correct response as an early-career staff member?

options.text: Comply immediately because the senior ecologist is responsible for the project.
Express concerns, refer to the documented safety plan and risk assessment, suggest postponement or additional controls, and escalate to the safety officer if necessary.
Ignore the senior and continue as planned.
Secretly alter the safety plan later without informing anyone.

questions.prompt: Which field protocol best supports both WHS and ecological ethics when collecting specimens in a remote area?

options.text: Collect as many specimens as possible to ensure identification accuracy without recording provenance.
Collect only when convenient and disregard permits if the need is urgent.
Collect only the minimum specimens required, use non-destructive methods where possible, record precise location and collection details, and secure permits before collection.
Allow each team member to collect specimens based on personal judgement.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate way to record an adverse weather forecast that forces survey cancellation in your project records?

options.text: Note 'cancelled due to weather' without additional details.
Do not record the cancellation to avoid appearing unproductive.
Only communicate cancellation verbally to the client.
Attach the forecast screenshot, note the cancellation decision, time/date, authorising person, planned mitigation and reschedule options in the project file.

questions.prompt: Which control is important for managing fatigue during multi-day remote surveys involving early starts and long drives?

options.text: Implement driving rostering limits, provide adequate rest breaks, limit consecutive early starts, and include accommodation planning to reduce cumulative fatigue.
Encourage team members to drink strong coffee and continue working.
Allow drivers to decide alone when they are too tired to continue.
Plan longer field days with fewer breaks to finish faster.

questions.prompt: You find a discrepancy between field GPS waypoint and handwritten plot location notes. What is the best immediate step to resolve it for data integrity?

options.text: Choose the GPS waypoint as ground truth without further checks.
Revisit the plot if safe to do so, cross-check GPS device, compare with photos and other metadata, and record the resolution method in the field log.
Discard both records and estimate the location mentally later.
Ask a colleague to pick one record at random to avoid delays.

questions.prompt: Which training or competence evidence should be required before allowing staff to conduct remote baited camera deployment alone?

options.text: A verbal assurance from the staff member that they have experience.
A client’s approval only.
Documented competency evidence: training records on camera deployment, bait handling, bait legal/ethical considerations, first aid, and documented field induction for the specific site.
No formal evidence; permit them to learn on the job.

questions.prompt: Which post-field documentation best supports escalation and corrective action after repeated near-miss reports on steep terrain?

options.text: A brief email acknowledging the near-misses with no follow-up.
Only informal verbal discussion at the next team social event.
A single anonymous note in the file with no details.
Consolidated incident and near-miss reports, root-cause analysis, recommended control changes, timelines for implementation, and assignment of responsibility for corrective actions.

questions.prompt: During a pre-field briefing for a vegetation survey in areas with known invasive plant species, what is the most appropriate hygiene step to include for staff entering each survey site?

options.text: Clean footwear and equipment with a boot brush and disinfectant at each site boundary before entry.
Wear disposable coveralls and change them only at the end of the day after visiting multiple sites.
Rinse boots with water from the nearest creek to remove soil before entering the site.
Leave vehicles running to prevent mud from drying on tyres while driving between sites.

questions.prompt: You discover fresh soil on a GPS unit brought from a previous property survey. What is the most appropriate immediate action to manage biosecurity risk?

options.text: Record the contamination and continue using the unit, noting the previous site in the project log.
Stop using the GPS unit, clean soil off with a brush and approved disinfectant, then log the incident and continue once dry.
Wipe the GPS unit with a cloth and carry on to avoid delaying the survey schedule.
Leave the unit in a sealed bag and use alternate devices without informing the supervisor.

questions.prompt: A client requests that ecology staff enter a property after recent livestock movement and a heavy rainfall event. What planning action best reduces biosecurity and environmental duty risks before entry?

options.text: Proceed with the planned survey immediately to meet the client timeline despite conditions.
Advise staff to wear normal PPE and rely on cleaning later at the field station.
Request recent property biosecurity reports and consult with the client about current ground conditions and any recent pest detections before scheduling entry.
Send only senior staff to minimise footprint, without adjusting protocols.

questions.prompt: Which record is most important to document immediately after completing field work where biosecurity procedures were used?

options.text: A brief note in a personal notebook that boots were cleaned at some point during the day.
An email to the client summarising findings without hygiene details.
A photo of cleaned boots saved on a team member’s phone.
A standard field hygiene log recording time, location, personnel, procedures performed, disinfectant product and dilution, and any contamination incidents.

questions.prompt: While surveying threatened fauna habitat, an ecologist finds a dieback-like fungal symptom on trees. What technical judgement should they make first?

options.text: Avoid disturbing the area, photograph symptoms, record GPS location, isolate tools and footwear hygiene, and escalate to a specialist for confirmation before sample collection.
Collect samples immediately and transport them in the same bag as soil samples to the lab.
Fence the area with flagging tape to prevent access and leave a note for landowners.
Spray visible symptoms with a fungicide from the vehicle to prevent spread.

questions.prompt: A field crew must move between two properties, one with identified weed infestations and one believed to be weed-free. What sequencing and hygiene practice best minimises cross-contamination risk?

options.text: Visit the weed-infested property first, then drive directly to the weed-free property and clean on arrival.
Schedule the weed-free property visit first and perform boot and equipment cleaning with disinfectant before entering the infested property only.
Visit the weed-free property first, then the known-infested property, and clean gear before returning to the weed-free property later in the day.
Avoid any cleaning to save time, assuming the vehicle prevents transfer.

questions.prompt: Which data record is most appropriate to support future audits regarding environmental duties after a field program with potential biosecurity hazards?

options.text: Daily task checklists listing only species observations with no hygiene entries.
An informal staff group chat summarising the day’s work.
Comprehensive field reports including hygiene logs, incident reports, photographic evidence, and chain-of-custody for any samples collected.
A single end-of-project summary stating that protocols were followed.

questions.prompt: During an induction, a new technician is unsure about the correct dilution for the field disinfectant. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Estimate the concentration based on label memory and proceed.
Ask a colleague to prepare it later without documenting the dilution.
Use undiluted disinfectant to ensure effectiveness.
Refer to the product label and the project biosecurity procedure, prepare the correct dilution, and document it in the field log.

questions.prompt: You need to collect soil samples for pathogen testing in a sensitive native remnant. Which handling approach best manages biosecurity and environmental duty risks?

options.text: Use clean, labelled sterile sampling tools for each sample, place samples into individual sealed bags, and record chain-of-custody and cleaning of non-disposable equipment.
Use the same spade at all sample points to save cleaning time, placing samples into a single container.
Collect samples directly into the vehicle boot to protect them during transit.
Leave sampling bags open to air-dry on-site before sealing.

questions.prompt: A landowner reports seeing a suspicious invertebrate on site that might be an exotic pest. What communication and escalation step should the ecologist take?

options.text: Ignore the report because identification is uncertain and continue the survey.

Collect clear photographs, record the location, isolate any specimens without contamination, notify the project lead and the appropriate biosecurity authority or specialist as required by the project procedure.
Tell the landowner to capture more specimens and hold them in their fridge until further notice.
Apply pesticides around the sighting area immediately to eradicate any possible pest.

questions.prompt: Which quality assurance check should be performed before starting a field day in an area with known aquatic weeds?

options.text: Ensure all team members can swim in case of water entry.
Pack extra food in case the day runs long.
Confirm boat and waders are cleaned, decontaminant stocked, and signage for cleaning stations are available and functioning.
Check weather forecasts only and assume equipment hygiene is adequate.

questions.prompt: On review of field records, you notice a discrepancy between the hygiene log and the times staff reported being on-site. What is the appropriate quality assurance action?

options.text: Delete the hygiene entries to match staff times for a tidy record.
Ignore the discrepancy since the project lead probably knows the truth.
Add a generic note stating ‘procedures followed’ without further detail.
Contact the field team to clarify timings, request corrected entries or explanations, and document any corrections and reasons in an audit trail.

questions.prompt: An ecologist must decide whether to enter a wetland area known to have a quarantine disease that spreads via mud on tyres. What risk-based technical judgement is best?

options.text: Avoid driving into the wetland, park at a designated clean parking area, and walk in using cleaned footwear or designated boardwalks to minimise tyre-mediated spread.
Drive into the wetland on low tyre pressure to reduce soil compaction.
Cross the wetland quickly to reduce time of exposure.
Ask the landowner’s permission and proceed without additional hygiene measures.

questions.prompt: Which communication method is most effective for ensuring subcontractors understand project-specific biosecurity requirements prior to fieldwork?

options.text: Send a long PDF of procedures and assume subcontractors read it.
Hold a mandatory pre-start meeting to go through key biosecurity tasks, provide a succinct checklist, and require confirmation of understanding and commitment in writing.
Rely on the client to brief subcontractors on your behalf.
Brief only the lead subcontractor and expect them to tell the rest.

questions.prompt: During a post-survey review, a team member reports they forgot to disinfect a soil auger between two sites. What review and corrective action is most appropriate?

options.text: Ignore the report to avoid paperwork.
Fire the team member immediately without further investigation.
Record the lapse in the incident log, assess potential cross-contamination impact, consult with a specialist if needed, and update procedures or training to prevent recurrence.
Clean the auger after returning to base and delete the incident from records.

questions.prompt: A contractor proposes using a high-pressure hose to clean vehicles between sites. What technical and environmental consideration should you advise?

options.text: Approve immediately because high-pressure washing removes all contaminants.
Suggest washing only in natural waterways to dilute contaminants.
Recommend using petrol or solvents to quickly clean tyres.

Advise that high-pressure washing can spread pathogens via runoff; recommend containment, proper waste capture and disposal, and use of approved disinfectants following cleaning rather than indiscriminate hosing.

questions.prompt: Which field evidence is most important to collect when documenting a suspected biosecurity incident affecting native vegetation?

options.text: High-resolution photos with scale, GPS coordinates, date/time stamps, brief description of symptoms, and notes of nearby human or vehicle activity.
A single distant-wide photo of the site without scale or location details.
A hand-drawn sketch made later from memory.
An eyewitness account without physical or photographic evidence.

questions.prompt: You must choose PPE for staff undertaking weed control that involves herbicide application near a creek. Which choice balances worker safety and environmental duty?

options.text: Provide only gloves and a disposable mask since the application is brief.

Use chemical-resistant gloves, splash-resistant eyewear, appropriate respirators if required by product label, and measures to prevent drift into water such as low-pressure application and buffer zones.
No PPE is needed because the herbicide is low-toxicity.
Require full body suits and respirators for all staff regardless of label instructions.

questions.prompt: Which planning document should be consulted first when determining site hygiene stations for a multi-day field program across several land tenures?

options.text: Local newspaper reports about weather.
Individual staff preferences for station locations.
The project’s biosecurity management plan and site-specific risk assessments.
A generic national checklist with no project tailoring.

questions.prompt: During a rapid response to a suspected pest plant, which chain-of-custody action is most important for physical specimens removed for identification?

options.text: Place specimens in unlabelled containers and deliver them at your convenience.
Leave specimens at the roadside for the lab to collect later.
Send specimens in multiple people’s backpacks without documentation to speed transport.
Label each specimen with unique ID, date, location, collector name, preserve appropriately, document transfer steps, and retain records of who handled the specimen.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist notices a senior staff member repeatedly skipping boot-cleaning between sites to save time. What is the appropriate escalation action?

options.text: Privately raise the concern with the project lead or safety officer, document the observation in the field log, and suggest a refresher briefing on hygiene procedures.
Confront the senior staff member aggressively on site.
Follow the senior staff member’s approach to avoid conflict.
Post about it on social media to embarrass them into compliance.

questions.prompt: Which method best verifies that a disinfectant procedure used in the field was effective against a target pathogen when lab confirmation is pending?

options.text: Assume effectiveness because the product was used.
Follow manufacturer contact times and dilution, ensure physical cleaning preceded disinfection, document procedures, and consult specialists or lab protocols for interim guidance.
Double the dilution to be safe without following instructions.
Rely solely on visual cleanliness as proof of disinfection.

questions.prompt: When planning sampling in culturally sensitive areas with biosecurity concerns, what is the appropriate approach to fulfil environmental duties and respect stakeholders?

options.text: Proceed with sampling without consultation to avoid delays.
Ask local contractors to handle it without involving traditional owners.
Engage native title holders or land custodians early, explain biosecurity measures, obtain consent for procedures, and incorporate their advice into hygiene planning.
Limit communication to a single email describing actions after the fieldwork.

questions.prompt: You must design an evidence trail for managing weed hygiene across multiple teams. Which element is most essential to include?

options.text: Verbal confirmations during morning briefings without recording.
A spreadsheet stored only on one person’s laptop with no backups.
A single paper note per week summarising activities.
A centralised digital log with time-stamped entries for each cleaning event, personnel involved, product used and photographic evidence of cleaned equipment.

questions.prompt: During an operational review, you find that disinfectant stockouts have occurred repeatedly. What risk management measure best addresses this recurring supply issue?

options.text: Implement minimum stock levels, assign responsibility for stock monitoring, identify alternative approved products, and include supply checks in pre-field QA.
Reduce cleaning frequency to conserve supplies until the next delivery.
Ask staff to share personal disinfectants from their vehicles.
Ignore the issue because suppliers will restock eventually.

questions.prompt: Which monitoring indicator is most useful to evaluate field hygiene compliance over a project?

options.text: Number of coffee breaks taken per team.
Proportion of field entries with completed hygiene logs, verified photos, and no recorded cross-contamination incidents.
Total kilometres driven during the project.
Average time spent on species identification tasks.

questions.prompt: A contractor offers a faster chemical for on-site decontamination that is not listed in your project biosecurity plan. What is the correct procedural judgement?

options.text: Use the chemical immediately to save time, and update the plan later.
Refuse any change and cancel the fieldwork.
Evaluate the product’s label, safety data sheet and efficacy for target organisms, consult the project lead and update procedures only if approved and documented prior to use.
Let the contractor use it on isolated equipment without informing the team.

questions.prompt: You observe sediment-laden water discharge from a vehicle wash area adjacent to a protected stream. What immediate action aligns with environmental duties?

options.text: Continue washing because vehicles must be clean.
Divert the flow into the stream to dilute contaminants.
Finish washing quickly and hope the impact is minor.
Stop washing immediately, contain runoff if possible, prevent further discharge into the stream, record the event, and arrange for appropriate remediation and disposal.

questions.prompt: Which training assessment is most appropriate to confirm competence in biosecurity hygiene for early career ecological field staff?

options.text: A combined approach of classroom instruction, practical demonstrations of cleaning and disinfection procedures, a supervised field assessment, and documented competency sign-off.
A one-hour online video with no assessment.
Relying on previous unrelated field experience without formal assessment.
Providing a single-page checklist and asking staff to self-declare competence.

questions.prompt: While preparing a methodological section for a survey report, how should you present biosecurity measures to support environmental duty transparency?

options.text: Omit hygiene steps because they are operational details.
Include a clear section describing hygiene protocols used, dates and locations of cleaning stations, disinfectant products and dilutions, and any incidents and mitigations.
Only mention that ‘standard hygiene was followed’ without specifics.
Provide a separate confidential file only available on request.

questions.prompt: An ecologist is designing a protocol for handling equipment after working in a declared biosecurity outbreak area. Which disposal or decontamination option is most appropriate?

options.text: Store contaminated gear with clean gear to save space.
Burn all equipment on-site to ensure sterilisation.
Segregate contaminated equipment, follow approved decontamination or disposal guidance, log actions taken, and consult the managing authority for any controlled wastes.
Send contaminated equipment home with staff for them to clean.

questions.prompt: Which risk control best addresses the hazard of seed transfer on clothing during multi-site terrestrial surveys?

options.text: Instruct staff to shake off visible seeds at the end of the day.
Require staff to wear only dark-coloured clothing to hide seeds.
Advise staff to remain in the field until all sites are completed to minimise clothing changes.
Use disposable or launderable outerwear between sites, perform on-site brushing and vacuuming of clothing at hygiene stations, and inspect garments before entry to new sites.

questions.prompt: You are asked to verify that field evidence collection followed biosecurity procedures before laboratory analysis. What verification step is most defensible?

options.text: Review the chain-of-custody documentation, hygiene logs, photographic evidence of cleaning, and interviewer notes to confirm procedures were followed prior to lab acceptance.
Trust verbal assurances from the collector without reviewing records.
Ask the lab to proceed and inform them to be cautious.
Discard specimens if any doubt exists without further inquiry.

questions.prompt: Which measure best minimises environmental impacts when establishing a temporary field hygiene station in a conservation area?

options.text: Install permanent concrete wash bays for convenience.
Use temporary, elevated platforms or matting to avoid soil disturbance, contain wash water in bunded trays for removal, and place stations on previously disturbed ground where possible.
Wash equipment directly on the ground to speed up operations.
Use chemical dispersants to neutralise wash water on-site.

questions.prompt: When reporting a non-compliance event where a team failed to implement buffer zones near a sensitive habitat, what should the report prioritise?

options.text: Minimising details to protect staff reputations.
Shifting responsibility to external factors like weather.
A factual account of what occurred, evaluation of ecological risk, immediate mitigation measures taken, notification of affected stakeholders, and actions to prevent recurrence.
Only reporting the event if an external auditor asks.

questions.prompt: An ecological consultant must choose between single-use disposable sampling gloves and reusable nitrile gloves laundered between sites. Which selection better meets biosecurity and environmental duties?

options.text: Always use single-use gloves to ensure cleanliness regardless of waste generation.
Use no gloves to reduce waste.
Allow staff to choose based on personal preference.
Select reusable gloves if they can be reliably decontaminated between sites and laundering is managed to avoid cross-contamination; otherwise use disposables with proper waste management.

questions.prompt: Which element is most critical when determining whether to postpone fieldwork due to elevated biosecurity risk indicators (e.g. recent pest detection, wet conditions)?

options.text: A documented risk assessment weighing the likelihood of spread, potential ecological impacts, availability of mitigation measures, and stakeholder consultation before deciding to proceed or postpone.
Whether the team is eager to complete the task.
Only the client’s deadline pressures.
Assumption that quick work reduces risk and therefore proceed.

questions.prompt: A field team must transport potentially contaminated gear across public roads. What control best balances public safety and environmental compliance?

options.text: Load gear uncovered to save time.
Contain gear in sealed, labelled containers or tarpaulins, segregate contaminated items from general cargo, and display appropriate warning labels if required by procedure.
Leave contaminated gear unsecured in the back of an open tray.
Ask the public to avoid the area rather than securing gear.

questions.prompt: Which review practice most effectively identifies systemic weaknesses in biosecurity hygiene across multiple projects?

options.text: Relying on isolated incident reports without aggregation.
Assuming current procedures are adequate if no one complains.
Conducting periodic cross-project audits that analyse incident trends, compliance records, training gaps, and supply chain issues, and then updating policies and training accordingly.
Only reviewing projects when a regulator requests documentation.

questions.prompt: How should an ecology consulting team demonstrate due diligence for biosecurity when providing advice to a client about rehabilitation planting materials?

options.text: Recommend any locally available seeds without verification to save time.
Require the client to source materials themselves and absolve the team of responsibility.
Suggest collecting seed on-site regardless of potential contamination.
Advise using certified seed or propagation material, verify provenance and any quarantine status, document checks undertaken, and recommend quarantine or testing if provenance is uncertain.

title: Ecological Data Management and File QA

questions.prompt: You receive field data sheets from a contractor surveying vegetation plots. Several sheets have illegible handwriting for species codes and some GPS coordinates are missing. What is the best immediate action to ensure data integrity before entering data into the master database?

options.text: Contact the field crew to clarify species codes and request corrected GPS coordinates or metadata about locations.
Enter legible parts and flag the ambiguous entries as 'uncertain' for later review.
Discard sheets with missing coordinates and proceed with the rest of the dataset to avoid delays.
Assign new location IDs based on plot order and interpret species codes using the most common species list for the area.

questions.prompt: During QA you notice that a night's acoustic bat recordings are timestamped in UTC but your database expects local time. What should you do before performing temporal analyses?

options.text: Leave timestamps as recorded and note the timezone mismatch in the methods section of analyses.
Convert the timestamps from UTC to local time consistently, documenting the conversion method and any daylight-saving adjustments.
Randomly shift timestamps within the same night to approximate local times and avoid systematic bias.
Delete the timestamps and use night-number identifiers instead to simplify analyses.

questions.prompt: A dataset includes species abundance values where a few plots have negative numbers due to a data-entry error. What is the most appropriate QA step?

options.text: Replace negative values with zero, assuming no individuals were recorded.
Remove the entire plots from analysis to avoid dealing with erroneous values.
Flag those records and check original field notes or photographic evidence to confirm correct values before correcting the database.
Convert negative values to absolute values to retain data magnitude.

questions.prompt: A colleague hands you a CSV with species names that mix scientific names, common names and abbreviations. For consistent data management, what is the best immediate practice?

options.text: Convert all names to common names to be more accessible to stakeholders.
Leave the mixed names as-is and use them during analyses, relying on manual interpretation when needed.
Replace all names with species codes generated from spreadsheet row numbers.
Standardise names to the organisation's authority list or a recognised taxonomy, keeping the original name column as raw input.

questions.prompt: Your project requires storing sensitive locations for a threatened species. Which file-management practice best balances security with usability for the team?

options.text: Keep sensitive locations in a separate, encrypted file with access logs and document the process for authorised requests.
Store sensitive coordinates in the main project database but restrict read permissions to only senior staff.
Omit location coordinates entirely from project deliverables to avoid any risk.
Publish approximate coordinates publicly and keep precise coordinates on an external hard drive without backups.

questions.prompt: While merging two datasets, you find duplicate plot IDs that represent different physical locations. How should you resolve this before finalising the merged dataset?

options.text: Keep the IDs as-is and add a note explaining duplicates exist.
Create unique composite identifiers by combining original ID and site code, and retain original IDs in a separate column for provenance.
Overwrite one set of records with the other to remove duplicates.
Delete records from the dataset with fewer fields to reduce complexity.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist asks how long to retain raw field images and audio files after project completion. What is the appropriate advice consistent with good data management?

options.text: Retain raw media indefinitely, storing them on local hard drives only as they are large files.
Delete raw files after extracting results to save storage space, keeping only summary data.

Follow your organisation's records retention policy; if none exists, retain raw data for a defined period (e.g., minimum project archiving timeframe) and document storage location and access controls.
Compress and resample media to lower quality to reduce file sizes and then delete originals.

questions.prompt: You are preparing a deliverable dataset for a client who requests CSV and spatial shapefiles. Which metadata practice is essential before handing over files?

options.text: Only provide the files and give an oral explanation in the project handover meeting.
Embed minimal metadata within the file names to keep the dataset tidy.
Assume the client knows the conventions and omit metadata to speed delivery.
Include a README describing column meanings, units, coordinate reference system, and version/date of the dataset.

questions.prompt: During data import you discover inconsistent date formats (e.g., DD/MM/YYYY and MM/DD/YYYY) within a single column. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Standardise all dates to an agreed ISO format (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD) after verifying ambiguous entries against field notes.
Leave dates as-is and rely on analysts to interpret them contextually.
Convert all dates to text strings to avoid misinterpretation during calculations.
Remove all dates from records that show mixed formats to avoid contamination.

questions.prompt: A quality-review finds that several records lack the observer's name. For regulatory audits you need traceability. What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Leave the observer field blank and add a project-level comment about anonymous observers.
Attempt to recover observer information from field rosters, time sheets or GPS logger metadata, and document any records where observer cannot be confirmed.
Assign a generic observer name (e.g., 'FieldTeam') to all missing entries.
Remove records without observer names from the dataset used for regulatory reporting.

questions.prompt: You notice a spatial layer has an undefined coordinate reference system (CRS). Which step should you take before overlaying it with other layers?

options.text: Assume the layer uses the same CRS as the other project layers and proceed with overlays.
Reproject the layer to a common CRS without documenting the assumed source CRS.
Contact the data provider to confirm CRS; if unavailable, inspect metadata, original software exports, or sample coordinates to infer and test likely CRS before assigning.
Convert coordinates to lat/long by treating values as decimal degrees regardless of units.

questions.prompt: A biodiversity database contains a field 'SampleType' with inconsistent values like 'Soil', 'soil sample', 'SMP', and blanks. For database standardisation, what is the most defensible step?

options.text: Replace all entries with a single term 'Sample' to avoid ambiguity.
Leave values unchanged to preserve original field terminology.
Delete rows with blanks to ensure every record has a SampleType.
Create a controlled vocabulary for SampleType and map existing values to it, keeping original entries in a raw_input column.

questions.prompt: You are asked to create a backup schedule for active ecological monitoring data. Which schedule best balances risk and operational practicality?

options.text: Full backups weekly with daily incremental backups, stored offsite and tested quarterly for restorability.
Only manual backups taken before major analyses to save storage and avoid redundancy.
Automated hourly full backups stored on the same server for quick access.
No backups during field season to prevent accidental overwrites, then one full backup at season end.

questions.prompt: A contractor uses different species coding conventions than your organisation. For QA of an integrated dataset, what should you do?

options.text: Overwrite contractor codes with your organisation's codes without keeping a mapping record.
Develop and apply a documented crosswalk mapping contractor codes to the organisation's standard codes and retain both code columns for traceability.
Remove all species codes and rely on common names to merge datasets.
Accept contractor codes as authoritative to avoid extra work.

questions.prompt: You discover that a large telemetry dataset contains several improbable location jumps likely due to GPS errors. What QA filtering approach is most appropriate before analysis?

options.text: Automatically remove all points with high displacement jumps without inspection to clean the dataset quickly.
Interpolate positions between all points to smooth the track, removing jumps by averaging.
Apply speed and plausibility filters (e.g., maximum movement per time) to flag suspect points, then inspect flagged segments and consult field notes or device logs before removing or correcting data.
Keep all raw points and conduct analyses that ignore movement metrics to avoid bias.

questions.prompt: A reviewer requests the original raw data files to verify an analysis but you used derived datasets. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Provide only the derived datasets used in the analysis to avoid sharing large raw files.
Refuse to share raw data citing confidentiality without offering alternatives.
Send screenshots of raw files as evidence rather than full datasets.
Provide access to raw files via the data repository or controlled file transfer, with documentation showing how derived datasets were produced from raw files.

questions.prompt: While reviewing spreadsheets you find formulas embedded directly next to raw field values rather than in a separate processing script. For long-term QA, what is the best practice?

options.text: Extract all processing formulas into documented scripts with version control and convert spreadsheet cells to values linked to those scripts.
Leave formulas in-place and add comments describing them in the spreadsheet.
Convert formulas to values immediately to avoid accidental changes.
Hide all formula columns so casual users cannot modify them.

questions.prompt: A dataset includes abundance estimates with different methods annotated (e.g., visual count, capture-recapture, acoustic index). For combining data, what is the most defensible approach?

options.text: Pool all abundance values without adjustment but note method differences in the report.
Standardise or model method-specific biases where possible, keep method metadata intact, and avoid naïve pooling unless methods are comparable.
Exclude all but the most common method to ensure consistency.
Convert all methods to ranks (e.g., low/medium/high) to harmonise data.

questions.prompt: You are preparing to archive project data. Which documentation is essential to include with the archive?

options.text: Only final cleaned datasets and the final report to save space.
Only raw data since cleaning can be redone later if needed.
Raw data, cleaned datasets, metadata, data processing scripts, version history, and data access procedures or restrictions.
A single PDF summarising methods with no data files.

questions.prompt: You detect that two team members have different assumptions about units for soil moisture (percentage vs volumetric fraction) in an active dataset. What's the correct immediate step?

options.text: Assume percentage and convert all values accordingly without consulting the team.
Keep both units in the dataset and let analysts choose which to use.
Drop the soil moisture variable to avoid confusion.
Pause analyses that depend on soil moisture, review metadata and field protocols to confirm units, standardise units across the dataset, and document the conversion.

questions.prompt: A field surveyor reports that a batch of camera traps failed to record during part of the deployment. What data-management record should you update immediately?

options.text: Update deployment metadata to record device downtime, timestamps of failure, serial numbers affected, and any remedial actions taken.
Leave camera deployment table unchanged and note failure in a separate email thread.
Remove the camera trap entries from the dataset to avoid incomplete records.
Estimate missing detections based on nearby cameras and fill the data gaps.

questions.prompt: You must combine species observation records from multiple consultants with differing certainty codes (e.g., confirmed, probable, possible). How should you manage these certainty levels in the integrated dataset?

options.text: Ignore certainty codes and treat all observations equally for simplicity.
Standardise certainty categories to a common scheme, retain original certainty codes in a separate field, and document how categories map across consultants.
Downgrade all observations to 'possible' to be conservative.
Delete records marked as 'possible' to avoid uncertain data.

questions.prompt: A regulatory reviewer asks for evidence that your bird survey timing met daylight constraints. What record best supports your claim?

options.text: A summary statement in the methods section saying surveys were done at appropriate times.
An email from the project manager confirming schedule adherence.
Time-stamped field logs or GPS trackfiles from surveyors showing start and end times for each survey with local time specified.
Aerial photos of the site taken on survey days without timestamps.

questions.prompt: While QA'ing taxonomic identifications, you find several specimens identified to genus only but photos exist that could allow species-level ID. What is the proper QA workflow?

options.text: Update identifications to species based solely on photos without expert validation.
Leave identifications at genus level to avoid potential misidentification.
Delete photo files to avoid confusion and keep the genus-level record.
Flag specimens for expert review, attach photo evidence and original determinations, and record any changes with justification and reviewer name.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet contains hidden rows and columns; QA must ensure no data are obscured. What is the recommended action?

options.text: Unhide all rows and columns, inspect them for data or formulas, and document any hidden content that influenced calculations.
Trust the visible sheet and proceed with QA on visible data only.
Delete hidden rows and columns to simplify the sheet before QA.
Copy visible cells into a new sheet and ignore hidden content.

questions.prompt: You are drafting data-sharing terms for a dataset that includes Aboriginal cultural knowledge locations. What is the appropriate course of action for data handling and sharing?
