options.text: Share the dataset widely with minimal restrictions but remove explicit place names.
Engage with the relevant Traditional Owners/representatives to determine culturally appropriate access arrangements and document agreed restrictions in the metadata and access protocols.
Refuse any sharing of the dataset to avoid potential breaches.
Encrypt the dataset and provide the decryption key only to the project manager.

questions.prompt: A dataset's column labeled 'presence' contains integers 0,1 and some blanks. For automated modelling pipelines, what data-cleaning step is most appropriate?

options.text: Convert blanks to 1 to maximise presence records.
Remove rows with blanks in 'presence' to ensure models run without NA values.
Investigate and fill blanks by cross-checking field forms; convert the column to a binary boolean with documented handling of uncertain or missing values.
Treat blanks as a separate category 'unknown' and assign them a numeric value like 2.

questions.prompt: You need to review a contractor's data pipeline that automatically imports and processes camera-trap images. What QA focus is most important during review?

options.text: Check that images are compressed to save storage before processing.
Ensure the pipeline deletes raw images immediately after processing to maintain a tidy system.
Confirm that only high-resolution images are processed to improve species ID accuracy.
Verify reproducibility by reviewing code/scripts, confirming version control, checking error-handling for failed uploads, and ensuring metadata (timestamps, device IDs) are correctly parsed.

questions.prompt: A colleague recommends normalising elevation values from different DEM sources by subtracting a global mean to harmonise datasets. What is the correct QA judgement?

options.text: Assess differences among DEM sources, test for systematic bias, document vertical datum and resolution differences, and apply a documented correction only if justified.
Apply the suggested subtraction as a simple harmonisation step without further checks.
Discard the lower-resolution DEM to avoid harmonisation problems.
Convert all elevations to relative ranks to avoid datum issues.

questions.prompt: You are training new staff on naming conventions. Which rule is most essential to include for ecological data files?

options.text: Use long descriptive file names that include full project narratives to be self-explanatory.
Adopt concise, consistent names including project code, data type, date (YYYYMMDD), and version number, and document the convention in a README.
Name files only by date to keep file lists sorted chronologically.
Use team members' initials in file names to indicate authorship.

questions.prompt: A senior ecologist asks whether to include QA flags in the main dataset or in a separate QA log. What is the best practice for downstream users?

options.text: Keep QA flags only in a separate QA log to avoid cluttering datasets.
Do not include QA flags; instead correct data silently to present clean data.
Include QA flags as fields within the main dataset and maintain a detailed external QA log describing each flag and corrective actions.
Add QA flags as comments in spreadsheet cells so they are visible but not part of the data table.

questions.prompt: You identify a coding bug in a script that produced an influential result reported to a client. What is the immediate professional step?

options.text: Correct the bug silently and update subsequent reports without notifying stakeholders.
Ignore the bug if the client is unlikely to notice minor changes.
Blame the contractor who supplied the script and refuse responsibility.
Inform project management and the client of the error, provide corrected analysis with documented impact assessment, and update archived scripts with a versioned fix.

questions.prompt: A QA check shows a sudden drop in detection rates for a survey day across many sites. Which investigative step is most appropriate?

options.text: Investigate potential causes by checking weather logs, survey effort records, equipment logs, and observer notes to determine whether the drop reflects real change or an artefact.
Exclude that day's data from all analyses as anomalous.
Adjust detection rates upwards using the dataset average.
Replace the day’s data with values interpolated from surrounding days.

questions.prompt: You are compiling a metadata record and must specify the point of contact for data queries. What is the most appropriate selection?

options.text: List the project lead's personal email without providing an organisational backup.
Provide a designated data custodian's contact (role and email) plus a secondary organisational contact and hours of availability.
Provide a generic departmental inbox only, with no named individual.
Omit contact details and instruct users to consult published reports for questions.

questions.prompt: A third-party app used for species identification exports results in a proprietary binary format. For long-term accessibility, what should your data-management plan require?

options.text: Keep the proprietary files only and rely on the app for future access.
Convert proprietary files to PDF summaries to preserve content.
Export and store open-format outputs (e.g., CSV or JSON), retain original proprietary files, and document the software version and export procedures.
Delete proprietary files after exporting summary statistics to reduce storage.

questions.prompt: An external auditor requests logs showing who edited the master dataset. What is the correct data-governance response if you do not currently capture edit history?

options.text: Tell the auditor edit history is not recorded and provide the current dataset.
Fabricate an edit history to satisfy the auditor's request.
Refuse to provide any data until a full audit trail can be generated.
Acknowledge the gap, start capturing audit logs immediately, reconstruct edit history where possible from backups and emails, and document limitations in the response.

questions.prompt: You’re asked to QA georeferenced vegetation quadrats that show improbable clustering at exact coordinate values (e.g., many sites at X=0.000). What is the best explanation to explore and step to take?

options.text: Investigate whether default or truncated GPS values were used, check raw GPS logs or field forms, and correct coordinates where provenance supports it.
Assume aggregations represent true field hotspots and proceed without change.
Randomly jitter coordinates to spread points for visualisation.
Delete any points with coordinate values that repeat more than once to avoid clusters.

questions.prompt: A peer reviewer asks for the decision rules you used to filter out low-quality drone imagery from analyses. How should you present these rules?

options.text: Provide a brief verbal summary during a meeting.
Share a documented, version-controlled filtering protocol with explicit thresholds (e.g., blur, exposure, overlap), code used, and examples of included/excluded images.
Provide the excluded images only and let the reviewer infer rules.
State that exclusions were subjective and cannot be documented.

questions.prompt: You must escalate a suspected data breach where unauthorized access to a file containing species locations occurred. What is the correct escalation path in professional practice?

options.text: Silently restore from backups and notify only the IT department.
Postpone notification until you can confirm the full extent of the breach personally.
Immediately notify your line manager and organisation's data-security/IT incident response team, record the incident details, and follow any legal or organisational reporting requirements.
Publicly disclose the breach to stakeholders to preserve transparency before internal escalation.

questions.prompt: A deliverable requires a reproducible analysis workflow. Which of the following best meets reproducibility standards for an ecological data analysis?

options.text: Provide the final figures and a high-level description of methods used.
Provide only the processed data and a ZIP of the analysis software used locally.
Provide screenshots of code outputs and step-by-step manual instructions to reproduce results.
Provide raw and processed data, annotated scripts or notebooks with environment/package versions, and a README explaining how to run the workflow end-to-end.

questions.prompt: During a site walk for habitat assessment, you encounter a vegetation community that appears to grade gradually into another. What is the most appropriate immediate field action to characterise the boundary for later mapping?

options.text: Locate and record multiple GPS waypoints along the transition, take photographs at regular intervals and note dominant species and structural changes.
Draw a single line on the map where the visual change seems greatest and note species names observed.
Estimate the average width of the transition zone and assign the entire area to the closest dominant community type.
Mark only the start and end points of the transition and rely on aerial imagery later to define the boundary.

questions.prompt: You must assess habitat value for fauna in a remnant patch of native vegetation on private land. Which initial evidence gathering approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Conduct a single rapid flora survey and assume fauna value matches plant diversity.
Combine targeted flora and structural vegetation assessments with a short set of fauna detection methods (e.g., call playback, nocturnal spotlighting or camera deployment) appropriate to likely taxa.
Use only desktop records of threatened species occurrences from museum databases without field verification.
Interview the landowner for anecdotal observations and base assessment primarily on their recollections.

questions.prompt: While planning a vegetation community survey, you discover the client expects species-level lists but timeframe and budget only allow a rapid assessment. What is the correct action to manage expectations?

options.text: Proceed with the rapid assessment and deliver a species list that may be incomplete without informing the client of limitations.
Refuse to proceed unless the client agrees to the full species-level survey regardless of time and budget.
Advise the client that a rapid assessment will provide community-level descriptions and a prioritized list of likely additional surveys, and propose a staged approach with costs.
Estimate species by extrapolating from nearby conserved areas and provide those as if surveyed on site.

questions.prompt: During a plot-based vegetation survey you record species cover estimates. Which practice best reduces observer bias in cover estimates across multiple observers?

options.text: Allow each observer to use their preferred method and average their estimates afterwards.
Assign the most experienced observer to estimate cover and others to only record species presence.
Use verbal descriptions of abundance rather than quantitative classes to keep it simple.
Provide a standardised cover class chart and train observers on applying classes in a calibration exercise before fieldwork.

questions.prompt: You find an unusual plant that you suspect is a threatened species while conducting vegetation community mapping. What is the immediate professional action?

options.text: Document location with GPS, take high-quality photos of diagnostic features, collect minimal material only if permitted, and flag the finding in the field notes for verification and escalation following project protocol.
Collect a specimen without permission to confirm identification later.
Ignore the find since identification is uncertain and continue mapping community boundaries.
Move the plant to a more accessible area for better photographs and specimen collection.

questions.prompt: For ecological vegetation community mapping, you must choose sampling locations. Which strategy most appropriately captures community heterogeneity?

options.text: Place all plots near the access point to save time and still represent the site.
Use a stratified-random approach across identifiable community units, disturbance gradients and topographic variation to place plots.
Place plots at equal distances on a grid ignoring visible community boundaries.
Place plots only in areas with the highest conservation value to demonstrate best-condition vegetation.

questions.prompt: You are preparing the methods section of a habitat assessment report. Which description best supports reproducibility and QA for vegetation community mapping?

options.text: We surveyed the vegetation thoroughly and mapped communities based on field judgement.
We visually estimated communities and created maps from memory after fieldwork.

We conducted plot-based surveys using 10 m x 10 m quadrats across stratified units; recorded species, cover classes, GPS coordinates (±3 m), photos, and followed the project QA checklist for data entry and taxonomic validation.
We collected data as needed; consultees can contact us for further details.

questions.prompt: While entering field data into the project database you notice several species names with uncertain spelling. What is the correct immediate course of action under quality assurance?

options.text: Enter the names exactly as written in the field notes and correct them later during report writing.
Replace uncertain names with common names to avoid spelling issues.
Delete ambiguous entries to avoid introducing errors into the dataset.
Cross-check uncertain names against a current botanical authority (e.g., national or state flora), flag entries requiring verification, and record the source used for taxonomic authority.

questions.prompt: During a vegetation community assessment, you must decide whether to map a small 20 m by 10 m patch of intact native understory within a cleared paddock. What is the most defensible mapping decision for habitat assessments?

options.text: Map the patch as a discrete vegetation community and document its size, condition and connectivity rationale for inclusion.
Exclude the patch because it is too small to matter for regional mapping.
Merge the patch with the surrounding cleared paddock on the map to simplify outputs.
Ignore the patch in the field notes but photograph it for later reference.

questions.prompt: You are assessing a riparian vegetation community and need to evaluate habitat connectivity for terrestrial fauna. Which evidence-based metric is most appropriate to record in the field?

options.text: Record only the length of the stream because water presence alone indicates connectivity.
Estimate the linear distance of contiguous vegetation to the nearest remnant and record structural continuity (e.g., canopy cover, understorey continuity) and barriers (e.g., roads, fences).
Document connectivity solely by asking local stakeholders about animal movement.
Assume good connectivity if the riparian vegetation appears relatively dense at the sample point.

questions.prompt: You detect evidence of feral predators in a high-value vegetation community. What is the appropriate risk evaluation step to include in your report?

options.text: List feral predators as a general concern without linking to habitat features.
Recommend immediate eradication without consultation given the potential threat.
Describe observed signs, map locations, assess likely impacts on fauna using literature and local context, and recommend targeted management or follow-up monitoring.
Omit mention to avoid alarming the client and focus on native species only.

questions.prompt: A botanist on your team suggests aggregating two mapped vegetation communities because they share several species. What technical judgement best supports whether to aggregate?

options.text: Combine them because any species overlap justifies a single map unit.
Keep them separate regardless of similarity to maximise map complexity.
Decide by which community appears more extensive and label the whole area accordingly.

Compare structural characteristics, ecological function, dominant species, soil, hydrology and management relevance; aggregate only if these aspects align and the distinction is not important for assessment objectives.

questions.prompt: During nocturnal fauna surveys adjacent to mapped vegetation communities you obtain camera images of a species typically using dense understorey. What is the appropriate way to integrate this finding into your vegetation habitat assessment?

options.text: Document the species occurrence with camera metadata, spatially link the detection to the mapped community, and discuss how understorey structure likely provides habitat and any implications for management.
Add a generic note that fauna were observed near the survey area without linking to vegetation features.
Exclude nocturnal detections from vegetation-based reports as they relate to fauna only.
Assume the species uses other areas and do not alter habitat value ratings.

questions.prompt: You must produce an accuracy statement for your vegetation community map. Which content is essential to include?

options.text: A general claim that the map is accurate without supporting data.
Description of mapping methods, source data and dates, GPS accuracy, minimum mapping unit, known limitations and an estimate of positional and thematic uncertainty.
Only the mapping scale and a disclaimer that users should be cautious.
A statement that the map supersedes any previous maps in the region.

questions.prompt: A client requests you to use a different vegetation classification system than your team usually uses. How should you respond professionally?

options.text: Refuse and insist on using the team's preferred system without discussion.
Agree without checking and apply the new system regardless of compatibility.
Evaluate the requested system's compatibility with project objectives, advise on implications for continuity and reporting, and offer to map to both systems if feasible within scope.
Apply a hybrid of both systems without documenting the translation method.

questions.prompt: You find ground-truthing results differ substantially from remote-sensed vegetation classes. What is the correct QA step?

options.text: Override the field data with remote sensing if the imagery looks consistent overall.
Discard the remote-sensing dataset and rely solely on field observations.
Assume misclassification is due to temporary seasonal differences and ignore the mismatch.
Investigate discrepancies by reviewing field notes, revisit key sites if needed, assess imagery dates and processing, and document reconciliation methods for the final map.

questions.prompt: While conducting a vegetation community assessment in wet conditions, you must record soil saturation levels. Which approach gives the most reliable field evidence for hydric conditions?

options.text: Record water table observations (e.g., surface water, saturation within the root zone), soil colour, redoximorphic features, and recent flooding indicators at each plot.
Note that the ground feels wet without further detail.
Rely on local rainfall reports to infer soil saturation.
Only record hydric vegetation species presence and infer soils from that.

questions.prompt: You are preparing to assess vegetation communities on Aboriginal land where access requires cultural protocols. What is the best planning action?

options.text: Enter without notifying Traditional Owners since the assessment is scientific.
Engage early with the right local Indigenous contacts to obtain permissions, understand any culturally sensitive areas, and incorporate their knowledge into planning and field methods.
Rely on the landowner's real-estate agent for permission and skip cultural engagement.
Only seek permission on the day of fieldwork to avoid delays.

questions.prompt: You must rank vegetation community condition for a report. Which set of metrics is most appropriate to include for defensible condition scoring?

options.text: Only plant species richness and a subjective overall score.
Only canopy height and leaf area index measurements.
Native species richness, exotic species cover, recruitment of natives, structural integrity, extent of disturbance (e.g., grazing, weeds, clearing) and representative benchmarks for the community.
Photographs alone to represent condition without quantitative metrics.

questions.prompt: In the field you find a small wetland within a mapped vegetation community that was not on client-provided maps. For regulatory or habitat assessments, what is the appropriate immediate documentation?

options.text: Ignore it because it was not on the client's maps.
Assume it is ephemeral and note nothing further.
Estimate its size by pacing and describe it qualitatively without coordinates.
Record its GPS location, extent, hydrological indicators, vegetation composition, photograph it, and flag it for verification against regulatory definitions with recommended follow-up if needed.

questions.prompt: You are training an early-career colleague on assigning vegetation community labels. Which training emphasis will best reduce future misclassification?

options.text: Provide field decision rules linking diagnostic species, structure, soil and hydrology, practice with example sites and review their labels against an expert during initial surveys.
Tell them to prioritise familiar species when labelling communities even if structure differs.
Advise them to defer all decisions to the senior ecologist without attempting to classify.
Encourage creative labelling to capture nuance without standard references.

questions.prompt: Your survey encountered mapped private property where the owner denied access mid-survey. What is the correct next step regarding vegetation community mapping for that parcel?

options.text: Proceed to enter the property anyway to finish mapping.

Cease surveying the parcel, document access denial with time/date and attempts made, use remote data and adjacent field data to infer communities, and clearly note limitations and uncertainty in the report.
Exclude the parcel entirely from the report without mention.
Estimate communities based on memory from a distance without documenting access denial.

questions.prompt: When assessing vegetation communities, how should you treat historically cleared areas undergoing natural regeneration in terms of map units?

options.text: Label them as intact native community immediately because seedlings are present.
Treat them as cleared land until they reach mature canopy height regardless of species composition.
Classify them as regenerating or secondary succession, document vegetation structure, recruitment rates and management history, and map them with a distinct label reflecting successional stage.
Ignore successional areas because they are not relevant to habitat assessments.

questions.prompt: You need to decide whether to recommend targeted flora surveys for cryptic species reliant on particular vegetation communities. What drives the decision most appropriately?

options.text: Recommend surveys only if the community has the highest cover score.
Never recommend additional surveys to avoid costs to the client.
Recommend surveys for all cryptic species regardless of likelihood to be present.
Base the decision on habitat suitability indicators (presence of diagnostic microhabitats and host plants), known range and timing for detectability, and potential impact of proposed works.

questions.prompt: During mapping you must choose a minimum mapping unit (MMU). Which rationale best justifies the chosen MMU for vegetation communities?

options.text: Select an MMU based on project objectives, scale of heterogeneity observed, positional accuracy of base data, and management usefulness, and document this choice and limitations.
Choose the largest MMU possible to simplify the map without discussing implications.
Use an arbitrary MMU of 1 hectare because it is round.
Match the MMU of an unrelated previous project regardless of site conditions.

questions.prompt: A junior assessor reports high weed cover in a mapped community but did not note the weed species. What quality assurance instruction should you give?

options.text: Accept the observation as ‘weedy’ without further detail since cover is more important.
Request the assessor return to identify dominant weed species, or provide photographs and GPS points for identification, because species identity informs management priorities.
Delete the entry since it lacks species names.
Estimate likely weed species based on general regional knowledge and record those names.

questions.prompt: You are asked to produce a map legend for vegetation communities. Which element is most important to include for end-users assessing habitat values?

options.text: Only community names with no description to keep the legend concise.
Colours only, assuming users will refer to the report text for details.
Community names, brief descriptions of dominant species and structure, mapping confidence level, and MMU to help users interpret habitat value.
A detailed botanical key in the legend for field identification.

questions.prompt: During stakeholder consultation, a local volunteer group claims a mapped vegetation community used to support a rare bird historically but not recently. How should you incorporate this information into your habitat assessment?

options.text: Discard anecdotal historical reports as unreliable.
Assume the species is present and adjust habitat value upwards without further evidence.
Note the claim but state it is irrelevant to the current assessment.

Record the historical observations with dates and source, consider their implications for habitat restoration potential, and recommend targeted surveys or archival record checks to verify current status.

questions.prompt: You detect soil compaction and rabbit warrens affecting understorey within a mapped community. Which management-focused recommendation is most appropriate in the report?

options.text: Recommend specific management actions: targeted rabbit control, soil decompaction where feasible, and monitoring of understorey recruitment, with suggested priorities based on habitat importance.
Do nothing; natural processes will recover the understorey.
Recommend complete exclusion of the area from public access without further actions.
Advise replacement of understorey with exotic grasses to stabilise soil.

questions.prompt: When producing final vegetation community maps, what is the correct process for handling third-party spatial data layers supplied by the client?

options.text: Integrate them without checking provenance since the client provided them.
Assess the provenance, currency, projection and accuracy of third-party layers, document how they were used or modified, and clearly state limitations in the map metadata.
Discard third-party layers and recreate everything from scratch to avoid liability.
Merge them into the final map and remove any attribution to protect client confidentiality.

questions.prompt: A proposed development overlaps multiple vegetation communities with varying quality. Which approach to cumulative habitat impact assessment is most appropriate?

options.text: Assess impact based only on the highest-quality community present.
Assume impacts are minor since the area is small and do not quantify.
Quantify area and condition of each community affected, evaluate functional connectivity losses, species-specific habitat requirements, and aggregate impacts to describe cumulative effects.
Only consider impacts to communities listed as threatened in state documents.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether to collect voucher specimens for difficult-to-identify grasses in a mapped community. What is the correct practice?

options.text: Never collect plant material under any circumstances.
Collect abundant material to ensure identification even if it impacts local populations.
Skip collection and rely solely on photographs for identification of grasses.
Collect minimal voucher specimens following permits and ethical guidelines, label them precisely with GPS and habitat data, and submit to a recognised herbarium for identification and archiving.

questions.prompt: While reviewing a peer’s vegetation community map, you find classification labels inconsistent with the agreed project taxonomy. How should you proceed?

options.text: Discuss the inconsistencies with the peer, reference the agreed taxonomy, request corrections or a clear justification for deviations, and document the review outcome.
Approve the map to avoid conflict and let the client decide.
Replace labels unilaterally without informing the peer to speed up delivery.
Reject the entire map and ask for a complete redo.

questions.prompt: Your field team identifies multiple small patches of a community that collectively form an important corridor but individually fall below the MMU. How should you reflect this in the report and map?

options.text: Omit them because each patch is below the MMU.
Map them as sub-MMU features or annotate their presence and connectivity value in the report, and consider composite mapping for corridor assessment while noting MMU constraints.
Combine them artificially into a single large patch on the map ignoring intervening cleared areas.
Represent them only in text without any spatial reference.

questions.prompt: A landowner asks for management advice to enhance habitat values of a degraded vegetation community. Which initial recommendation is most appropriate from you as the assessor?

options.text: Provide a detailed multi-year restoration plan including budgets without further site-specific analysis.
Recommend immediate planting of exotic fast-growing species to bulk up vegetation cover.

Offer prioritized, practical short-term actions based on observed threats (e.g., weed control, fencing to exclude grazing, enhancement planting of local provenance species) and recommend a follow-up site-specific restoration plan.
Advise waiting several years to see if natural regeneration occurs before any action.

questions.prompt: You are estimating habitat suitability for a small mammal that requires dense groundcover. Which field data will most directly inform your suitability rating?

options.text: Canopy height only.
Distance to the nearest town as a proxy for disturbance.
Number of bird species recorded at the site.
Groundcover percent, understorey structure, leaf litter depth, and presence of refugia (e.g., logs, rock crevices) measured at sample plots.

questions.prompt: Which communication approach is best when reporting uncertain vegetation community boundaries due to seasonal phenology differences?

options.text: Explain the seasonality-related uncertainty, provide dates of fieldwork, suggest the likely extent of variation, and recommend timing for additional surveys to reduce uncertainty.
Present the boundaries as definitive and omit mention of seasonality.
Delay the report indefinitely until boundaries are definitively known.
Provide multiple contrasting boundary maps without narrative to let the client decide.

questions.prompt: A regulatory officer requests verification of your mapped vegetation community that might meet a statutory definition. You lack authority-specific thresholds. What is the appropriate professional response?

options.text: State that the community meets the statutory definition without checking details.

Provide the measured evidence (species composition, structure, extent, hydrology), specify that you have not applied authority-specific legal thresholds, and recommend that the officer or a specialist verify the fit to statutory criteria or that you can perform that verification if provided with the exact thresholds.
Refuse to provide any data until the officer confirms legal thresholds.
Tell the officer the community does not meet any statutory definitions to avoid regulatory complications.

questions.prompt: During a peer review of vegetation survey data you find inconsistent GPS accuracies across plots. Which corrective action aligns with good data quality practice?

options.text: Ignore the inconsistencies because the general locations are sufficient.
Replace all GPS coordinates with site centroid coordinates to standardise.
Document the varying accuracies, evaluate whether positional errors affect mapping or interpretation, revisit critical plots if necessary, and include GPS accuracy metadata in the dataset.
Delete coordinates for plots with low accuracy to avoid confusion.

questions.prompt: You must finalise recommendations for monitoring vegetation community condition after proposed works. Which monitoring design element is most critical to detect change reliably?

options.text: Only take random photos annually without fixed points.
Monitor only once immediately after works and assume future status.
Rely on anecdotal reports from site staff to assess condition over time.

Establish fixed monitoring plots with standardised methods, representative of different community conditions and controls, include clear metrics and sampling frequency tied to expected response times.

title: Targeted Survey Planning and Effort Design

questions.prompt: You are planning a targeted nocturnal survey for a threatened microbat species known to forage along riparian corridors on a development site. Weather forecasts predict light rain and 10–15 km/h winds on survey nights. What is the best planning action to maximise survey value?

options.text: Reschedule surveys to nights with no rain and winds below 5 km/h, and document the rationale for changing dates.
Proceed with night surveys as scheduled because microbats continue to forage in light rain and wind is moderate.
Replace field surveys with additional automated sound recorders deployed for two weeks regardless of weather.
Carry out a single-night survey during the forecast conditions and supplement with daytime habitat assessment only.

questions.prompt: A client asks you to design targeted surveys for a ground-dwelling reptile that shelters under fallen logs. The proposed development area is large but resources are limited. Which sampling approach best balances coverage and effort?

options.text: Search every fallen log across the entire development area once during a single season.
Stratify the site by habitat type, randomly select representative plots in each stratum, and conduct repeated timed searches of logs in those plots.
Focus only on areas closest to the proposed construction footprint because developer impacts are concentrated there.
Place artificial cover boards only in areas with the most logs and leave other areas unsurveyed.

questions.prompt: While designing effort for a targeted aquatic invertebrate survey, you need to justify the number of replicate samples. What is the most defensible way to determine replicates?

options.text: Select a fixed number of five replicates because it's commonly used in ecological studies.
Use one replicate per site to maximise the number of sites sampled.
Base replicates on a pilot study to estimate within-site variance and use power analysis to meet detection or comparison objectives.
Decide replicates by budget limits and accept lower statistical power.

questions.prompt: You must plan surveys for a cryptic ground bird whose detectability peaks at dawn. The client wants daytime habitat assessments only to save costs. What is the appropriate professional response?

options.text: Agree to daytime assessments and note that detection probability may be lower in the report.
Suggest using remote cameras placed during the day as a full replacement for dawn surveys.
Recommend conducting a literature review instead of field surveys to infer presence.
Explain that targeted dawn surveys are required to meet objectives and offer a costed option for dawn detection surveys with justification.

questions.prompt: During planning you identify an introduced predator that could affect survey detection of small marsupials. How should this risk influence survey effort design?

options.text: Increase survey duration and trap replicates in areas where predator activity is high to offset reduced detectability, and record predator signs as covariates.
Ignore the predator because it is part of the current ecosystem and surveys should reflect present conditions.
Avoid surveying areas with predators to prevent biased low detection results.
Conduct surveys only after predator control has been implemented by the client.

questions.prompt: You plan to use automated acoustic loggers for a cryptic frog species. What key metadata should you include in the survey design to ensure data usability?

options.text: Logger make and model only, since recording capability is standard across devices.
Deployment location coordinates, start/stop times, sampling schedule, microphone orientation, and calibration details.
Only the number of loggers deployed per night because spatial coverage is the main concern.
Photographs of logger locations without timestamps because visual context is sufficient.

questions.prompt: A threatened plant flowers irregularly; detectability is highest during bloom. The client demands a single fixed-date survey next month. What is the most appropriate technical judgement?

options.text: Proceed with the single fixed-date survey and assume absence if not detected.
Replace field surveys with remote imagery to capture flowering regardless of timing.
Advise that multiple surveys timed to phenology and environmental cues are necessary, propose flexible-survey windows, and outline contingency triggers for follow-up.
Delay all work indefinitely until the plant is guaranteed to bloom.

questions.prompt: You're designing surveys for a nocturnal mammal and must decide how many survey nights per site. Which rationale is most defensible?

options.text: Use a single night per site because logistical constraints and even one detection is sufficient.
Survey every night available until the species is detected once at each site.
Rely on historical records rather than multiple survey nights to infer presence.
Schedule multiple nights per site, spaced across different lunar phases and weather conditions to capture temporal variability in activity.

questions.prompt: You find existing records from a community database showing a target frog species 3 km from the study area from ten years ago. How should this influence targeted survey planning?

options.text: Treat the record as supporting context, verify currency and habitat continuity, and include additional survey effort near potential habitat corridors.
Assume presence across the landscape and reduce survey effort accordingly.
Ignore community records because they are not professionally verified.
Only use those records to avoid surveying areas where the species was found historically.

questions.prompt: A targeted survey protocol requires observers to be 'experienced with species detection' but no formal training is specified. How should you operationalise observer selection and QA?

options.text: Hire any available field staff and assume experience is sufficient.
Specify minimum field experience, require training or calibration sessions, document observer IDs, and implement field QA checks like paired surveys.
Only hire senior ecologists regardless of cost to meet the requirement.
Use remote methods exclusively to avoid observer variability issues.

questions.prompt: The survey brief requests detection of an endangered bat roost. Access restrictions mean you cannot inspect some culverts. What's the most appropriate next step when planning effort?

options.text: Exclude inaccessible culverts and proceed with accessible locations only.
Assume inaccessible culverts are unsuitable and reduce survey effort accordingly.
Document access limitations, propose alternative methods such as endoscope inspections where safe and permitted, and escalate access needs to the client.
Delay the entire survey until all access issues are resolved by the client.

questions.prompt: You're designing effort to estimate occupancy of a woodland bird using call-playback. What is a key ethical and methodological consideration to include in your plan?

options.text: Use call-playback continuously for long periods to maximise detections.
Only use call-playback in high-quality habitat because disturbance elsewhere is unwarranted.
Avoid call-playback entirely because it always disturbs birds.
Limit call-playback duration and frequency to minimise disturbance, justify the protocol, and record playback timing as metadata.

questions.prompt: A proposed survey timing conflicts with breeding season restrictions from a local land manager. How should you integrate this constraint into your survey effort design?

options.text: Adjust survey windows to comply with land manager conditions, identify alternative methods outside the restricted period, and document the constraints and adaptations.
Ignore the restriction and proceed because detection during breeding season is important.
Request the land manager lift restrictions without providing alternative options.
Cancel survey planning because compliance is impossible.

questions.prompt: You must provide an evidence standard for presence/absence in your survey report. Which approach best supports a defensible conclusion?

options.text: Declare absence if the species is not observed during one site visit.
State presence if detected and for absence quantify effort, detection probability assumptions, and any limitations affecting inference.
Avoid making any presence/absence statements and only describe observations.
Use historical records to assert presence regardless of current survey results.

questions.prompt: During pilot surveys you observe strong fine-scale variation in microhabitat features that affect detectability. How should this influence your sampling design?

options.text: Ignore fine-scale variation and keep a coarse-scale sampling grid to maintain logistics.
Only sample the most common microhabitat to standardise detection.
Incorporate microhabitat stratification into sampling units or include microhabitat as covariates in analysis to account for detectability differences.
Increase sample size uniformly across the site without accounting for microhabitat.

questions.prompt: A landowner requests immediate results after a single day of targeted surveys for a small mammal. Which communication approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Give definitive absence statements based on that single day to satisfy the landowner.
Decline to communicate anything until the final report is delivered.
Send raw field notes without interpretation to avoid responsibility for conclusions.
Provide provisional observations but explain that formal results require synthesis of multi-night effort and QA checks, and outline the expected report timeline.

questions.prompt: You are choosing detection methods for a secretive arboreal mammal. Which combination best supports both detection and minimises disturbance?

options.text: Combine remote camera traps at canopy access points, acoustic recorders for calls, and targeted daytime habitat assessment of likely den trees, with disturbance-minimising protocols.
Use only intensive daytime ladder inspections of all trees in the site.
Set live traps in the canopy to capture individuals for identification.
Rely solely on community-reported sightings collected via social media.

questions.prompt: When designing targeted surveys you must estimate detectability to inform effort. What is a practical way to obtain detectability estimates when none exist for your site?

options.text: Assume perfect detectability to simplify analysis.
Run a short pilot study with repeated surveys to estimate detection probability and use those estimates to scale full survey effort.
Borrow detectability estimates from a different region with different habitat.
Ignore detectability and increase sample sites arbitrarily.

questions.prompt: Your survey design proposes the use of spotlighting along transects for nocturnal frogs. Which quality assurance step should you include to ensure data consistency between observers?

options.text: Allow observers to choose their own spotlight brightness and search pace.
Only assign the most junior staff to spotlighting and check results later.
Conduct a calibration session where observers survey the same transect together, compare detections, and agree standardised search protocols and pace.
Rotate observers randomly without standardisation to average out differences.

questions.prompt: A neighbouring property has recent records of a target species that likely moves across boundaries. How should this inform site selection for targeted surveys?

options.text: Ignore neighbouring records because your survey is confined to the development site.
Only survey deep interior areas of the site since edge habitat is irrelevant.
Assume species occurs site-wide and avoid rigorous sampling.
Prioritise survey effort along likely movement corridors and boundary-adjacent habitats to detect potential transients and inform impact assessment.

questions.prompt: You're designing a survey for a wetland-dependent bird outside its known breeding season. Which effort decision best supports detection while respecting seasonal behaviour?

options.text: Plan surveys to focus on non-breeding season behaviours like roosting and foraging, using appropriate methods and temporal windows tailored to those behaviours.
Conduct intensive breeding-season surveys regardless of timing because detectability is always highest then.
Skip surveys because outside breeding season detection is not useful.
Use playback of breeding calls to attract birds outside the season.

questions.prompt: A targeted survey protocol requires voucher specimens for identification, but the species is protected. What is the correct course of action in planning?

options.text: Collect voucher specimens regardless of protection status to confirm identification.
Use non-lethal alternatives such as high-resolution photographs, DNA swabs if permitted, or expert confirmation, and escalate permit needs to the client if specimen collection is necessary.
Refuse to proceed with surveys if vouchers cannot be collected.
Assume field identifications are sufficient without documentation.

questions.prompt: You need to specify spatial sampling resolution for a reptile survey over a heterogeneous landscape. What is an appropriate justification for your chosen grid spacing?

options.text: Use the finest grid spacing possible irrespective of time or resource constraints.
Adopt a generic 100 m grid because it is a common default.
Base grid spacing on species home range size, habitat patchiness, and logistical constraints, and justify how chosen spacing meets survey objectives.
Use random placement with no consideration of spatial scale because randomness removes bias.

questions.prompt: During design you discover a small area of high-quality habitat that you cannot cover with equal effort across all sites. How should you allocate effort?

options.text: Allocate equal effort per site regardless of habitat quality.
Exclude the high-quality patch to preserve even sampling.
Split effort proportionally by landowner preference rather than habitat value.
Prioritise higher effort in the high-quality habitat area and explicitly document the rationale and implications for inference across the wider site.

questions.prompt: A technician reports an unexpected nocturnal species detection during a daytime-only targeted bird survey. How should this be handled in your data records and planning?

options.text: Record the detection with full metadata, assess its relevance, and consider adjusting future survey methods to include nocturnal effort if warranted.
Ignore the record because it falls outside the survey method and timeframe.
Delete the entry to avoid complicating the dataset.
Flag the record as unreliable without further investigation.

questions.prompt: You must design repeatability checks for morphological identifications of similar frog species in the field. Which QA step is most appropriate?

options.text: Rely entirely on a single experienced observer's identifications without verification.
Collect photos or audio of each individual, have a second expert verify a subset, and document any disagreements and resolution methods.
Only identify to genus level in the field to avoid misidentification.
Use field keys but make no provision for independent verification.

questions.prompt: Your planned survey relies on volunteers to increase transect coverage. What management measure should you include in effort design?

options.text: Assign volunteers without training to maximise coverage quickly.
Use volunteers only for data entry after surveys are completed.
Provide training, pair volunteers with experienced staff, limit tasks to low-risk activities, and include supervision checks to ensure data quality.
Allow volunteers to design their own survey routes to encourage ownership.

questions.prompt: A client requests that you minimise survey duration by reducing replicate counts. How should you respond in your plan?

options.text: Accept the client's instruction and reduce replicates without comment.
Refuse to adjust and insist on full replicates regardless of budget.
Conceal the reduced effort in the final report to avoid client concern.
Provide an impact assessment showing how reduced replicates affect detection probability and offer alternative strategies to meet objectives within constraints.

questions.prompt: You need to document uncertainty in your targeted survey design. Which statement best describes an appropriate treatment of uncertainty in the design documents?

options.text: Explicitly list key uncertainties (e.g., weather windows, detectability), describe how they influence results, and outline contingency measures or adaptive approaches.
Ignore uncertainty and present the design as certain to reassure stakeholders.
State that uncertainty cannot be quantified and therefore is not discussed.
Replace quantitative targets with qualitative statements to avoid dealing with uncertainty.

questions.prompt: During planning you must decide whether to use daytime visual encounter surveys or night spotlighting for a crepuscular mammal. What decision criterion best aligns with targeted survey objectives?

options.text: Choose daytime surveys because day work is logistically easier.
Select methods informed by species activity periods and pilot data; if crepuscular peaks occur at dusk/dawn, schedule surveys then or include both methods to capture activity.
Run both methods equally regardless of species behaviour to be thorough.
Use daylight remote cameras only since they function 24/7.

questions.prompt: You prepare a targeted survey schedule requiring specific lunar phases. How should you manage scheduling risks related to lunar constraints?

options.text: Fix dates only to a single preferred lunar night and treat cancellations as unplanned delays.
Ignore lunar phase because its influence is negligible.
Build a schedule window that includes multiple acceptable lunar nights, identify backup dates, and record chosen lunar criteria in the protocol.
Schedule surveys across all lunar phases to guarantee coverage.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist proposes fewer but longer transects rather than many short transects for a dense shrubland survey. What is the most defensible evaluation of this proposal?

options.text: Accept longer transects because they reduce relocation time and increase detection.
Reject the proposal outright because it deviates from common practice.
Choose the option that minimises total walking distance regardless of detection considerations.

Assess species movement scales and detection decay along transects; if detectability declines with observer fatigue or habitat heterogeneity, a mix of shorter transects with adequate replicates may be preferable.

questions.prompt: You must design data recording forms for targeted reptile surveys. Which element is essential to ensure later quality assurance and analysis?

options.text: Include observer ID, start/finish times, GPS coordinates, microhabitat, detection method, and environmental conditions on each form.
Only record species names and counts to simplify fieldwork.
Use freehand notes with no standard fields and transcribe later.
Record only aggregate daily totals to reduce paperwork.

questions.prompt: A proposed survey uses baited camera traps which may alter animal behaviour. How should this potential bias be addressed in effort design and reporting?

options.text: Use baited cameras and omit discussion of behavioural bias because detection is the priority.
Evaluate bait effects in a pilot, consider unbaited controls, document bait type and deployment, and discuss how baiting may influence detections in the report.
Avoid camera traps entirely to remove any bias concerns.
Rotate bait types daily to minimise habituation without documenting changes.

questions.prompt: You need to escalate a planning issue: the proposed timing overlaps with indigenous cultural activities restricting access. What is the correct escalation action?

options.text: Proceed with scheduled surveys ignoring cultural activities.
Cancel the survey planning to avoid engagement complexities.
Raise the access conflict to the client and relevant stakeholders, seek guidance from the indigenous custodians, and adjust survey timing or methods in consultation with them.
Carry out surveys covertly during restrictions to avoid delays.

questions.prompt: Your project requires combining datasets from a previous consultant with different survey methods. How should you reconcile these for targeted survey conclusions?

options.text: Merge datasets without adjustment and treat them as equivalent.
Discard the older dataset because it does not match your methods.
Adjust your current methods to exactly match the old ones regardless of their suitability.
Assess methodological differences, quantify comparability where possible, use each dataset for context rather than direct comparison if methods differ substantially, and document limitations.

questions.prompt: You design surveys requiring repeated vegetation traverses that risk trampling rare orchids. How should survey effort mitigate this risk?

options.text: Design transects to avoid known orchid locations, use boardwalks or defined paths, limit foot traffic, and record any unavoidable impacts with mitigation measures.
Ignore trampling risk because surveys are brief.
Cancel vegetation surveys entirely to eliminate risk.
Allow unrestricted access but compensate with rehabilitation afterwards.

questions.prompt: A survey's statistical design relies on independence between sampling units, but field conditions create potential spatial autocorrelation. What planning change best addresses this?

options.text: Ignore autocorrelation because it is difficult to address in the field.
Modify sampling spacing to reduce autocorrelation, include spatial covariates in analysis, and document residual spatial dependence and implications.
Collect all samples clustered to simplify logistics.
Abandon statistical analysis and report raw counts only.

questions.prompt: You must present the survey effort plan to regulators who expect clear auditable records. Which element is essential to include in the submitted plan?

options.text: A verbal commitment that surveys will be adequate without written protocols.
Only a map showing planned transects with no supporting methodological detail.
A detailed field protocol specifying methods, number of replicates, timing windows, observer requirements, QA procedures, and contingency plans.
A summary statement that the team will follow best practice without specifics.

questions.prompt: After completing targeted surveys, you find unexpected detections that change impact risk. What is the correct escalation and next-step in your reporting?

options.text: Ignore the implications and finalise the report as originally scoped.
Delay informing stakeholders until after expensive analyses are completed to avoid alarm.
Remove the unexpected detections from the dataset to preserve original conclusions.
Inform the client and relevant authorities promptly, document the new findings and recommend additional targeted surveys or mitigation as appropriate.

title: GIS Requests Map QA and Spatial Interpretation

questions.prompt: You receive a GIS request from a project ecologist asking for a habitat suitability map for a listed vegetation community within a proposed development footprint. The request includes a shapefile of the footprint but no field data. What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Contact the project ecologist to clarify the objective, required spatial resolution, acceptable data sources, and intended use of the map.
Produce the habitat suitability map using existing regional vegetation extents and remotely sensed predictors, and flag assumptions in the metadata.
Schedule field surveys during the next available window and decline to produce any map until surveys are complete.
Use a national default habitat model and deliver it immediately to meet project timelines.

questions.prompt: While QA-checking a colleague’s landcover classification, you notice a cluster of pixels labelled ‘wetland’ over an area that aerial imagery shows as cleared agricultural paddocks. What is the best immediate QA action?

options.text: Accept the classification because the algorithm likely detected seasonal water that isn’t visible in the imagery.
Flag the anomaly, document the inconsistency, and ask the analyst to review the training data and recent imagery timestamps.
Manually reclassify the cluster to ‘agriculture’ without consulting the original analyst.
Remove the wetland label from the entire dataset to avoid further misclassification.

questions.prompt: A client requests a buffer map showing a 50 m setback from all mapped koala habitat polygons. The habitat layer is known to have positional uncertainty of up to 20 m. Which mapping approach best communicates spatial risk?

options.text: Create the 50 m buffer and add a note in the map legend that the habitat layer has positional uncertainty.
Increase the buffer to 70 m uniformly to account for uncertainty without additional explanation.
Generate a composite buffer that presents inner 30 m and outer 70 m bands representing the uncertainty envelope, and include metadata explaining assumptions.
Produce the 50 m buffer but also provide the raw habitat polygons without any buffering for the client to interpret.

questions.prompt: During spatial QA you find that a delivery includes mixed coordinate reference systems (CRS) — some layers in GDA2020 and others in an unknown projected CRS. What should you do before proceeding with spatial analyses?

options.text: Proceed using the majority CRS layers and ignore the few unknown ones since they are a small proportion of the dataset.
Convert everything to WGS84 geographic coordinates because it is universally understandable.
Deliver the raw files back to the requester and ask them to standardise CRSs before any work can be done.
Reproject all layers to a consistent, documented CRS (e.g., GDA2020 MGA zone) and verify alignment against control features.

questions.prompt: A spatial layer of threatened flora records has attribute fields for species name, survey date, and observer. You notice many records lack survey date. For map QA and evidence purposes, what is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Flag records missing dates, try to obtain the dates from the data provider, and if unavailable, clearly indicate the uncertainty in the dataset used for analysis.
Exclude all records lacking survey date from the dataset used for reporting without further enquiry.
Estimate dates based on surrounding records’ dates and document the estimations in metadata.
Assume missing dates are current and include them as present occurrences in the analysis.

questions.prompt: A junior mapper provides a species distribution map derived from presence points with no absence data. The project requires an impact assessment that quantifies habitat loss risk. What is the most defensible mapping advice?

options.text: Use the presence-only points to create a simple buffered zone around occurrences and state limitations clearly.
Recommend generating additional survey data for absences or using presence-only modelling methods with clear caveats and sensitivity testing.
Convert presence points into a presence-absence grid by randomly generating absences across the study area.
Interpolate a continuous distribution surface from the presence points using inverse distance weighting and proceed.

questions.prompt: While reviewing a map, you find a labelled ‘recorded habitat’ polygon that overlaps a proposed road alignment. The attribute table shows the polygon was digitised from a 2010 survey. What is the correct QA response?

options.text: Retain the polygon as current habitat because historical records are authoritative until proven otherwise.
Delete the polygon because it is likely outdated and not relevant to current planning.
Flag the polygon as historical, note the survey date in the map legend, and recommend current field verification before using it for impact decisions.
Automatically update the polygon using recent satellite imagery without documenting the change.

questions.prompt: You must deliver maps to a client who will use them to inform a biodiversity offset calculation. Which quality assurance element is least optional for this deliverable?

options.text: High-resolution printing of maps on glossy paper for presentation aesthetics.
Including a copyright watermark on all map layers to protect company IP.
A colourful hillshade background to make the maps visually appealing.
Clear metadata documenting data sources, dates, CRS, processing steps and known limitations.

questions.prompt: A spatial analyst used an automated rule to clip habitat polygons to a development boundary but notices thin sliver polygons remain along the edge. For map QA, what is the best corrective action?

options.text: Apply a topology rule to remove sliver polygons below a minimum area threshold and document the cleaning step.
Leave the slivers because they represent real edge habitat and altering them risks data loss.
Merge the slivers with adjacent polygons regardless of their attributes to remove them.
Re-run the clipping with a larger buffer around the development to force removal of slivers.

questions.prompt: An ecologist asks for a map showing likely movement corridors for a medium-sized mammal. You have telemetry points from five individuals collected over two seasons. What is the best mapping approach to address their request at this career stage?

options.text: Plot raw telemetry points only and label them as movement corridors since they indicate where animals were recorded.
Create kernel density estimates from the pooled telemetry points and overlay linear connectivity paths derived from least-cost analysis using known habitat preferences.
Generate straight-line connections between successive telemetry fixes and present them as definitive corridors.
Use a generic corridor template from another region and adapt it to the study area with no local data integration.

questions.prompt: You discover that two layers of the same feature (rock outcrops) were digitised by different analysts and have slightly different extents and attribute schemas. For a consolidated deliverable, what is the appropriate QA workflow?

options.text: Keep both layers separate in the deliverable to show all variations in digitisation.
Merge the layers into one without reviewing attributes to simplify the dataset.
Compare features, reconcile attribute schemas, standardise attributes, resolve geometric overlaps, and record decisions in metadata.
Discard the older layer and use only the most recent analyst’s layer as the authoritative source.

questions.prompt: An internal reviewer asks whether the map symbology adheres to accessibility standards for colour-blind stakeholders. What practical QA step should you take?

options.text: Ignore the concern because colour choice is an aesthetic issue not a QA matter.
Convert all maps to greyscale to avoid colour issues entirely.
Advise the stakeholder to view the map on different screens to ensure perceived colours are accurate.
Provide a version of the map with high-contrast and colour-blind safe palettes and include patterned fills for critical categories.

questions.prompt: While validating a remotely-sensed vegetation change layer, you notice an implausible sudden canopy gain in a utility easement unlikely to have regrown. Which data-check is most appropriate to determine if this is an artefact?

options.text: Compare the dates and sensors of input imagery, check for sensor differences or seasonal changes, and review recent field photos if available.
Assume the canopy gain is real because remote sensing detects vegetation dynamics better than field surveys.
Manually edit the change layer to remove the gain in the easement to match expected conditions.
Apply a smoothing filter across the whole study area to remove apparent abrupt changes.

questions.prompt: A contractor submits a fauna habitat suitability layer with no provenance for the environmental variables used in the model. For quality assurance, what should you request?

options.text: Accept the layer if the contractor is experienced and deliver without further verification.
Ask for complete documentation of input variables, data sources, processing steps, model parameters, and validation statistics.
Request only the raw input rasters so you can reproduce the modelling yourself later if needed.
Discard the layer and commission a new model from a different contractor.

questions.prompt: You are preparing maps for a statutory referral and must ensure no sensitive point locations (e.g., nesting sites) are exposed. Which is the best map-level mitigation?

options.text: Remove all sensitive point records from the spatial dataset before producing any maps.
Publish the exact locations only in low-resolution maps to reduce detail visibility.
Generalise and mask sensitive locations using coarser centroids or buffered areas and document the modification in metadata, while retaining original data in secure records.
Leave the locations intact but add a disclaimer that the map is for internal use only.

questions.prompt: A map showing proposed offsets uses a land tenure layer that appears out of date. You cannot verify the current tenure before the deliverable deadline. What is the most appropriate QA treatment?

options.text: Proceed and present the offsets as final, expecting tenure will not affect decision-making.
Remove the tenure layer entirely to avoid misleading stakeholders.
Make assumptions about likely tenure changes and update the layer accordingly without source verification.
Note the tenure layer’s date and potential for change in the map metadata and recommend tenure verification prior to implementation.

questions.prompt: You are asked to QA a habitat suitability model output that shows unexpectedly high suitability inside urban areas. What targeted check would best identify likely causes?

options.text: Inspect input covariates for urban areas (e.g., landcover, imperviousness), check for misclassified input layers or incorrect covariate weighting, and run sensitivity tests.
Assume the model is correct because urban records can occur near remnant patches.
Remove all urban cells from the model output to force realistic results.
Increase the threshold for suitability uniformly across the map to reduce urban suitability values.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder questions why a mapped buffer around a wetland uses Euclidean distance rather than hydrological connectivity. As the GIS QA reviewer, what is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Ignore the comment because Euclidean buffers are standard and simpler to produce.
Explain the rationale for the Euclidean buffer, assess whether hydrological connectivity would materially change outcomes, and recommend re-analysis if needed.
Replace the Euclidean buffer with a hydrologically-based buffer without further assessment because it is more ecologically realistic.
Advise the stakeholder that buffer methodology is outside the scope of GIS QA and refer them to the project manager.

questions.prompt: During QA you note that a spatial dataset contains duplicate records of fauna observations with identical coordinates but different observer names. What should you do?

options.text: Keep all duplicates because multiple observers increase confidence in the record.
Remove duplicates randomly to reduce dataset size.
Investigate differences, consolidate duplicates into a single record with combined provenance fields if confirmed duplicates, and retain originals in an archival table.
Merge duplicates by averaging observer names into a single field.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a quick map overlaying ecological constraints with zoning layers. You detect that the zoning layer has a known issue where a recent amendment isn’t included. What is the appropriate QA action?

options.text: Proceed with the outdated zoning layer and hope the amendment does not affect decisions.
Delay all mapping until the zoning amendment is verified even if it impacts project timelines.
Attempt to recreate the amendment by guessing its likely location based on other project documents.
Inform the client of the zoning layer’s currency issue, present the overlay with a clear caveat, and suggest verifying zoning before final decisions.

questions.prompt: You need to produce a map showing potential impacts on a migratory bird species during breeding season. The breeding season dates vary by region. How should you reflect temporal sensitivity in the spatial product?

options.text: Create maps for multiple breeding season windows reflecting regional variation, and include guidance on which window applies where in the metadata.
Use a single breeding season range from the literature without regional adjustment and label it as applicable everywhere.
Exclude temporal information and let stakeholders infer breeding season timing.
Select the longest possible breeding season to be conservative and apply it uniformly.

questions.prompt: A junior staff member used an automated landcover classification but did not produce an accuracy assessment. As the QA reviewer, what is the appropriate corrective instruction?

options.text: Accept the classification because automated methods are generally reliable.
Require an accuracy assessment using independent validation samples, report confusion matrix metrics, and assess whether accuracy meets project needs.
Suggest visual inspection only to confirm obvious classes and skip quantitative assessment.
Ask the junior staffer to rerun the classification with different parameters without conducting accuracy assessment.

questions.prompt: A consultant provides presence points for a rare plant species but omits uncertainty estimates in coordinates. For spatial interpretation, what is the correct QA step?

options.text: Assume coordinates are exact and use them directly in planning maps.
Exclude the records because uncertainty is unknown.
Add a standard positional uncertainty buffer (e.g., 10–50 m) determined by the survey method, document assumptions, and recommend field verification if needed.
Randomly jitter the points to simulate uncertainty without documenting the change.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing a GIS deliverable and find a processing script has hard-coded file paths to an analyst’s local drive. What QA action is necessary before distribution?

options.text: Leave the script as-is because it ran successfully on the analyst’s machine.
Replace the script with manual steps described in the map legend.
Delete the script to avoid exposing the analyst’s local paths.
Refactor the script to use relative paths or parameters, document dependencies, and include versioned input data in a shared repository.

questions.prompt: A map legend lists species names but uses different taxonomic synonyms across layers. For map QA and clarity, what is the best action?

options.text: Standardise to a current accepted taxonomic name across the deliverable, include synonyms in metadata, and cite the taxonomic authority used.
Leave synonyms as-is because different datasets may use different names.
Use common names only to avoid taxonomic confusion.
Remove species names from the legend entirely to avoid mislabelling.

questions.prompt: You must combine raster layers from different sensors for a change detection product. One sensor has nominal 3 m resolution and the other 1 m. For QA, how should you handle differing resolutions?

options.text: Resample the coarser 3 m raster to 1 m using nearest-neighbour to match resolutions without noting impacts.
Aggregate the 1 m raster to 3 m using an appropriate summary statistic, document resampling method and implications for change detection.
Keep both rasters at native resolution and conduct change detection ignoring scale mismatch.
Select only one sensor’s data and discard the other to avoid resolution issues.

questions.prompt: An external reviewer identifies a spatial overlap between a mapped endangered ecological community and a cleared paddock that is unlikely habitat. As the QA lead, what is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Defend the mapped community as correct since the source dataset is authoritative.
Erase the mapped community layer where it overlaps with cleared paddocks to avoid public confusion.
Investigate the source data and mapping methods, check recent imagery and field notes, and if necessary annotate the map to show possible misclassification pending verification.
Ignore the reviewer’s comment because external reviewers may not understand local conditions.

questions.prompt: You are asked to produce a derived layer of canopy cover percentage from LiDAR returns. The LiDAR provider reports points classified only as ground and non-ground with no vegetation classes. What is the best QA-informed approach to derive canopy cover?

options.text: Decline to produce canopy cover because vegetation classes are missing and cannot be inferred.
Apply a generic canopy percentage value based on region averages.
Use the non-ground returns directly as canopy cover percentages without processing.
Use ground and non-ground returns to estimate height above ground, classify vegetation height thresholds for canopy, and document assumptions and limitations.

questions.prompt: A client needs a simplified map for a community meeting; they ask to omit methodological caveats to keep the map understandable. What is the correct QA response?

options.text: Produce simplified map versions for the meeting but include a concise, non-technical caveat panel or handout explaining key limitations.
Remove all caveats to make the map as simple as possible for the public.
Refuse to produce any simplified maps without full technical metadata attached.
Provide the technical map only and advise the client to present it as-is.

questions.prompt: During final QA you detect that the scale bar on exported map PDFs does not update when users change map extent. How should you address this issue for reliable map products?

options.text: Instruct users to ignore the scale bar and refer to textual scale statements instead.
Fix the map export template to generate dynamic scale bars tied to map extent and include map scale in the metadata for assurance.
Remove the scale bar from all exports to avoid presenting incorrect information.
Add multiple scale bars for different common extents to cover potential use cases.

questions.prompt: You are QAing a dataset where polygon boundaries were digitised using low-resolution basemap imagery, producing imprecise boundaries. Which guidance should you give to the analyst for improving spatial accuracy?

options.text: Accept current polygons if they roughly represent features and focus on other datasets.
Slightly shrink polygon extents to mitigate overestimation risks without further sourcing imagery.
Refine digitisation using higher-resolution imagery, cross-reference cadastral or survey control where available, and note residual uncertainty in the metadata.
Convert polygons to centroids to avoid boundary issues.

questions.prompt: A mapping deliverable contains multiple map layers with inconsistent attribute field naming conventions. For QA and reproducibility, what action should you require?

options.text: Leave names as-is because field names are minor and do not affect visual outputs.
Remove attribute fields that are inconsistent to force uniformity.
Rename fields arbitrarily to shorter names for convenience without documentation.
Standardise attribute field names across layers using a documented data dictionary and maintain original fields in an archive table.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist requests a quick patch map overlaying species records and construction zones. You notice the species dataset includes records with datum 'unknown'. As QA reviewer, what is the correct course of action?

options.text: Pause the overlay, attempt to identify the datum from the provider or contextual metadata, and if unresolved, flag coordinate uncertainty before mapping.
Assume unknown datum is WGS84 and proceed with overlay to meet the quick request.
Apply a generic datum transformation to all unknown records to align them visually with the construction zones.
Exclude all records with unknown datum to avoid any positional errors.

questions.prompt: An automated QA report flags that 5% of polygons have no area attribute and cannot be used in calculations. What is the most appropriate remedial QA step?

options.text: Ignore the missing area attributes because 95% of data is complete.
Calculate and populate area attributes from geometry for those polygons, record the update in processing logs, and rerun dependent analyses.
Delete the polygons without area attributes to simplify the dataset.
Manually estimate areas for each polygon by eyeballing their extents and record approximate values.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder requests the raw GPS tracks from camera trap patrols to be included in public-facing materials. As part of QA and risk management, what should you do?

options.text: Provide the raw GPS tracks as requested to be fully transparent.
Refuse to provide any GPS data and state confidentiality concerns without further discussion.
Assess sensitivity of the tracks, remove or generalise sensitive portions (e.g., near known dens), and get client approval before public release.
Convert tracks into heatmaps that show intensity but still reflect exact locations.

questions.prompt: You are QAing an ESRI map package for delivery. One raster included is 5 GB and the package exceeds client file transfer limits. What is the appropriate QA strategy?

options.text: Remove the large raster without notifying the client to meet transfer limits.
Split the package into multiple emails and send sequentially without telling the client.
Convert the raster to a PNG image to reduce size, even if spatial attributes are lost.
Discuss alternatives with the client: provide a compressed or lower-resolution version, host the full raster on a secure server for download, and document what was changed.
