questions.prompt: An automated spatial overlay report shows a small percentage of habitat polygons intersecting with a heritage constraint layer. You know the heritage layer contains very coarse polygons. For interpretation, what is the best approach?

options.text: Assess the spatial resolution mismatch, review specific intersection locations with higher-resolution data or field checks, and qualify findings accordingly.
Treat the intersections as definitive and incorporate them into mitigation without further checks.
Remove the heritage layer from analysis because it is coarse and may produce false positives.
Increase habitat polygon sizes to ensure intersections are captured comprehensively.

questions.prompt: A map product includes a derived index layer that uses a threshold decided by the analyst with no justification. For QA, what should you request?

options.text: Accept the threshold because the analyst is experienced.
Request a justification for the threshold, evidence of sensitivity analysis, and alternative thresholded outputs if appropriate.
Apply a different threshold arbitrarily that seems more conservative.
Remove the thresholding from the deliverable and supply raw index values only.

questions.prompt: You observe that the map’s north arrow points slightly off true north because the map is in a projected coordinate system. The client requests true north orientation for field crews. What is the appropriate QA correction?

options.text: Leave the current north arrow and tell the client field crews will understand orientation issues.
Rotate the map until the north arrow aligns with true north without noting the change.
Add both grid north (projection) and true north indicators or convert the map to a projection that aligns with true north for the extent, and explain in the legend.
Remove the north arrow entirely to avoid confusion.

questions.prompt: A new starter asks how to escalate a suspected critical spatial error that could materially affect an environmental approval. What escalation path should you advise for this module?

options.text: Fix the error quietly and do not escalate to avoid alarm and delays.
Post the issue to the team chat and wait for someone to respond.
Contact the regulatory authority directly to inform them of the error before informing internal management.
Immediately notify the project manager and senior ecologist, provide documented evidence of the error and potential impacts, and suspend downstream deliverables until assessed.

title: Construction Ecology and Pre clearing Compliance

questions.prompt: You are planning a pre-clearance site inspection for a proposed road widening. Which action best ensures you meet statutory pre-clearance timing requirements when exact authority notification periods are unclear in the project briefs?

options.text: Contact the relevant regulatory authority to confirm required notice periods and obtain written confirmation before scheduling clearing activities.
Proceed with clearance if project timeline is tight, and document attempts to notify authorities later.
Assume a standard 48-hour notice period to all authorities and schedule works accordingly.
Ask the contractor to obtain any required approvals and rely on their confirmation verbally.

questions.prompt: During a vegetation assessment before clearing, you find an unrecorded hollow-bearing tree within the footprint. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Cut down the tree immediately to prevent potential safety risks to crews.
Mark the tree for avoidance and proceed with clearing elsewhere, documenting the finding in the report.
Continue inspections and note the hollow-bearing tree only in the final report without altering plans.
Consult the construction supervisor on-site for their opinion before documenting anything.

questions.prompt: A contractor asks you for a species-specific mitigation measure for a frog species potentially on site, but you lack species-level survey data. What is the best course of action?

options.text: State that no mitigation is necessary until species is confirmed by DNA analysis.
Advise delaying all works for six months to allow natural migration without surveys.
Recommend broad amphibian exclusion fencing and timing constraints while scheduling targeted surveys to confirm species presence.
Provide a mitigation plan for the most common local frog species without further surveys.

questions.prompt: While compiling pre-clearance records, you notice the contractor's daily clearing logs are missing start and end times. What should you do to ensure records meet compliance needs?

options.text: Accept the logs as-is because other details are present and file them.
Create estimated times yourself based on crew size and submit the amended logs.
Discard the logs and instruct the contractor to restart record-keeping next month.
Request corrected daily logs with accurate start and end times and attach an interim note explaining the discrepancy.

questions.prompt: You are supervising fauna spotter-catcher operations during pre-clearing and spot a protected bat roost being disturbed by workers. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Stop works in the immediate area, secure the site, and notify the project environmental manager and the licenced bat handler.
Tell workers to work more carefully and continue while you document the disturbance.
Relocate the bats yourself to speed up works, since you observed them flying out.
Complete the rest of your supervision tasks and report the disturbance at the end of the day.

questions.prompt: You need to decide where to place fauna exclusion fencing prior to clearing an area adjacent to wetlands. Which factor is most important to determine fence alignment?

options.text: The contractor’s desire to maintain machinery access routes through the wetland edge.
Topography and likely animal movement corridors identified during habitat assessment, to reduce animal entrapment and maintain connectivity.
Maximising cleared area to speed construction works.
Placing fencing in straight lines to simplify installation regardless of vegetation.

questions.prompt: A pre-clearing inspection identifies several individuals of a plant listed as threatened in the local council database, but not on-site records. How should you proceed with ecological risk assessment?

options.text: Assume the plants are not threatened since they are absent from recent on-site records and proceed with clearing.
Transplant the plants immediately to a nearby remnant vegetation patch without documentation.
Flag these individuals as potential listed species and escalate to a senior ecologist to verify conservation status and advise on avoidance or salvage options.
Ignore the council database and rely solely on your field identification.

questions.prompt: Your pre-clearance guideline requires photographic evidence of pre-clearing conditions. Which photographic protocol best supports later compliance audits?

options.text: Take a single wide-angle photo of the area before clearing without geotagging or timestamping.
Rely on contractor smartphone images taken sporadically during works with informal captions.
Photograph only any obviously large trees and ignore understorey and ground features.
Capture multiple geotagged, timestamped photos from consistent reference points showing microhabitats and key features including scale indicators and exclusion fence locations.

questions.prompt: A surveyor’s pre-clearing map shows nesting habitat within the clearing footprint but no nests were observed during your field check. How should you handle this discrepancy in your report?

options.text: Document both the map indication and your current field observations, recommend targeted nest searches and, if necessary, schedule a follow-up survey during appropriate seasonal windows.
Delete the surveyor’s note and state no nesting habitat was present to avoid confusion.
Assume the map is outdated and proceed with clearing based on your field check alone.
Record only the map’s indication and disregard your field observations as temporary.

questions.prompt: When preparing a pre-clearing checklist for contractors, which element most directly reduces risk of harming ground-dwelling fauna?

options.text: Require that all heavy machinery operate at maximum speed to finish early.
Include a requirement for hand-searching and habitat manipulation (e.g., gentle raking) in sensitive microhabitats immediately before mechanical clearing.
Mandate that only supervisors carry torches during nocturnal works.
Specify that contractors can skip pre-clearing checks on cooler days under 15°C.

questions.prompt: You observe that fauna handling during translocation is being done by unlicensed personnel. What is the correct compliance action?

options.text: Allow the activity to continue after a quick briefing since delays are costly.
Let the unlicensed personnel finish and submit a retrospective licence application.
Stop the translocation activity immediately and arrange for a licensed fauna handler to take over while documenting the incident and notifying the client and regulator if required.
Replace translocation with on-site euthanasia to avoid needing a licence.

questions.prompt: A contractor proposes clearing at night to avoid disturbing diurnal birds. Which assessment is most relevant before approving night works?

options.text: Whether night works reduce labour costs for the contractor.
Whether the project will finish earlier overall regardless of ecological factors.
If night clearing is common practice on other projects in the region.
Potential impacts on nocturnal fauna, availability of licensed night-time fauna handlers, lighting effects on wildlife, and required permits or noise restrictions.

questions.prompt: You need to demonstrate due diligence in pre-clearing training for a subcontractor’s crew. Which documentation best supports this?

options.text: A toolbox talk attendance sheet, a signed site-specific induction that covers species identification, exclusion zones, and incident reporting procedures, plus training records for spotter-catchers.
A verbal briefing given once with no sign-in sheet.
An email sent to the subcontractor listing topics to cover, without proof of crew receipt.
A generic company induction from five years ago provided by the contractor.

questions.prompt: While reviewing pre-clearance survey data, you find GPS points that cluster but have no metadata. What is the best next step to validate those data for compliance reports?

options.text: Include the points in the report without qualification to meet deadlines.
Contact the surveyor to obtain metadata (device type, datum, accuracy, timestamp) and verify ground-truth locations before including them in compliance documentation.
Delete the GPS points because they are unusable without metadata.
Assume a standard positional accuracy and proceed.

questions.prompt: A client requests that protected vegetation be cleared to maintain project schedule, claiming mitigation will be done later. What is the appropriate professional response?

options.text: Agree and allow clearing now to avoid contractual penalties, with a promise to retrofit mitigation later.
Ignore the client and proceed according to your own timeline.
Refuse to permit clearing until appropriate approvals and mitigation plans are in place, and escalate to the project environmental manager and client with documented reasons.
Perform selective clearing tonight and document it as emergency works.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether to retain a patch of native grassland within a construction zone as a micro-reserve. What technical judgement factor is most important?

options.text: Whether the contractor’s equipment can be re-routed without cost.
Whether the patch can be converted into a landscaped area post-construction.
If the patch is visible from the main road for aesthetic purposes.
The ecological value of the patch (species diversity, presence of threatened taxa, connectivity) balanced against construction constraints and maintenance feasibility.

questions.prompt: During pre-clearing, you observe erosion risk on a slope adjacent to the work area. Which mitigation action should you prioritise immediately?

options.text: Install sediment control (silt fence or wattles) downslope of clearing to trap sediment and schedule revegetation as soon as practicable.
Proceed with clearing and rely on future landscaping to manage erosion.
Divert stormwater directly into a nearby creek to avoid pooling on site.
Ignore erosion risk if current weather is dry.

questions.prompt: A field crew reports a live animal casualty found during pre-clearance. What documentation and next steps are required for proper compliance?

options.text: Bury the carcass immediately and record only the location in the daily log.

Record species (or best estimate), GPS location, time, cause if apparent, photograph the casualty, notify the licenced fauna officer and the project environmental manager, and retain evidence where safe and legal.
Transport the carcass to the office without documentation for later disposal.
Ask the contractor to dispose of the carcass and only note the disposal in the invoice.

questions.prompt: You must produce a pre-clearing compliance report for a regulator. Which approach gives the most defensible evidence of adherence to pre-clearing controls?

options.text: A narrative summary without supporting field records, relying on memory.
A brief email to the regulator stating controls were implemented.
An integrated report combining signed checklists, timestamped and geotagged photos, fauna handling logs, GPS fence alignment files, and incident records.
A contractor's invoice claiming pre-clearing precautions were taken.

questions.prompt: A seasonal floodplain survey window is approaching but access will be limited due to vehicle constraints. What is an appropriate adjustment to the survey plan?

options.text: Cancel the survey until full vehicle access is available later in the year.
Replace the survey with desktop habitat mapping and defer field checks indefinitely.
Complete the survey only along fenced access roads and ignore inaccessible areas.
Adapt methods to include foot transects, remote sensing (drones) where permitted, and coordinate with landowners for alternative access to complete the survey within the window.

questions.prompt: You find historic cultural heritage markers in the clearing zone during pre-clearing. How should you integrate this into ecological compliance?

options.text: Stop works in the immediate area, notify cultural heritage representatives and integrate their guidance into revised clearing plans and compliance records.
Continue with clearing but avoid the markers without consulting heritage specialists.
Remove the markers and store them off-site for later reinstallation.
Document the location and proceed because cultural heritage is outside ecological scope.

questions.prompt: A fauna spotter notes that exclusion fencing is damaged during clearing. What is the best immediate operational step?

options.text: Ignore the damage and continue until daily maintenance checks.
Cease clearing near the breach, secure the gap to prevent fauna ingress/egress, document the damage, and arrange for repair before resuming work.
Move the clearing zone away from the fence and continue without repair.
Wait for the contractor to notice and repair whenever convenient.

questions.prompt: When deciding whether to undertake pre-clearing photomonitoring using drones, what constraint must you confirm before deployment?

options.text: Whether the drone pilot prefers morning flights.
That drones will capture prettier images for the client’s marketing.
Regulatory approvals for drone use in the area, site-specific safety and fauna disturbance risk assessments, and no-fly zones including nearby airspace and sensitive species breeding sites.
That drones are cheaper than walking the site.

questions.prompt: A field team reports conflicting species identifications for a small mammal captured during pre-clearance. What is the correct approach to resolve identification uncertainty?

options.text: Release the animal immediately and exclude all records for that incident.
Assign the most common species in the region to simplify reporting.
Dispose of the specimen and note only the capture time.

Photograph diagnostic features, retain clear measurements and photographs, secure the animal appropriately if permitted, consult a senior ecologist or taxonomic expert, and record uncertainty in the report.

questions.prompt: The client asks for a rapid salvaging of understory plants prior to clearing. Which factor must be prioritised to ensure ecological salvage is appropriate?

options.text: Identification of target species, appropriate timing, suitable recipient site conditions, and whether permits or specialist techniques are required to maximise salvage survival.
Speed of removal over plant health to meet tight schedule.
Using the nearest patch of soil regardless of compatibility to limit transport distance.
Transplanting during the hottest part of the day to reduce staffing needs.

questions.prompt: You review pre-clearing risk registers and see wildlife strike risk from vehicles listed without control measures. What control measure is most practical to add for pre-clearing works?

options.text: Prohibit vehicles on site entirely during daylight hours.
Implement speed limits, designated routes avoiding high-value habitat, driver awareness training, and signage to reduce wildlife strike risk during clearing operations.
Require drivers to sound horns continuously while on site.
Allow higher speeds to minimise time spent on roads.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist proposes a novel technique for relocating a lizard species during clearing. Before approval, what must you verify?

options.text: That the technique is popular on social media.
That the contractor agrees to try it without oversight.
That the technique is supported by evidence or expert opinion, aligns with licence conditions, minimises stress and mortality, and has contingency measures if it fails.
That it will reduce project costs regardless of outcomes.

questions.prompt: During review, you find the pre-clearance fauna handling log lacks signatures from the licensed handler. What is the appropriate correction?

options.text: Add your signature as the ecologist in charge without consulting the handler.
Ignore the omission if the rest of the log is complete.
Create a forged signature to meet audit expectations.
Return the log to the licensed handler to sign, request a dated attestation, and note the initial omission in the record to maintain traceability.

questions.prompt: You discover a discrepancy between the authorised clearing boundary and the contractor’s flagged boundary on site. Which action best addresses immediate compliance risk?

options.text: Halt clearing in the disputed area, verify authorised boundaries using plans and GPS, and clarify with the client and regulator before resuming.
Allow clearing up to the contractor’s flagged boundary to maintain schedule.
Adjust authorised plans to match the contractor’s flags without consultation.
Ignore the discrepancy and proceed where flags indicate.

questions.prompt: A statutory authority requests additional fauna survey data beyond what was in the brief. What is the responsible way to respond?

options.text: Ignore the request and submit the original report to keep to schedule.
Acknowledge the authority’s request, assess scope and feasibility, propose an amended survey plan and timetable, and seek client approval and resourcing to meet the authority’s requirements.
Provide fabricated additional data to satisfy the request quickly.
Tell the authority that additional surveys are impossible without offering alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which quality assurance step most effectively reduces observer bias in pre-clearing habitat assessments carried out by multiple ecologists?

options.text: Allow each ecologist to use their own preferred assessment method.
Average all ecologists’ subjective scores without calibration.
Use standardised survey protocols, provide training to ensure consistency, and conduct periodic inter-observer calibration checks.
Rotate ecologists between sites daily without standard methods.

questions.prompt: You must communicate pre-clearing restrictions to site workers with limited English proficiency. What is the most effective strategy?

options.text: Provide only English written instructions and expect comprehension.
Rely on a single bilingual worker to interpret informally as needed.
Hold a one-off briefing and distribute technical reports for later reading.
Use translated materials, pictograms for exclusion zones, a bilingual supervisor or interpreter, and practical demonstrations to ensure understanding of restrictions.

questions.prompt: A client requests that your pre-clearance monitoring omit negative incidents to maintain project reputation. How should you proceed ethically and professionally?

options.text: Refuse to omit incidents, document all occurrences accurately, explain legal and ethical obligations, and escalate if pressured to alter records.
Agree and remove negative incidents from the report to protect the client.
Delay the report until negative incidents are forgotten.
Create a separate confidential file for negative incidents not shared with regulators.

questions.prompt: When drafting a pre-clearing rehabilitation plan, which measure most directly supports return of native ground flora after clearing?

options.text: Covering the site with imported turf for immediate aesthetics.
Collecting topsoil and seedbank during clearing, storing it properly, and re-spreading it on regraded surfaces to retain native propagules.
Applying a generic commercial seed mix with no provenance matching.
Seeding only with fast-growing exotic grasses to stabilise soil.

questions.prompt: A fauna detector dog is proposed to assist pre-clearing surveys. Before including the dog in the methodology, what is the principal consideration?

options.text: Whether the dog will impress the client during site demonstrations.
Dog’s availability on weekends only.
Handler qualifications, dog certification for target species detection, potential disturbance to wildlife, and suitability of site conditions for safe dog deployment.
That dogs always increase detection rates regardless of context.

questions.prompt: Post-clearing audit reveals a small patch of retained invasive species within the cleared area. What remedial action best aligns with pre-clearing compliance objectives?

options.text: Leave the invasive patch as it is to avoid further disturbance.
Cover the patch with mulch and ignore it in monitoring reports.
Transplant the invasive species to an off-site nursery for later sale.
Remove the invasive patch promptly using appropriate methods, dispose of material to prevent spread, and update weed management records and future monitoring plans.

questions.prompt: You must decide whether to implement a pre-clearing requirement for fauna handling PPE. Which consideration is most important when specifying PPE?

options.text: Selecting PPE that protects handlers and animals (gloves, bite-resistant sleeves, hoods) without restricting dexterity, and matching PPE to species-specific handling protocols and welfare requirements.
Making PPE as minimal as possible to reduce heat stress regardless of handling risks.
Specifying only provided contractor-branded PPE.
Requiring full hazmat suits for all fauna handling.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist suggests deferring a nocturnal bat survey because weather forecasts predict strong winds on the planned night. What is the best judgement call?

options.text: Proceed regardless of conditions since survey windows are limited.
Defer the survey to a later suitable night because strong winds reduce detection probability and would compromise data quality, and document the decision and reschedule.
Replace the nocturnal survey with a daytime habitat assessment only.
Use automated detectors during the windy night without validation.

questions.prompt: You are preparing to escalate a significant non-compliance found during pre-clearing to the regulator. What information must you include to make the escalation effective?

options.text: Only a brief statement that a non-compliance occurred without details to avoid blame.
Only the contractor’s name and a demand for immediate investigation.
A clear description of the non-compliance, location (GPS), timing, actions taken to stop harm, potential impacts, supporting evidence (photos, logs), and proposed remediation steps.
A speculative estimate of impacts with no supporting evidence.

questions.prompt: After pre-clearing, monitoring shows reduced native ground cover compared with pre-clearing photos. Which analysis best supports corrective action planning?

options.text: Rely on anecdotal recollection of workers about pre-clearing conditions.
Assume weather caused the reduction and postpone any action for a year.
Apply a generic fertiliser across the site and monitor informally.

Compare geotagged pre- and post-clearing photos, reference baseline vegetation surveys, analyse topsoil movement and rehabilitation records, and identify causative factors to design targeted remediation.

title: Ecological Reporting Field Data to Draft

questions.prompt: You’ve completed a morning of targeted vegetation plots and have raw species lists with cover estimates and GPS tracks. What is the best next step to prepare these field data for inclusion in a draft ecological report?

options.text: Consolidate and standardise species names, transcribe plot metadata, check GPS track quality, and store datasets in the project’s agreed data folder before drafting.
Immediately import raw GPS tracks and species lists into the report draft to save time, then tidy entries during report writing.
Email the raw photos and handwritten notes to the project manager and wait for their instructions before processing any data.
Discard any ambiguous records and only keep the species identifications you are confident about to avoid errors in the draft.

questions.prompt: During reconnaissance you record a potentially significant fauna observation but cannot confirm the species in the field. For the draft report, what is the most appropriate approach to reporting this observation?

options.text: List the species as confirmed in the draft because the observation was made in the likely habitat.
Record the observation as an unconfirmed sighting with details of evidence, methods used, and recommended verification steps.
Omit the observation from the draft until laboratory confirmation is available.
Replace the species name with a genus-level identification to avoid misreporting.

questions.prompt: You have several audio recordings of dusk amphibian calls of variable quality. When preparing them as evidence for a draft habitat assessment, what is the best practice?

options.text: Include all recordings in the draft report appendix regardless of quality to demonstrate effort.
Only include a summary statement about amphibian presence without linking to the audio to avoid confusing readers.
Select representative high-quality extracts, annotate call times, methods, surveyor notes, and describe limitations of recordings in the draft.
Submit full-length unedited files as primary evidence and note that quality control will occur later.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist transcribed quadrat data into a spreadsheet but you notice inconsistent cover-scale entries (e.g. percent vs. Braun-Blanquet codes). For the draft report dataset, how should you handle this?

options.text: Leave the spreadsheet as-is and explain inconsistencies in the methodology section of the draft.
Delete entries with Braun-Blanquet codes and only use percent cover rows to avoid conversion errors.
Average the different cover metrics numerically without conversion and present the mean values in the draft.
Convert all entries to a single agreed cover metric after consulting the project documentation and note original values in metadata.

questions.prompt: You are drafting the vegetation results and must report on habitat condition assessments performed using a client-specified scoring method you are less familiar with. What should you do before finalising the draft text?

options.text: Contact the client to ask for their preferred wording and examples of previous reports using the scoring method, and validate your scoring with a senior ecologist.
Use your best interpretation of the scores and include an author note that scores were estimated.
Replace the client method with a more familiar standard assessment and note the substitution in the draft.
Omit numerical scores and provide only qualitative descriptions of habitat condition.

questions.prompt: You find a hand-drawn fence line on a landowner’s map that differs from the cadastral boundary in government data. For mapping the project’s ecological survey areas in the draft, what should you do?

options.text: Use the landowner’s hand-drawn fence line as the survey boundary since it reflects on-ground features.
Annotate both features in the draft maps, describe the discrepancy in the methods, and recommend ground-truthing or confirmation with the client.
Use the cadastral boundary only, because official spatial data are authoritative.
Create a merged boundary by averaging the two lines and use that for area calculations.

questions.prompt: While compiling species lists you encounter two different common names for the same taxon across field sheets. How should you present species names in the draft report?

options.text: Use the common name most frequently encountered in field sheets and ignore the alternate name.
Present only common names to make the report more accessible to non-specialist readers.
Standardise to the accepted scientific name with a preferred common name in the report and list alternate common names in metadata.
Show both names together for every species entry to avoid choosing between them.

questions.prompt: You need to include detection probability considerations for nocturnal mammal camera-trap results in the draft. Which approach is most appropriate to include at the drafting stage?

options.text: Assume detection probability equals one and report raw detection counts as occurrence.
Exclude any interpretation of detection probability and only report presence/absence based on at least one detection.
Apply a default literature-based detection probability value without local calibration and use it to adjust abundance estimates.
Describe survey effort, camera deployment details, and acknowledge detection limitations, recommending statistical analysis if required for final reporting.

questions.prompt: You are drafting a section on threatened species and have a single record within the project area from a historic dataset but no recent local detections. How should this be reported?

options.text: Report the historic record with its date and source, describe recent survey efforts and absence of current detections, and discuss implications and recommended follow-up.
Treat the historic record as current evidence of presence and list the species as present.
Omit the historic record to avoid confusing readers about current status.
Assume the species is absent and state that surveys confirmed its absence.

questions.prompt: An intern transcribed audio notes into narrative text and included subjective comments like ‘site looks degraded’. When preparing the draft ecological site description, what is the appropriate action?

options.text: Keep the intern’s narrative verbatim to reflect field impressions.
Convert subjective phrases into objective descriptions supported by measured indicators or provide them clearly as professional opinion with supporting evidence.
Remove any subjective comments and present only raw measurements to maintain objectivity.
Add stronger negative language to emphasise potential impacts to influence decision-makers.

questions.prompt: You must summarise waterbody condition data but some measurements were taken during heavy rain and are likely atypical. How should these data be handled in the draft report?

options.text: Exclude the rainy-day measurements from analysis to avoid skewing summary statistics.
Average the rainy-day values with other measurements without comment to maintain simplicity.
Include the measurements but flag them as collected during atypical conditions, describe how they affect interpretation, and consider separate analysis if necessary.
Replace rainy-day measurements with predicted dry-weather values based on literature.

questions.prompt: You are preparing to map flora survey plots in the draft, but GPS waypoint accuracy differs between devices. What is the correct course of action before finalising draft maps?

options.text: Use the highest-precision device’s coordinates for all plots to standardise positions.
Average coordinates across devices to smooth discrepancies.
Ignore reported accuracy values and rely on visual fit to aerial imagery.
Document device types and reported accuracy for each waypoint, apply reasonable spatial adjustments where justified, and include positional uncertainty in the draft maps and metadata.

questions.prompt: A client requests that you not include raw photographs in the draft because of privacy concerns. How should you respond in the draft materials?

options.text: Include redacted or cropped photographs that remove identifiable features, and provide image metadata and a note on privacy considerations.
Exclude all photographs and provide only textual descriptions to respect privacy.
Include full photographs in a password-protected appendix linked in the draft without notifying the client further.
Refuse the client’s request and state that photographs are critical evidence that must be included.

questions.prompt: While drafting the methods section, you realise some survey nights deviated from the protocol (different start times and weather). What is the appropriate way to document this?

options.text: Omit mention of deviations to present a cleaner methodological narrative.
Record the deviations, explain why they occurred, and discuss potential effects on results in the draft methods and limitations.
State that the protocol was followed and provide no further detail.
Rewrite the protocol in the draft to match what was actually done so it appears fully compliant.

questions.prompt: You need to present a time-series of vegetation cover measurements but several earlier years’ raw data are in incompatible file formats. For the draft, what is the best action?

options.text: Exclude earlier years from the draft and only use the years with compatible files.
Reformat current files to match the older formats to avoid conversion work.
Convert earlier files into compatible formats, document conversion steps, and include quality checks before presenting the time-series.
Manually transcribe earlier data into the current spreadsheet without documenting the process.

questions.prompt: A draft map shows a patch of remnant vegetation that may be a candidate for biodiversity offset. You are unsure of the legal definitions used by local authorities. How should you handle statements about offset eligibility in the draft?

options.text: Make a tentative classification based on your field assessment and assert likely offset eligibility.
Omit any discussion of offsets to avoid providing misleading advice.
State the patch is ineligible for offset because it is small and fragmented without checking definitions.
Provide a factual description of vegetation attributes, cite observed criteria relevant to offsets, and recommend escalation to the compliance specialist or authority for legal determination.

questions.prompt: You are finalising an evidence table of survey effort and outcomes; one surveyor’s name is missing from the field roster. What should you do before including the table in the draft?

options.text: Confirm the roster with the field team, update the table to include the missing surveyor, and record their role and dates in the metadata.
Leave the name blank and add a footnote that some surveyors are unnamed.
Replace the missing name with the project manager’s name since they oversaw the project.
Remove individual names entirely to avoid confidentiality issues.

questions.prompt: You must summarise incidental observations (e.g. opportunistic sightings) across multiple surveys for the draft. What is the correct way to present these data?

options.text: Integrate incidental observations into formal survey occurrence tables without differentiation.
Create a separate table for incidental observations, include date, observer, location precision, and a note about their opportunistic nature.
Discard incidental observations to focus on structured survey data only.
Convert incidental observations into presence-only records and use them as quantitative evidence of abundance.

questions.prompt: During QA of field forms you find several species entries where identifiers marked ‘cf.’ or ‘sp.’ were later confirmed by a taxonomic expert. In the draft species list, how should these be presented?

options.text: Leave the original ‘cf.’ and ‘sp.’ designations to preserve field authenticity.
Replace the entries with family-level identifications to be conservative.
Update the species names to the expert’s confirmed identifications and note original field designations and expert verification in the metadata.
Remove the entries to avoid presenting uncertain identifications.

questions.prompt: You are drafting an impacts section and must present likelihoods of species displacement due to a proposed development. Which approach is most defensible at the draft stage?

options.text: Give precise probability percentages for displacement without site-specific modelling.
State that displacement will definitely occur to emphasise precaution.
Avoid any likelihood statements and only describe habitat overlap.
Provide qualitative likelihood categories tied to evidence from surveys, habitat attributes, and relevant literature, and identify uncertainties.

questions.prompt: You discover duplicate photo filenames from different field days in the project photo library. What is the appropriate action before including images in the draft?

options.text: Rename files using a consistent convention that includes date, location ID, and photographer initials, and add a photo index with metadata.
Keep original filenames and add a note that duplicates exist.
Delete older photos to avoid duplication.
Embed the photos directly into the draft text to bypass file management.

questions.prompt: An external dataset used for habitat mapping has licensing restrictions that require attribution and prohibits redistribution. How should you handle use of this dataset in the draft report?

options.text: Reproduce the maps using the dataset and include full-resolution layers in the report appendix.
Use the dataset to produce maps in the draft, include required attribution, and note any redistribution limitations in the metadata and cover letter.
Avoid using the dataset and attempt to recreate similar data from public sources without checking comparability.
Provide the dataset as a downloadable attachment to the client regardless of license to expedite review.

questions.prompt: You need to present uncertainty around vegetation extent mapped from imagery, because shadows and recent clearing complicate interpretation. The best way to convey this in the draft is:

options.text: Provide a single definitive polygon and state that it represents mapped extent.
Omit any boundary mapping and only describe vegetation qualitatively.
Display core mapped polygons plus buffers or uncertainty bands, explain interpretation challenges, and recommend ground-truthing to refine boundaries.
Use older imagery to avoid recent clearing complexity and present that extent as current.

questions.prompt: You are drafting recommendations and want to prioritise mitigation actions based on field observations. What is the best way to structure these priority recommendations?

options.text: List mitigation actions alphabetically to avoid perceived bias.
Provide an exhaustive list of possible mitigation measures without prioritisation.
Leave prioritisation to the client and present only raw suggestions from field notes.
Rank actions by ecological risk and feasibility, provide brief justification for each ranking, and indicate which require further investigation or approval.

questions.prompt: An unusual plant community was encountered but lacks adequate literature references for classification. For the draft classification, what is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Describe community attributes in detail, avoid definitive assignment, and recommend targeted taxonomic or vegetation classification studies.
Assign the nearest published community name and state it as definitive.
Omit classification and treat the area as non-native scrub to simplify reporting.
Invent a new community name to use consistently in the draft.

questions.prompt: While drafting, you must summarise stakeholder communications about access restrictions during surveys. What is the correct way to present this in the draft?

options.text: List stakeholder names and verbatim private communications without consent.
Summarise access restrictions, cite the stakeholder role and date of communication, and note any conditions that affected survey coverage.
Exclude mention of access issues to avoid complicating the report.
State that access was unrestricted even though some areas were not surveyed.

questions.prompt: You identify potential biosecurity risks (weed seed spread) associated with field equipment. How should you document and act on this in the draft?

options.text: Ignore biosecurity risks in the draft since they are operational matters.
Describe the risk as severe and demand immediate cessation of all fieldwork.
Document observed biosecurity risks, note decontamination measures taken in the field, and recommend standard operating procedures for future surveys.
State that the client is responsible for biosecurity and do not include recommendations.

questions.prompt: A field dataset contains location coordinates with missing coordinate reference system (CRS) metadata. For the draft spatial analysis, what is the appropriate step?

options.text: Assume WGS84 and proceed with mapping.
Randomly test common CRS options until the coordinates overlay aerial imagery correctly, then record that CRS.
Exclude the dataset from the draft to avoid CRS uncertainty.
Trace back to the GPS device or field notes to confirm the CRS, document the confirmed CRS in metadata, and transform data if needed.

questions.prompt: You are writing the draft quality assurance section. Which statement best reflects appropriate QA practice for field-to-draft data workflows?

options.text: Describe staged QA checks including data transcription review, taxonomic verification, spatial accuracy checks, and sign-off by a senior ecologist prior to finalisation.
Quality assurance is performed only after the draft is complete to avoid rework.
Rely on automated spell-checkers and assume data accuracy.
Delegate QA responsibility entirely to the client to reduce consultant workload.

questions.prompt: During drafting you need to present limitations related to seasonal timing of surveys. What is the best way to handle this?

options.text: Omit seasonal limitations to avoid weakening conclusions.
Explicitly state seasonal timing, explain how it affects detectability of taxa, and suggest additional seasonal surveys if needed.
Claim surveys were representative of all seasons without evidence.
Recommend cancelling any further surveys as seasonality cannot be overcome.

questions.prompt: You must report on the chain of custody for biological samples collected. Which action is appropriate to include in the draft?

options.text: Provide a high-level statement that samples were collected and sent to a lab without records.
Omit chain-of-custody detail because laboratories handle sample verification.
Include a chain-of-custody log showing sample IDs, collection dates, handlers, storage conditions, and lab receipt timestamps.
List only the sample types collected without identifiers.

questions.prompt: A junior staff member drafted a risk matrix using subjective likelihoods and consequences without evidence. Before including it in the draft report, what should you do?

options.text: Include the matrix as-is to reflect team judgment.
Remove the matrix and replace it with narrative descriptions only.
Swap the likelihood and consequence axes to present different outcomes.
Review and revise the matrix to align likelihood and consequence ratings with documented survey data, literature, and clearly state assumptions.

questions.prompt: You are asked to provide preliminary recommendations for monitoring effectiveness of mitigation measures in the draft. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Propose specific, measurable indicators, monitoring frequency, methods, and trigger thresholds for adaptive management, with a note that details can be finalised after consultation.
Recommend vague monitoring like ‘regular checks’ without metrics.
Advise the client to use existing industry monitoring templates without tailoring them to site conditions.
Defer all monitoring recommendations to the final report and omit them from the draft.

questions.prompt: You need to communicate a technical uncertainty to a non-technical client in the draft. What is the best practice?

options.text: Use minimal technical detail and assert confidence to avoid alarming the client.
Explain the uncertainty in plain language, quantify it where possible, and describe how it affects decisions and recommended next steps.
Include the full technical analysis without simplification and expect the client to interpret it.
Avoid discussing uncertainties and focus on positive findings.

questions.prompt: An external reviewer flags a small methodological error in your dataset alignment after you have included it in the draft. What is the correct immediate action?

options.text: Ignore the reviewer and proceed to finalise the draft.
Blame the external reviewer and state their comment is outside scope.
Investigate the flagged error, correct the dataset if necessary, document the correction in the draft change log, and notify the review team of the update.
Withdraw the entire draft and restart data processing from scratch.

questions.prompt: You must escalate a biosecurity non-compliance observed in the field (e.g. gear not cleaned) while drafting. Which escalation path is most appropriate?

options.text: Include the incident only in confidential internal notes and do not mention it in the draft report.
Publicly name the field staff responsible in the draft to ensure accountability.
Ignore it as an isolated minor issue and make no mention in the draft.
Record the non-compliance in the draft, notify the project manager and health/safety or biosecurity lead, and propose immediate corrective actions.

questions.prompt: You are preparing to include a statistical summary (e.g. diversity indices) in the draft, but some sample sizes are very small. What is the appropriate way to present these results?

options.text: Present the indices but include caveats about small sample sizes, confidence intervals where possible, and avoid over-interpretation.
Report the indices without qualification to provide consistency across sites.
Exclude diversity indices entirely because of small sample sizes.
Aggregate small samples across unrelated sites to increase sample size without noting the aggregation.

questions.prompt: When drafting, you need to ensure accessibility of data files for future review. Which practice should you include in the draft data management statement?

options.text: State that raw data are available on request but provide no details on format, structure, or access conditions.
Describe file naming conventions, folder structure, file formats, metadata standards used, and how authorised parties can request access.
Publish data openly without checking for sensitive or licensed content to maximise accessibility.
Note that data will be deleted after the project to protect privacy.

questions.prompt: A field crew reported an unusual mortality event observed adjacent to the study area. For the draft report, what is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Exclude the observation as it occurred outside the study boundary.
Assume the event is unrelated to the project and make no mention.
Document the mortality event with location, evidence, photos, and any immediate steps taken, and recommend escalation to relevant authorities and further investigation as needed.
Speculate on probable causes in the draft without supporting data.

questions.prompt: You must prepare a draft appendices index linking datasets, maps, photos and survey forms. Which approach best ensures usability of the draft appendices?

options.text: List appendix titles only without descriptions or file references.
Embed all appendices sequentially without an index and rely on the table of contents.
Provide only hyperlinks to internal project drives assuming all readers have access.
Provide an index that lists each appendix item, brief description, file name, file format, date, creator, and cross-reference to sections of the draft where it is cited.

questions.prompt: You are preparing to meet a private landholder for a site inspection to assess vegetation impacts. Before arrival, which action best demonstrates client-focused preparation specific to this module?

options.text: Send the landholder a brief agenda and confirm access points, timing and any biosecurity requirements.
Prepare a detailed ecological survey methodology document to present on site.
Ask the landholder to provide written permission only when you meet them in person.
Contact neighbours for their opinion about the landholder’s property before visiting.

questions.prompt: During a handover with a landholder, they ask for immediate advice about spot-filling a small bare patch that may affect fauna. What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Provide detailed planting species and soil mix recommendations on the spot.
Explain you can offer general guidance now but defer specific recommendations until you’ve recorded observations and checked relevant records.
Decline to discuss anything until you submit a formal report.
Tell them to wait until the next seasonal survey to take any action.

questions.prompt: A landholder becomes upset during the inspection about previous contractor damage. How should you manage the conversation to maintain trust and professional boundaries?

options.text: Agree with the landholder that the previous contractor was negligent and advise immediate legal action.
Change the subject to avoid conflict and continue the inspection silently.
Acknowledge their concern, note factual details, offer to document the damage in your site report, and explain the process for escalation if required.
Tell the landholder not to worry and that you will fix everything yourself without involving anyone else.

questions.prompt: You discover a potential threatened-ecology indicator on private land but are uncertain of identification. What is the most appropriate next step regarding the landholder?

options.text: Tell the landholder it is definitely a threatened species to ensure it gets protected immediately.
Keep the finding confidential and only note it in your personal field notes without informing the landholder.
Ask the landholder to remove or relocate the organism to avoid complications.
Explain your uncertainty, avoid speculation, record clear photos and GPS location, and tell the landholder you'll verify identification and follow up promptly.

questions.prompt: A landholder asks you to start work beyond the agreed scope during the inspection. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Politely decline and explain the agreed scope, offer to note the request and provide a scope amendment and cost estimate after returning to the office.
Agree immediately and start the extra work to please the client.
Tell them your employer would never allow changes and ignore the request.
Complete the extra work without recording it and include it in the final invoice.

questions.prompt: Which record should you prioritise capturing on-site to support later communication with the landholder about findings?

options.text: A detailed written narrative of your impressions without photographs.
High-resolution photographs of key features with time and location metadata, plus brief field notes describing context.
Only GPS coordinates without context or images.
A voice recording summarising the inspection but without location information.

questions.prompt: You need to explain potential ecological risks of proposed earthworks to a landholder who is unfamiliar with technical terms. Which approach is most effective?

options.text: Provide them with a copy of the technical assessment and ask them to read it thoroughly.
Tell them that the consultants and regulators will handle all risks and no action is needed from them.
Use plain language, local examples relevant to the property, and simple diagrams if needed to explain likely risks and mitigation options.
Discuss only regulatory penalties without explaining ecological consequences.

questions.prompt: A landholder requests copies of your raw field data immediately. How should you respond professionally?

options.text: Provide raw spreadsheets immediately without explanation.
Refuse to share any information until the invoice is paid.
Tell the landholder to request the data from your supervisor and avoid further discussion.
Explain the data will be provided in an appropriate formatted report after quality checks, offer summary findings now, and discuss any urgent concerns.

questions.prompt: During a site meeting a landholder reveals cultural information about the site that may affect assessment and confidentiality. What is your immediate responsibility?

options.text: Acknowledge the information, explain confidentiality limits and how you will handle sensitive details, and seek guidance from appropriate cultural liaison or supervisor before including specifics in reports.
Record the details in the public report without question to ensure completeness.
Ignore the cultural information since it is outside ecological scope.
Share the information with all team members immediately to expedite assessment.

questions.prompt: A landholder asks for an estimate of how long your full report will take during the inspection. Given constraints, what is the most appropriate reply?

options.text: Promise an unrealistically short turnaround to secure client satisfaction.
Provide a realistic timeframe based on the agreed scope, explain factors that could change it, and offer to update them if any delays occur.
Refuse to give any timeline until the report is delivered.
Tell them the report will be ready only when regulatory authorities approve it.

questions.prompt: On arrival you find the landholder is not present and access is via an unlocked gate. What is the best practice for entry and initial site communication?

options.text: Enter immediately and begin the inspection without leaving any notice.
Leave and reschedule without attempting any documentation of the situation.
Confirm prior permission for access, take photos of the gate and property boundary, proceed cautiously and leave a note explaining your visit plus contact details.
Call local neighbours to ask if they know the landholder’s whereabouts before entering.

questions.prompt: During an assessment the landholder asks you to photograph their livestock for their own records. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Refuse to take the photos because livestock are unrelated to ecology.
Take photos without telling the landholder to avoid delays.
Recommend they ask a family member to photograph the animals instead.
Explain you can take photos for the landholder’s records if they consent, ensure images are stored separately from client sensitive data, and record that you took them with permission.

questions.prompt: A landholder asks for advice on timing of vegetation clearing to avoid impacting fauna. You are not certain of seasonal species presence. What should you advise?

options.text: Advise a precautionary approach: avoid clearing during suspected breeding seasons, document uncertainty, and propose targeted surveys or liaising with ecological specialists for definitive timing.
Provide specific months for clearing based on your intuition without field data.
Tell them there is no need to consider seasonality for clearing.
Recommend clearing immediately to pre-empt any future impact claims.

questions.prompt: After an inspection, a landholder asks for verbal findings immediately but you need to verify some identifications. What is the best immediate reply?

options.text: Refuse to discuss anything until the final report is submitted.

Offer a preliminary verbal summary of non-sensitive observations while stating that species identifications and regulatory implications require verification and will be provided in the written report.
Provide final conclusions including legal implications even though identifications are unverified.
Tell the landholder to wait for regulators to contact them directly.

questions.prompt: You observe evidence of recent illegal clearing on a client’s neighbour’s property visible from the client site. The client asks whether you will report it. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Agree to report it immediately to the media at the client’s request.
Decline to report anything because it involves a neighbour.

Explain your professional duty is to report observed significant environmental harm, advise the client on what you can report and offer to document and escalate the observed evidence following company procedures.
Encourage the client to take matters into their own hands and confront the neighbour.

questions.prompt: Which communication method is most appropriate for delivering a draft report to a landholder who prefers plain English and limited technical detail?

options.text: Deliver the full technical draft only and ask them to consult a solicitor if they have questions.
Provide only the executive summary and withhold technical appendices.
Print the complete report and leave it at the property mail box without contact.
Send the draft report with a one-page plain-language summary highlighting key findings and actions, and offer a follow-up meeting to discuss details.

questions.prompt: During a site walk the landholder mentions planned future works that were not in the brief. What should you document and communicate back to the client?

options.text: Record the planned works, note potential ecological interactions, explain that these are outside the current scope, and propose an addendum assessment or separate advice.
Ignore the remark as irrelevant to the current brief.
Include the future works in your current report without additional approval.
Warn the landholder they cannot proceed with any future works under any circumstances.

questions.prompt: A landholder asks how you will protect their property biosecurity during survey work. Which immediate action best addresses their concern?

options.text: Assure them biosecurity is not your responsibility and will not be addressed.
Explain the company’s biosecurity procedures (clean boots, vehicle checks, weed hygiene) and demonstrate practical steps you will take on site.
Tell them biosecurity measures are only necessary on public lands.
Suggest they sign a waiver absolving you of responsibility for any biosecurity risk.

questions.prompt: You need to escalate a client concern about potential habitat for a species protected by regulation but are unsure of the legislative detail. What is the most appropriate escalation step?

options.text: Tell the landholder nothing until you have memorised the legislation.
Advise the landholder to ignore regulations because they rarely apply.
Document the observed evidence, notify your supervisor and request they liaise with the regulatory specialist to confirm requirements before advising the landholder.
Directly contact the regulator with unverified observations without internal review.

questions.prompt: A landholder requests immediate photographs of sensitive flora to share on social media. What is the best response?

options.text: Provide geotagged photos to help them promote their property.
Refuse to take any photos as a matter of principle.
Take photos and post them to social media yourself to control the message.
Explain the risks of publicising sensitive locations, offer non-location-tagged photos if appropriate, and discuss consent and sensitive information handling before providing images.

questions.prompt: You are preparing notes from a site meeting and want to ensure accuracy before sending them to the landholder. What is the best verification step?

options.text: Summarise the key points and send them to the landholder asking for confirmation or correction within a specified timeframe.
Assume your notes are correct and send them without checking.
Send the landholder only a terse one-line summary to minimise follow-up.
Wait until the final report before sharing any site meeting notes.

questions.prompt: A landholder is concerned about how long survey equipment will remain on their property. Which approach best addresses this concern?

options.text: Place equipment without notice and hope the landholder does not notice.
Explain the planned equipment schedule, the reasons for placement, measures to secure equipment, and agree on contact procedures if the landholder has concerns.
Tell the landholder equipment will be left indefinitely.
Deny responsibility for any equipment maintenance or security arrangements.

questions.prompt: While recording field data a landholder asks whether their proposed fence line will impact native vegetation. You have only preliminary notes. What is the appropriate reply?

options.text: Provide a definitive judgement now and sign off on the design.
Refuse to comment on design matters as they are outside ecology entirely.
Offer a provisional observation based on what you’ve seen, note the limitations, and recommend a targeted assessment of the fence line prior to construction.
Tell them fences never affect vegetation and they can proceed freely.

questions.prompt: A landholder requests that your report omit certain observations that reflect poorly on their management. What is the correct professional response?

options.text: Agree to omit the observations to maintain a good relationship.
Threaten to withdraw from the project if they push further.
Alter the observations without telling anyone to avoid conflict.
Explain you must report observations objectively, discuss how findings will be presented, and offer to include contextual information provided by the landholder.

questions.prompt: You discover a previously unrecorded weed species on the client’s property. The landholder asks if it’s a serious problem. What is the best immediate response?

options.text: Describe what you observed, indicate potential management concerns based on the weed’s characteristics, and recommend control options or specialist verification before major actions.
Tell them it’s not a problem and no action is needed.
State it is an emergency and require immediate eradication without further assessment.
Advise them to ignore it as weeds commonly appear spontaneously.

questions.prompt: A client calls after hours worried about machinery noise disturbing nocturnal animals during works. What should you do first?

options.text: Tell them no action will be taken because work schedules are fixed.
Listen to the client, acknowledge their concern, document the timing and specifics, and advise you will investigate and follow up promptly with options to mitigate impacts.
Tell them to contact the media if they are unhappy.
Ignore the call until regular working hours.

questions.prompt: You must obtain informed consent from a landholder to place monitoring cameras. What details are essential to include in your communication?

options.text: Only the general purpose of monitoring without specifics on data handling.
Provide technical camera specifications but no information on data use.
Purpose of cameras, placement locations, data captured, storage and access arrangements, duration of deployment, and options to withdraw consent.
Ask for consent verbally only and proceed without written documentation.

questions.prompt: A landholder disputes the location of a boundary tree you recorded that may be habitat-critical. How should you proceed?

options.text: Insist your original location is correct and refuse any further discussion.
Remove the tree from your records to avoid conflict.
Advise the landholder to seek legal boundary clarification before you act.
Document the landholder’s view, re-check your GPS and photo evidence, note any discrepancies, and propose a joint site re-survey or refer to cadastral records if needed.

questions.prompt: You are required to leave a short field instruction with the landholder for contractors who will work in sensitive habitat. What should that instruction include?

options.text: Clear map of sensitive areas to avoid, practical mitigation steps, contact details for reporting issues, and agreed work hours to minimise disturbance.
A single sentence stating 'Be careful around vegetation'.
Only the contact details of your supervisor without site instructions.
A technical specification of vegetation indices without practical instructions.

questions.prompt: A landholder requests a change in the preferred method of communication from email to text messages for quick updates. What is the best professional response?

options.text: Refuse and insist all communication must be by email only.
Agree to text updates for time-sensitive items, confirm what types of messages will be sent by text, and retain email for formal records and detailed documents.
Switch entirely to text messages for all communications including formal reports.
Ignore the preference and continue with your usual communication methods.

questions.prompt: You need to evidence that you sought landholder permission for site access. Which combination of records best supports this?

options.text: Only a verbal recollection of permission noted in your memory.
A note in your personal notebook without landholder signature or timestamp.
A dated email or signed form granting access, GPS-tagged photos from the visit, and a field note referencing the permission conversation.
A photo of the gate without any written permission.

questions.prompt: During an inspection you identify potential asbestos material on site. The landholder asks you to remove it immediately. What is your correct immediate response regarding client communication and safety?

options.text: Agree to remove it yourself to save time.
Tell the landholder it's harmless and continue the inspection.
Ignore the finding and hope nobody notices.
Prioritise safety: stop work in the area, advise the landholder not to disturb the material, document the finding, and escalate to your supervisor and licensed asbestos removal specialists.

questions.prompt: A landholder requests immediate follow-up actions to reduce erosion after your verbal advice. Which action demonstrates proper documentation and client communication?

options.text: Provide a short written action list based on your verbal advice, prioritise urgent tasks, include estimated timelines, and schedule a follow-up visit to assess progress.
Tell them to implement any measures they prefer and you will not be involved.
Delay any written communication until the final report is issued.
Give verbal instructions only and leave the details vague.

questions.prompt: Which is the most appropriate way to record consent from a landholder for a minor on-site survey when time is limited?

options.text: Proceed without any record because the landholder verbally agreed.
Obtain verbal consent witnessed by a colleague, record the time, purpose, and summary of consent on site, and follow up with an email confirming details.
Refuse to proceed unless the landholder completes a lengthy formal consent form on the spot.
Ask the landholder to sign a blank page to formalise consent later.

questions.prompt: A landholder asks for an explanation of uncertainty in your ecological judgement about potential habitat value. Which explanation best meets client needs?

options.text: State uncertainty cannot be explained and avoid the discussion.
Claim full certainty to avoid confusing the landholder.
Explain the sources of uncertainty (limited seasonality, identification limits, mapping resolution), how these affect confidence levels, and what additional data would reduce uncertainty.
Provide a technical essay on statistical error without referencing the site.

questions.prompt: You identify a safety hazard on a client site during inspection that could affect contractors. What is the most appropriate communication action?

options.text: Note the hazard in your final report only and take no immediate action.
Ignore it because it is not part of the ecological brief.
Tell others about the hazard informally without recording or notifying the landholder.
Immediately inform the landholder and any on-site contractors, mark or restrict the hazardous area if safe to do so, and document the hazard and recommended controls.

questions.prompt: A landholder requests that survey data be shared with a community group. What is the correct approach before releasing data?

options.text: Confirm data ownership and confidentiality obligations, seek landholder consent in writing, redact sensitive location details if necessary, and document the release agreement.
Provide all raw data publicly without checking ownership or sensitivity.
Refuse outright to share any data regardless of permissions.
Ask the community group to contact you directly and ignore the landholder’s request.

questions.prompt: You need to record a site meeting where several action items were agreed. Which follow-up communication best closes the loop with the landholder?

options.text: Assume everyone remembers the discussion and take no further action.
Send a concise meeting minutes email listing agreed actions, responsibilities, deadlines, and contact details, and ask the landholder to confirm or amend.
Provide a lengthy technical annex without a clear action list.
Wait until the final report to mention the action items.

questions.prompt: A landholder expresses distrust because previous consultants misrepresented findings. How should you differentiate your communication approach to rebuild trust?

options.text: Promise better outcomes without showing evidence to reassure them.
Criticise the previous consultants to reassure the landholder of your superiority.
Be transparent about methods and limitations, share evidence (photos, data) where appropriate, invite questions, and agree on checkpoints for collaborative review.
Avoid sharing detailed information to prevent further disputes.

questions.prompt: You identify an urgent ecological risk on a landholder’s property outside your competence to manage. What is the most appropriate escalation and communication action?

options.text: Ignore the issue and wait until you can handle it personally.
Tell the landholder the risk is not urgent to avoid alarm.
Contact external authorities directly without informing your supervisor.
Explain the nature of the urgent risk to the landholder, document observations, immediately escalate to your supervisor and relevant specialists, and provide interim risk-reduction advice where safe.

questions.prompt: A mid-level ecology consultant is scoping a new development site with several habitat types. What is the best initial action to inform project resourcing and timing?

options.text: Conduct a desktop review of existing ecological records, aerial imagery and known seasonal constraints to draft a preliminary effort estimate.
Request a fixed daily rate from field staff and allocate five days by default.
Book the first available survey team for the next week to secure scheduling.
Assume standard survey effort for the area size and rely on adaptive scheduling once on site.

questions.prompt: During programming, a client asks for a single survey window to save costs, but the site has both migratory birds and a threatened frog species with different peak periods. What is the most defensible programming decision?

options.text: Prioritise the birds and schedule surveys during the bird window only to reduce costs.
Schedule separate targeted survey windows for each taxon according to their peak activity and advise the client of the increased cost and why it is necessary.
Combine surveys into one generalised visit and collect opportunistic data for both taxa.
Delay all surveys until next year to attempt to capture both species simultaneously.

questions.prompt: You are preparing a scope for nocturnal mammal surveys. Which resource estimate most appropriately accounts for technical and safety considerations?

options.text: One surveyor per night for 2 nights across 8 sites to minimise field days.
Three surveyors per night for 1 night across 12 sites to complete work quickly.
Two surveyors per night for 3 nights across 4 sites, including vehicle fuel, torches, thermal camera hire and a night work safety officer.
One surveyor per night without specialist equipment to reduce budget.

questions.prompt: A client requests that you use internal staff only for a niche botanical assessment, but your team lacks taxonomic expertise. What is the appropriate escalation or action?

options.text: Accept the client's request and proceed, noting limitations in the report.
Attempt the assessment and seek post-hoc peer review if issues are identified.
Refer the client to another consultancy.
Engage or subcontract an external botanist with appropriate taxonomic accreditation and inform the client of revised costs and timelines.

questions.prompt: While planning aquatic fauna sampling, you discover local fish passage works may affect seasonal migration. How should this influence your sampling program?

options.text: Adjust sampling timing and methods to capture potential migration periods, and include targeted assessments upstream and downstream of the works.
Ignore the works since they are unrelated to your scope and proceed with standard sampling dates.
Cancel sampling until the works are finished.
Only sample downstream where species densities are expected to be higher.

questions.prompt: You must prepare a program for detecting a cryptic nocturnal frog. Limited historical records exist. What is the best data/records approach to inform survey effort?

options.text: Rely solely on the sparse historical records and use standard survey effort.
Search scientific literature, local databases, council records, and consult local experts to build a more complete picture before finalising effort.
Survey multiple sites broadly without prior information to increase chance of detection.
Only use community-sourced smartphone sightings as current records.

questions.prompt: A project's scope includes vegetation mapping that will inform impact assessment. Which quality assurance measure should you include in the program?

options.text: Have a single surveyor map all vegetation types to maintain consistency.
Outsource mapping to a junior staff member to reduce cost and then accept their outputs.
Include a field validation session where a senior ecologist reviews a subset of mapped polygons to check classification accuracy.
Rely on remote-sensing outputs without any ground-truthing.

questions.prompt: You are scoping an urban redevelopment where several stakeholders require different report formats and levels of detail. How should you handle communication and deliverables in your project plan?

options.text: Produce one comprehensive report and tell stakeholders to extract what they need.
Provide only the minimum statutory report and ignore additional stakeholder needs to save time.
Send preliminary data and ask each stakeholder to specify later what format they want.
Identify stakeholder requirements during scoping, set a deliverables schedule with tailored summaries and technical appendices, and confirm acceptance criteria with the client.

questions.prompt: During field programming, seasonal access restrictions to a neighbouring reserve mean you might lose planned sample sites. What is the best risk mitigation strategy?

options.text: Identify alternative sites with similar habitat, negotiate temporary access early, and include contingency days in the schedule.
Proceed without contingency and hope access becomes available.
Cancel all surveys that relied on those sites.
Reduce sample size and continue with the remaining sites without adjusting the analysis plan.

questions.prompt: You're programming a flora survey in a region with a short flowering window. A client requests a rapid cost reduction. What is an appropriate technical judgement?

options.text: Shorten field time and rely on non-flowering specimens for identification.
Explain that reducing field time will reduce detection reliability, propose cost-saving alternatives such as targeting core areas and prioritising high-value habitats, and outline trade-offs.
Replace specialist botanist with general ecologist to save costs.
Delay the survey indefinitely until budget increases.

questions.prompt: A field team reports that one of two acoustic detectors failed during a bat survey night. How should you document and respond in the project records?

options.text: Ignore the failure and proceed without noting it in records.
Assume neighbouring detector data compensates and do not replace the failed unit.
Record the equipment failure, log affected sample nights, reschedule recording nights to replace lost data, and update the client and data quality log.
Replace the failed unit after the entire survey is finished without rescheduling.

questions.prompt: While scoping, you identify a potential conflict with cultural heritage surveys that may restrict ground disturbance. What is the correct program adjustment?

options.text: Proceed with planned soil-based surveys irrespective of heritage concerns.
Replace soil sampling with fewer plot-based surveys without consultation.
Proceed but mark out sensitive areas on the day in the field.
Pause any ground-disturbing activities, liaise with cultural heritage specialists and authorities, and sequence ecological surveys to avoid conflict or obtain clearances before disturbance.

questions.prompt: A junior ecologist proposes a cheaper method for nocturnal marsupial trapping that reduces trap nights by half. As the mid-level consultant, what is your response regarding technical judgement and quality?

options.text: Review detection probability implications, consult species-specific guidance, and only accept reduced trap nights if statistical power and detection likelihood remain adequate; otherwise propose alternative savings.
Approve the change to save budget without further consideration.
Reject the junior’s idea outright as inexperienced.
